16ad119b8cbd.text: Department of Homeland Security employees were instructed to access state voter databases in ways a whistleblower alleges violate state law, according to a new report. Why it matters: The policy signals the Trump administration's persistence in trying to root out purported voter fraud by any means necessary. Driving the news: The whistleblower report , released by Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), details a protected whistleblower disclosure that "reveals serious allegations of illegal and inappropriate activities" within DHS' Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate. Employees have been asked to access sensitive voter information in state voter databases of people flagged by DHS as potential "unlawful voters," the report says. The whistleblower says the process can result in errors involving naturalized U.S. citizens, potentially subjecting them to secondary customs screenings at airports, or criminal referrals to Homeland Security Investigations. Zoom in: Some states, such as Virginia and Florida, require users signing onto the databases to legally confirm that they are the voter or an expressly authorized representative, meaning federal officers are effectively making false statements to access private records, the report says. Officers are also under tremendous pressure to review and verify a person's citizenship status in 12 minutes and enter it into a law enforcement record. The whistleblower says officers were told to rely on data they knew could be inaccurate, and employees' training on the new procedures amounted to a less-than-two-hour video. As a result, U.S. citizens are being investigated through the initiative "without their knowledge or ability to correct erroneous data," the report says. When officers questioned the practice, they were told individual officers would not be held personally liable for the searches, which the report says could indicate that the agency "is aware that the activity may be illegal." What they're saying: "The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump's long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it," Schumer said in an emailed statement. "This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans," he said. "Trump may try to steal this election, but we will make sure he can never be successful." DHS and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: The whistleblower report comes as the administration has been trying — and failing — to obtain sensitive voter information. The administration is seeking information such as driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers, demanding that every state hand over voter registration lists, previous election ballots and access to voting equipment. Federal courts have repeatedly rejected the DOJ's attempts to force states to turn over voter data, though litigation is ongoing in some states. 16 others voluntarily provided or agreed to provide voter files. Attorneys suing the government say the requests raise privacy and security concerns and likely violate various state and federal laws. Multiple audits have found no evidence of widespread voter fraud in America or proof that large numbers of noncitizens are voting . What we're watching: Schumer and Padilla want DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to stop the initiative and brief Congress on its activities—it's unclear whether he will agree to do so. Rules aimed at limiting pollution from coal and gas power plants are being scrapped, the head of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has announced.
The agency says that getting rid of the majority of the Biden-era rules, aimed at improving health and curbing climate change, will save $310bn (Â£223bn) and lead to a decrease in energy prices.
"The reality is that America produces energy better and cleaner than anywhere else in the world, and our power plants should not be unfairly targeted," the head of the EPA, Lee Zeldin, said.
Some have criticised the move, arguing it will affect public health and set back progress on developing renewable energy sources.
Fossil fuels, which include coal and natural gas, are by far the largest driver of global climate change, according to the United Nations.
The EPA said in a statement that it found the rules on power plant emissions that were introduced under former President Joe Biden had "exceeded the agency's authority" by "requiring control technologies that are not adequately demonstrated, effectively forcing plants to retire rather than setting standards they could actually meet".
The EPA is also seeking to get rid of all other greenhouse gas rules for the power sector.
The changes were proposed last year by Zeldin, who said they would "ensure affordable and reliable energy supplies and drive down the costs of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing while boosting our national security".
The Biden-era regulations called for a major reduction in carbon emissions from power plants, as well as vehicles and industrial facilities. It was predicted that the measures would stop 4,500 premature deaths annually.
"Any potential public health harms are too uncertain, conjectural, remote, and convoluted to tie specifically to the US power sector," the EPA said on Monday.
Nathaniel Keohane, president of the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions â an independent environmental organisation â described the move as "a giant step backward".
"In repealing carbon pollution standards for power plants, EPA has ignored sound science and economics and abdicated its responsibility to protect public health and welfare," Keohane added.
The US is currently the second-biggest emitter of planet-warming greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, behind China.
And the power sector makes up about a quarter of US emissions, at roughly 1.5 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent each year, according to the latest available estimates.
That means the US power sector emissions are higher than the total emissions of all but a handful of countries.
US power sector emissions have been generally falling over the past couple of decades, albeit with a slight uptick last year, as coal use has fallen.
But Trump has long argued for a resurgence in coal power and has regularly criticised renewables such as wind and solar.
The precise consequences of today's announcement for US emissions - and global climate change - are uncertain.
Some researchers question whether coal will ever make the resurgence that Trump hopes for. They point to the sharp falls in costs of many clean technologies such as solar power over the past decade.
Previous modelling by the independent Rhodium Group suggested rolling back US climate regulations would slow - but not reverse - emissions cuts there.
In 2022, the EPA lost some of its powers to limit greenhouse gas emissions when the Supreme Court ruled in favour of 19 states and some of the nation's largest coal companies, which were worried about the economic cost of the policy and argued the agency did not have the authority to limit emissions across whole states.
Monday's announcement is the latest move by President Donald Trump's administration to walk back policies designed to combat global warming and climate change.
In February, the EPA reversed a landmark Obama-era scientific ruling, which held that greenhouse gases were a threat to public health. This was challenged by several states and local governments.

159fb727b127.text: Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) is facing swift and intense anger from his Democratic colleagues after announcing plans to force a vote to impeach President Trump this week. Why it matters: This is a messaging headache the party did not need going into the House's last week in session before midterm Election Day, frustrated House Democrats told Axios. "It's fucked up," said a senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid criticism of a fellow Democrat. Fumed a second lawmaker: "There's a reason why Al Green isn't coming back. This is exactly what people don't want. People want us focusing on affordability and AI, not on starting this futile impeachment game." Green said in an interview: "People are dying, and they are talking about strategy." Driving the news: Green said in a letter to Trump, which he cc'd to fellow members of Congress, that he will exercise his privilege to force a House impeachment vote "during the legislative business of September 14-17." He said the vote will be based on the killings of Renée Good , Alex Pretti , Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration officers. "You are condoning, supporting, and covering up these unjustified killings. The American people deserve more from their leader," Green wrote to Trump. Between the lines: Green, who lost his primary to fellow Rep. Christian Menefee (D-Texas) in May, has positioned himself as one of the president's most obdurate critics in Congress. He was escorted out of Trump's speech to a joint session of Congress last year and his State of the Union this year, both times for heckling. He mounted rogue efforts to impeach Trump in 2017 , 2018 , and twice last year , but all of his attempts were quashed in bipartisan procedural votes . What we're hearing: A third House Democrat vented that "Rep. Green appears to only be thinking about himself. Not about strategy. Not about building a coalition." "We need serious people in our caucus focused on the mission: flipping the House to end this national nightmare," the lawmaker said. A fourth House Democrat told Axios: "Sure, he will excite the non-strategic activist crowd. But why is he empowering Trump?" "Every time you swing and miss at the guy, his approval rating goes up. Look for other ways to get attention," they added. Between the lines: Others, including party leadership, are brushing the vote off as a distraction. "Another day, another Al Green moment," a Democratic leadership source said. A fifth House Democrat told Axios: "Obviously, he is looking to keep his profile up. Don't think this fundamentally changes anything." The other side: "Where is the fight in the Democrats that are speaking anonymously? ... They don't have the courage to stand up and face me," Green told Axios. "I would challenge any one of them or all of them to debate me." he added. Green also pushed back on the argument that his impeachment vote is pointless: "Rosa Parks didn't know she was going to win. In fact, Rosa Parks knew she wouldn't win the night she took a seat on that bus." "Not one of them indicated that the president's actions are not impeachable, yet these Democrats are going to vote to stall and/or prevent the president from being impeached," the Texas Democrat said. The intrigue: Some Democrats who privately dislike Green's impeachment push likely will vote for it anyway for fear of backlash from the party base. "If he forces it, I have no choice but to vote for it," acknowledged the third House Democrat. There are also some true believers like Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.), who is also leaving Congress next year after losing his primary and told Axios: "Obviously I will be voting for [it]." What to watch: While Democrats can easily shrug off this vote as a farce, they will face a very real dilemma next year if they retake control of one or both chambers of Congress, as Axios previously reported . House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is toeing a careful line on the issue, saying in a CNN interview last month, "We haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out." His public ambivalence reflects genuine divisions among House Democrats as to whether it is worth trying to impeach Trump a third time.

754c11d6217f.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-celebrates-his-71st-birthday-but-its-vatican-employees-who-get-the-gift Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope celebrates his 71st birthday but it's Vatican employees who get the gift World Sep 14, 2026 4:30 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV celebrated his 71st birthday on Monday but it was Vatican employees who got the gift. The Vatican published a papal decree repealing 2021 salary cuts that Pope Francis had imposed on many Vatican employees as part of the Holy See's COVID-19 cost-saving measures. In the decree, Leo said the salary-containing measures "can now be overcome, in the certainty that the institutions of the Holy See and the Vatican City State will continue, through various means, their commitment to ensuring economic sustainability." The unpopular salary cuts had included a 10% cut on pay for cardinals and smaller percentage salary cuts for office heads and lower-ranking priests and nuns. Biennial pay raises were frozen for senior lay employees, though lower-ranking lay employees continued to receive raises. Francis had reasoned at the time that the cuts were necessary to save jobs, given the Holy See was also facing a structural deficit, estimated then at around 70 million euros, and a 1 billion euro ($1.14 billion) pension fund shortfall. The pandemic closed the Vatican Museums for months, depriving the Holy See of one of its main sources of revenue. The Vatican's coffers also suffered from investment and currency fluctuations. Leo, a math major and former superior general of his Augustinian religious order, is known to be adept at financial matters and reading balance sheets. His brother, John Prevost, recently told Italian broadcaster Mediaset that the pope helped him out recently with a question he had about filing his taxes. Soon after he was elected, Leo said the Vatican's financial situation wasn't nearly as bad as he thought and that Francis had made some important reforms. However, Leo has spent much of his early pontificate amending or outright reversing some of Francis' financial decisions. In another decree published Monday, Leo canceled Francis' plans to move some of the Vatican's secret archives and library holdings out of the city state and onto the grounds of a pontifical university across town. Francis had decided on the move because the material was outgrowing its current storage spaces, which include a vast underground bunker. Leo said "unprecedented opportunities have arisen to create new spaces" within Vatican City itself. He ordered the construction of a new building on a current parking lot to house the material, which includes ancient manuscripts and entire archival collections from past popes, religious congregations and benefactors. Leo visited the Vatican Apostolic Library on Monday, and noted that it was particularly fitting to be celebrating his birthday with its staff since his mother was a librarian. "I'd just like to say that God, in His providence — and sometimes with a touch of humor — always reminds us that he is with us," Leo told the staff. "Many of you may not know that my mother was a librarian, and today I'm here on my birthday specifically to say hello to all of you." The library and archive are open to scholars and researchers for study. A small exhibition space is also open on a weekly basis to the general public in the library, with reservation and pre-purchased tickets. Leo was at the library Monday to inaugurate an exhibition about water, the first installment in a new five-year cycle entitled "Catastrophe and Marvel." It features a giant design of a wave attached by scaffolding to the library's facade by the French artist JR. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. eef21b984446.text: By — Sophie Bates, Associated Press Sophie Bates, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/man-pleads-not-guilty-in-the-hanging-death-of-tasia-fortune-in-mississippi Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Man pleads not guilty in the hanging death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi Nation Sep 14, 2026 4:25 PM EDT JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — A man charged with murder in the hanging of a Black woman in Mississippi pleaded not guilty Monday at his first court appearance. The body of Tasia Fortune, 29, was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned home in the state's capital city, Jackson, on Aug. 3. On Friday, police arrested 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, who is also Black, on a murder charge after the state medical examiner deemed her death a homicide. READ MORE: What we know about the death of Tasia Fortune in Mississippi During Monday's brief hearing in Municipal Court, a judge denied bond for Ratliff, who told the court he's not guilty. Ratliff's attorney at the hearing left the courthouse without speaking to reporters. The case has attracted widespread attention because the manner of Fortune's death recalled lynchings in the Southern state, which has a tumultuous civil rights history stained by episodes of racial violence. Police and prosecutors haven't given a suspected motive or said whether they think race played any role. Police Chief RaShall Brackney said Friday that Ratliff, 51, had an "association" with Fortune, but she didn't elaborate. She also said additional arrests are expected in the case. Prosecutors on Monday offered few new details in court, though they said Fortune had been hanged with a "black cable cord" and that Ratliff had tried to hide from officers in a vehicle the day of his arrest. Brackney and other police officials who attended Ratliff's hearing Monday declined to comment afterward. A Kentucky native, Fortune had a Black father and a white mother, though she identified as Black, said Christy Spivey, the dead woman's mother. Fortune had been living in Jackson for about 10 years, according to relatives. Fortune had four children, Spivey said, adding she rarely saw two of her grandchildren. Spivey wasn't sure where Fortune was living when she died, but she said her daughter had struggled with homelessness in recent years. a3eeb711a4a2.text: By — Cinar Kiper, Associated Press Cinar Kiper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/turkish-authorities-launch-crackdown-on-lgbtq-and-hiv-support-groups Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Turkish authorities launch crackdown on LGBTQ+ and HIV support groups World Sep 14, 2026 6:05 PM EDT ISTANBUL (AP) — Turkish authorities cracked down on multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals early Sunday morning, detaining dozens of members, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts. In an escalation of its decade-long hostility toward LGBTQ+ groups, particularly in the lead-up to elections, simultaneous police raids beginning at 1 a.m. took place in the major cities of Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Aydin and Mersin. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced on social media that the investigation into 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses was to "protect children, the institution of the family, and public order" in line with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's 10-year executive order relating to families and children. "As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!" Gurlek said. The raids targeted both current and former members of multiple prominent LGBTQ+ rights and HIV awareness groups. The organizations' websites were also blocked. Gurlek also noted that such associations were found to receive significant funding from international sources and agencies. The Human Rights Association condemned the raids. "This is not a judicial investigation; it is a political operation aimed at forcing society into a monolithic family model and purging LGBTI+ and independent civil society under the guise of protecting the family and children," it said. "To include unrelated charges such as 'forming a criminal organization,' 'drugs,' 'prostitution' and 'obscenity' serves not to reveal the truth but to incriminate the entire community." The religious conservative Justice and Development Party has been increasingly vocal against LGBTQ+ groups to play up to the more conservative elements of its base. In 2015, it banned Istanbul Pride, which had tens of thousands of attendees in previous years prior. Since then, authorities have violently dispersed any attempted gatherings for Pride. This summer, an LGBTQ+ cruise ship that tours the Mediterranean and has docked in Turkey multiple times in the past was refused permission to dock there. The Ottoman Empire, predecessor to the modern republic of Turkey, decriminalized homosexuality in 1858, however there is still significant social discrimination. A free diver has said he "couldn't believe his luck" after spotting a giant jellyfish off the Welsh coastline.
Iestyn Morgan, from Pembrokeshire, said the lion's mane was the "length of a bus" with a size of about 10 to 15 metres (32ft 8in to 49ft 2in).
The 21-year-old conservationist, who records footage for social media to raise awareness about the "threats our seas are facing", said it was the first lion's mane he had seen in Wales.
More commonly found in the colder waters off Scotland, a marine biologist said although the lion's main sting was "nasty", it was not dangerous.
Morgan said he was swimming near Trefin Beach in Pembrokeshire when he spotted the tentacles in the water.
"Three turned to 10, and then to 20. They just kept on coming," he added.
The jellyfish was so big the tentacles went "beyond the range of visibility".
He initially thought it was a compass jellyfish, which are native to UK waters, before realising it was too big.
"It must have been the length of a bus or small train. I couldn't believe how big it was."
The Wildlife Trusts, external said the lion's mane jellyfish gets its name from its long tentacles, and have "all the beauty and bite of a lion".
They can grow up to 3m (9ft 8in) in length, but the tentacles - which are used to catch their prey - can exceed 30 to 36.5 metres (98ft 4in to 119ft 8in) making it one of the longest animals on Earth.
Marine biologist Dr Cathy Lucas, from the University of Southampton, said Morgan's video showed the animal's incredible length.
"The tentacles are so long and so fine you might not even see them," she said, recalling how during field work in Scotland divers would get bits of tentacles on them when there were no jellyfish around.
"They still sting after they break off," she said, adding that while the sting was "nasty" and "the worst in the UK", it was not dangerous.
"The advice is not to touch them and if you get a bit of tentacle on your skin flick it off with a stick and wash in warm water to neutralise," she said.
Lucas said lion's manes "occasionally" reach the Welsh coast later in the summer or autumn, according to jellyfish sightings recorded by the public, but their main habitat in the UK was Scotland.
Morgan feels we should be "grateful" they were in Wales, adding they were not "big scary monsters" as some people may think.
"Your biggest problem is if you swim into them. You don't want to get stung by a lion's mane."
Morgan said he was seeing "more and more" jellyfish coming into Welsh waters as he was filming.
He said it was part of a theme in which he was noticing warm water species "becoming more abundant".
"I don't have enough summers to compare it to, but I put down a camera a few weeks ago and saw a Triggerfish, which is native to the Mediterranean," he added.
Morgan said creating his content has been "very rewarding" as he wanted to make aquatic environments "more accessible" to people.
But he was always conscious that he never wanted to harm the animals as part of his project.
"I don't want to turn it into something that I'm going out to hunt the animals or anything," he said.
"I just get in the water, film and swim."

The UK could supply half of its oil and gas needs without imports if the government showed more support for the sector, an industry report claims.
Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) said changes to the windfall tax on energy firms and approval of the controversial Rosebank and Jackdaw fields could unlock 111 projects, attracting investment worth Â£50bn.
North Sea output has been falling and projections suggest that the UK's domestic supplies will meet only about a third of demand until 2050.
Environmental group Uplift branded the report a "fantasy" and said that the Prime Minister should not listen to "self-interested demands" of oil companies.
The OEUK report sets out the industry's case for supporting domestic production of oil and gas and displacing imports, which have increased.
It calls for the current Energy Profits Levy (EPL), a windfall tax on oil and gas producers which is due to be replaced in 2030, to be scrapped by next January.
The replacement Oil and Gas Revenue Levy would be triggered only when prices spike.
The sector has long said the EPL has significantly stifled investment because it remains in place even when wholesale oil and gas prices fall.
Last year, for the first time since the North Sea began producing oil and gas, not a single exploration well was drilled.
OEUK said the oil and gas industry supported 180,000 jobs in 2024 across the UK.
The report said that "fiscal reform and a pragmatic approach to licensing could unlock investment and improve long-term energy security".
It said that boosting domestic energy production was vital for "protecting households, businesses and the wider economy from global shocks".
Policy Director Enrique Cornejo added: "Britain is at a critical juncture. Our industry is ready to invest and deliver more homegrown oil and gas, but the window for action is narrowing.
"Without urgent policy decisions, the UK risks increasing its dependence on imports, losing high-value jobs."
The second demand from the industry is a signal of long term support for domestic oil and gas production.
In essence, that means supporting the controversial Rosebank and Jackdaw developments which are currently being considered for permitting by the industry regulator.
Both projects had already been given the go-ahead under the previous Conservative government but were successfully challenged in the Scottish courts on environmental grounds.
It has meant all other potential projects have essentially been put on hold under the decisions are taken.
Energy security
One of the environmental groups which brought the legal challenges, Uplift, has described OEUK's calls for support as a "fantasy" and says the North Sea is an "ultra-mature" basin with very little reserves left.
It said that instead of listening to the "self-interested demands" of the oil companies, Andy Burnham should instead be listening to people whose homes were destroyed in the summer's wildfires.
Director Tessa Khan added: "The UK has burned most of its gas and what's left is mostly oil, the vast majority of which is exported and sold on international markets. New drilling will do nothing to bring down bills and little for energy security.
"The science is clear that the world already has far more oil and gas than can ever be safely burned if we are to limit warming."
Among the projects which could be unlocked is a second phase of the Rosebank development, the Cambo field and Clair South - all of which sit west of Shetland.
The UK Labour government has banned the issuing of new exploration licenses in UK waters.
But OEUK says most of the 111 projects identified are within existing licenced areas.
A UK government spokesperson said: "We're giving the sector and its investors the long-term certainty to plan, invest and support jobs with plans to replace the EPL when it ends by 2030, or earlier if its price floor is triggered.
"We are also making sure the North Sea has a prosperous and sustainable future through record investment that helps deliver the next generation of skilled jobs while growing the clean energy industries of the future."

The Iowa Utilities Commission is moving toward hearings on the second phase of a proposed carbon dioxide pipeline, which would add hundreds of miles of lines to a project already stuck in a legal quagmire.
Summit Carbon Solutions initially intended to carry CO2 from ethanol plants across the Corn Belt to North Dakota for underground storage, but that’s been derailed by court challenges over their plan to use eminent domain to acquire land for the pipeline.
The utilities commission heard comments Monday on the proposed hearing schedule for additional sections of Summit’s planned route. The panel approves permits for hazardous liquid pipelines and evaluates whether projects can seize portions of private property along the route to install pipeline infrastructure. The commissioners cannot approve any docket unless they find that the project will “promote public necessity,” said Sarah Martz, chair of the panel.
Summit Carbon Transport, an affiliate of Summit Carbon Solutions and the company leading the second phase of the project, asked the commission to expedite the draft schedule, which currently sets the final hearing in late February, and instead reach a decision on the dockets by the end of the year. The Iowa Farm Bureau and Iowa Renewable Fuels Association, both recognized as official parties in the case, backed Summit’s request for quick decision-making.
But multiple landowners along the proposed pipeline route argued that it’s too soon for the commission to even set a hearing schedule.
“We shouldn’t even be here today. We have the proverbial cart before the horse,” said Deborah Main, whose family farm outside Sioux City falls along the route. “What exactly is the purpose of this project?”
The Summit pipeline faces significant legal challenges, including South Dakota’s recent ban on eminent domain for carbon pipelines and a North Dakota judge revoking the company’s permit to store CO2 underground in the state.
Now, Summit has said it is considering destinations in Nebraska, Wyoming, Colorado and Kansas. “We’re asking for permission to explore all options,” said Bret Dublinske, an attorney for the company, in an Iowa district court hearing last September.
According to the project website, those options will likely include using the carbon dioxide, a byproduct of ethanol production, for enhanced oil and gas drilling. Linking Iowa ethanol plants to domestic fossil fuel production would be a sharp departure from Summit’s original, climate-conscious pitch for the pipeline.
Also in September 2025, Summit petitioned the Iowa Utilities Commission for permission to amend the terms of its permit and remove language specifying a route or destination for the pipeline. The commission has yet to rule on that petition.
Meanwhile, an Iowa district court is still hearing a case brought by landowners challenging the commission’s approval of phase one of the pipeline.
At the scheduling hearing Monday, many landowners with property along the route argued that Summit should decide on the pipeline’s final destination before any additional dockets are heard.
“This is a pipeline to nowhere,” said Kerry King, who owns farmland in Dickens, Iowa. “There should be no hearings until there is a completed route. That would just make common sense to me.”
Brant Leonard, an attorney representing Summit Carbon Transport, told the commissioners that hearings for the dockets in phase two could be expedited as the company’s evidence “would be very similar, if not identical” to evidence that’s been presented to the commission in previous hearings for the pipeline.
The connection between phase two dockets and previous Summit pipeline hearings is hardly a consolation, Main said: “This docket is dependent on the original project that’s now entangled in chaos and litigation.”

Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.
The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.
"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.
"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."
Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.
The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.
The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.
"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.
Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".
"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.
Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.
Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.
"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."
Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."
"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."
Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.
He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.
Robert Gordon Mackie was born in Monterey Park, California, in 1939.
His design career started as a sketch artist for Jean Louis, a French-American costume designer. One of Mackie's early assignments saw him sketch the dress that Marilyn Monroe wore when she delivered her breathy rendition of "Happy Birthday Mr President" to John F Kennedy in 1962.
He married Hollywood singer and actress Lulu Porter in 1960, but they divorced three years later. They had a son together, Robin, who died in his early thirties from an Aids related illness.
Mackie was in a relationship with Iranian fashion designer, Ray Aghayan, from 1963 until Aghayan's death in 2011.
"I think I'm the oldest living designer in Hollywood," Mackie told The Guardian in 2018. When asked if he'd ever retire, his answer was simple - "I hope not."

Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the Senate on Monday for the first time since June 14, when he was hospitalized after a fall in his home. The Republican senator returned to the Senate on Monday to cast his first vote since being hospitalized in June. Watch the moment in the player above. McConnell's three-month absence from the Senate generated a flood of criticism and online speculation, as the Kentucky senator initially remained quiet for weeks about his condition. The 84-year-old senator eventually disclosed that he had been "briefly unconscious" due to the fall and had also been treated for mild pneumonia in the hospital. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier," McConnell said in a statement Monday. "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." The concerns over McConnell's absence highlighted increasing public concern about the age of lawmakers and their capacity to carry out their duties. Speculation about his condition grew so intense at one point that Kentucky's Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear took the extraordinary step of issuing a public letter asking McConnell to update the public in a "transparent manner." McConnell's absence was also felt over the summer as Republicans were unable to advance a farm bill out of committee. His return could give GOP leaders a needed vote as they try to advance legislation on cryptocurrency regulation and college sports. McConnell, who holds the distinction of being the longest-serving Senate leader, is in his final months of his four decades in office. He is retiring at the end of January after one of the most consequential careers in modern politics. Republicans have nominated U.S. Rep. Andy Barr to replace him, while Democrats have nominated former state lawmaker Charles Booker. McConnell said he is determined to finish out his term. A history of health problems Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., waves at reporters outside the Senate Chamber after he returned to Capitol Hill on Monday. Photo by Evan Vucci/Reuters McConnell had polio in his early childhood and has long acknowledged difficulty as an adult in walking and climbing stairs. The physician's office in Congress in the July statement said McConnell has "experienced several falls through the year" due to his "post-polio condition." The office said his physical therapy was aimed at reducing the risk of him falling again. "A comprehensive evaluation by a multidisciplinary team determined that he had no fractures, cardiac abnormalities, stroke, tumor, or hemorrhage," the physician's office said. McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1984 and was the Republican leader from 2007 until last year, serving as both majority and minority leader during that period. He has remained active as a rank-and-file senator, showing up for work when the chamber is in session, often using a wheelchair to get around. But the senator's physical condition has visibly declined in recent years. He was hospitalized with a concussion in March 2023 and missed several weeks of work after falling in a Washington hotel. He twice froze up during news conferences after he returned, staring vacantly ahead before colleagues and staff. A year later, he fell and sprained his wrist while walking out of a GOP luncheon. 9c78000664a2.text: By — Hannah Grabenstein Hannah Grabenstein Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/more-than-1-2-million-children-have-lost-snap-benefits-since-last-july-experts-explain-why Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter More than 1.2 million children have lost SNAP benefits since last July. Experts explain why Nation Sep 14, 2026 6:29 PM EDT More than 1.2 million children lost access to food aid through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program between July 2025 and 2026, according to a new analysis. While it's too early to know exactly why so many children have lost SNAP eligibility in the past year, experts say that the drop is a cause for worry. They also told PBS News that it's unlikely that the need for food assistance has dropped. WATCH: Millions lose SNAP benefits as One Big Beautiful Bill's stricter requirements kick in "For kids to lose that benefit is really devastating," said Priya Fielding-Singh, director of policy and programs at George Washington University's Global Food Institute. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research group that tracks enrollment rates, considers its estimate to be an undercount. The number actually could be more than 1.5 million children who have lost food aid, CBPP believes. Experts attribute the drop in participation to cuts made by President Donald Trump's big tax and spending bill, which became law more than a year ago and slashed at least $1 trillion in federal spending from the nation's social safety net. Among the changes, the law imposed stricter work requirements for adults on SNAP and shifted more of the program's costs to states, based on their payment error rates. Nationwide, some 5 million people overall have lost SNAP access. "SNAP is not, despite the name, supplemental," Fielding-Singh said. "SNAP is essential. SNAP is critical. SNAP is how families feed their kids enough food." A closer look at the data The decline is particularly alarming because it's been so rapid, said Joseph Llobrera, CBPP's senior research director for food assistance. SNAP enrollment traditionally rises and falls in response to the strength of the economy and the amount of need. With a strong economy, SNAP participation drops. But the current economic conditions don't indicate that people don't need assistance, Llobrera told PBS News. "The data that we're seeing now is that the declines are so significant and rapid that it's really unlikely that this is because there's a reduced need," Fielding-Singh said. There's been no dramatic change in unemployment or improvement in living wages to indicate fewer people need SNAP, she added. CBPP analyzed data from the 25 states where it is publicly available and tracked enrollment from July 2025 through each state's most recent published month. In those states, which account for roughly 60% of all SNAP participants, the analysis found: Children make up 43% of the total drop in SNAP participants Around 1.2 million fewer children have SNAP benefits Children account for between 28% and 77% of those who were disenrolled from SNAP To estimate the number of children in the remaining states, CBPP took the low end of that range and applied it to the total number of people who lost SNAP benefits over the remainder of the year. The estimate is a conservative one, Llobrera said. Some critics of the massive food safety program are touting the major drop as a win, indicating a reduced reliance on federal assistance. Others argue many of the people who've lost benefits were part of a COVID-19 pandemic-era expansion, including waived work requirements and a temporary increase in benefits. With the expiration of those changes, SNAP enrollment should be dropping, said Lauren Bauer, a fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, but "not as much as it is." Why have children lost benefits? Trump's sweeping law directly removes some children from the SNAP rolls, but other changes under the law might be having an indirect effect. Some legal immigrants, including refugees and people granted asylum, lost SNAP eligibility at the end of last year. The administration's broader immigration crackdown may have also had a "chilling effect" on eligible or current participants seeking the aid because they fear drawing attention to their immigration status, according to a July brief produced by researchers at Center for Science in the Public Interest and George Washington University's Global Food Institute. Undocumented immigrants remain ineligible for SNAP, although they can apply if their children are U.S. citizens. Please check your inbox to confirm. Experts say two major changes in the bill likely bear most of the responsibility for fewer children having food aid as a new school year starts: the implementation of expanded work requirements and heightened scrutiny over how states are managing the program. The administrative burden of both work requirements and additional state certifications could affect families' ability to stay in the program. People enrolled in SNAP between the ages of 18 and 64 who are also able to work and whose youngest child is 14 or older must now demonstrate that they're working or in a work program for 80 hours in a month within three months of receiving benefits. If the requirements are not met, people will lose their benefits for the next three years until they come into compliance. That can be a tough requirement, since many people sign up for SNAP after becoming unemployed, Bauer said. Some families may have lost benefits after adults with older children weren't able to meet the requirements or had difficulty documenting their work, she added. 6f5d7e6301e9.text: The Supreme Court struck down the U.S. Postal Service's rule restructuring mail-in voting Monday, halting a major Trump administration priority. The big picture: The 7-2 decision is a major win for voting rights advocates and the states that challenged the administration's plan; it also reverses the Supreme Court's earlier green light for President Trump's mail-in voting order. The justices' prior unsigned order allowing the rule to proceed was not a ruling on the merits — but this time around, they decided the government is "unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge." The rule would require states to submit lists of eligible voters to USPS, and the agency would then verify that those voters were receiving mail-in ballots before sending them out. The rule also had strict requirements on envelope design. Driving the news: While the court rejected the administration's stance, at least one concurring justice disagreed on the merits of the case. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with fellow Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority" but that applying the proposed rules would be "arbitrary and capricious" for the midterm elections as state and local officials "do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule." Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented in a separate opinion. In their opinion, they called the filings claiming harm by some plaintiffs "cryptic" and that the USPS has the authority to implement a rule because Congress has empowered it to do so. Zoom out: The decision is likely the final say on the rule during this election cycle, with even U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani saying from the bench earlier this month that it was unclear how the government would implement the plans with November just around the corner. Steven Monteith, executive vice president at the Postal Service, said in a declaration filed Sept. 3 that the agency continues to make "refinements" to the portal, which he predicted would be available for "voluntary use by sometime next week." He added that under Talwani's restraining order, USPS was not mandating design review for state mail but has made review available for states that want to "voluntarily submit" envelopes to ensure they comply with the rule. The case has been full of legal twists and turns, with Talwani blocking key parts of the rule last month and a second judge doing the same earlier this week . Friction point: While the administration has dismissed concerns, a USPS whistleblower recently alleged that the agency defied court orders and rushed to build out the new ballot system, putting thousands of mail ballots at risk. The whistleblower said the Postal Service built the system in weeks, not the nine months to a year typically needed for a project of this complexity, Axios' Andrew Pantazi and Donica Phifer reported. The bottom line: The rule is just one front in the myriad ways the administration has tried—at times, unsuccessfully—to reshape elections, as seen in attempts to obtain state voter rolls and redraw congressional maps . Some of those efforts have been snuffed out in the courtroom, while others could have real impacts in November. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional information throughout.

5e123564e1fc.text:
On the heels of the hottest summer on record and a United Nations report warning that global temperatures are likely to push climate risks to “increasingly dangerous heights,” the Trump administration overturned most of a Biden-era rule limiting climate pollution from power plants, the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions.
The Environmental Protection Agency announced a final plan Monday that guts the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which the agency said exceeds its authority under the Clean Air Act by requiring control technologies “that are not adequately demonstrated.” The agency also proposed revoking “all remaining GHG emissions requirements for power plants,” arguing their emissions “have no material impact on climate change.”
The plan to revoke the Carbon Pollution Standards was initially revealed last spring.
In 2007, the Supreme Court ruled that the Clean Air Act’s definition of air pollutants includes greenhouse gases, which cause climate change, and that if the EPA concludes that GHGs pose a danger to human health and the environment, it must act to reduce those emissions. The EPA made that “endangerment finding” in 2009.
“The Trump administration is now kicking the legs out from under the entire legal framework for regulating climate pollution by arguing that climate pollution does not harm human health or welfare,” said Zealan Hoover, a former senior advisor to the EPA during the Biden administration.
Hoover and other environmental and climate experts have not yet had a chance to review the specific arguments the agency is making to justify its actions.
Maggie Coulter, senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, expects the Trump administration to make a “non-endangerment finding” so they don’t have to regulate greenhouse gas emissions at all. “That goes against really well-established science,” Coulter said. “Will this stand up in court? We would argue, definitely not.”
Experts on the fossil fuel industry’s decades-long attempts to deny the reality or consequences of climate change see the same tactics in the Trump administration’s latest actions. President Donald Trump called climate change the “greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world” last year during a speech at the United Nations.
“Who needs Big Oil to deny climate science, undermine science-based decision-making and endanger peoples’ lives and livelihoods when the U.S. government will do it for them?” asked Geoffrey Supran, director of the Climate Accountability Lab at the University of Miami.
“The government can choose to deny reality,” said Ben Franta, an associate professor of climate litigation at the University of Oxford, who has highlighted the role of false solutions in delaying action on climate change. “But the real damages from global warming will continue to accumulate, from heat waves and fires to superstorms and floods, and calls for accountability will only increase.”
Since returning to office, Trump has overseen a multi-pronged attack on the legal and regulatory framework to protect public health and the environment from the climate-warming consequences of greenhouse gas emissions.

In February, the EPA overturned the endangerment finding that underpinned its authority to regulate greenhouse gases from motor vehicles, the largest source of climate pollution. The same month, the agency attacked states’ rights to pass stricter climate regulations by using a parliamentary trick to revoke decades-old Clean Air Act waivers that underpinned California’s vehicle emissions standards, though a federal judge has temporarily blocked that move. And now, in going after the Carbon Pollution Standards, the agency aims to remove limits on power plants.
Part one was repealing the endangerment finding, Hoover said. Now that that’s done, they’re working on part two, rolling back different regulations that relied on the endangerment finding, and part three, which would prevent future efforts to regulate climate pollution.
The first Trump administration repealed a bunch of public health regulations, then Trump lost his re-election bid, and the Biden administration reinstated many of them, he said. Now, they are not just repealing them “but burning them to the ground,” in an effort to make it incredibly hard for a future administration to come back in and re-regulate public health pollution, Hoover said. “It’s really quite pernicious.”
EPA spokespersons did not respond to a request for comment about what science they are using to support the claim that greenhouse gas emissions don’t contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution.
The climate and health benefits of the Carbon Pollution Standards “substantially outweigh the compliance costs,” Biden’s EPA announced in June 2024. The agency pointed to a regulatory impact analysis that projected reductions of 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon pollution through 2047, the equivalent of preventing nearly a year of emissions from the entire U.S. electric power sector or avoiding the annual emissions of 328 million gas-powered cars.
The entire regulatory framework is based on cost-benefit analyses, Hoover said. But so far, the Trump administration is “heavily discounting, if not completely refusing” to quantify public health benefits in regulations, he said.
In announcing the power plant regulations repeal, Trump’s EPA said only that by unleashing coal and natural gas, its new rule will save $310 billion and its proposal to rescind “every remaining greenhouse gas standard for the power sector” would save an additional $370 million in direct compliance costs. It also said the rules would save American families and businesses billions more.

0553244f5e7b.text: Majority Leader John Thune is asserting Congress' prerogative to act on AI — but he's urging a "light touch" even in the face of "consequential risks." Why it matters: On his first day back after a five-week break, Thune (R-S.D.) outlined his vision for congressional action on an issue President Trump has dismissed as a " hoax ." "Congress has a job to do," Thune said. "I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI," Thune told reporters when asked if he believes AI poses an existential threat to humanity. He added, "Guardrails there make sense to me" about cutting-edge, frontier AI models. But Thune also said that "there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there." Driving the news: An AI panic is rippling through Congress, but mostly on the Democratic side, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) calling to "slow down the pace of development" of AI to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome. Publicly, Trump is professing not to be concerned and insists that he should have the sole authority to regulate AI. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he posted on his Truth Social account Monday morning. Zoom out: Republicans aren't questioning Trump's ability to lead the country's approach to AI regulation, but they are suggesting that Congress has a role to play. And they aren't ruling out legislation. "So we may need to do something," Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said. "But there are existing guardrails, and corporate responsibility is a big part of this." Zoom in: Thune said he spoke with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) on Saturday night about their AI bill, which would force companies creating frontier AI models to guard against catastrophic risks and submit to federal oversight. Thune said he has been working with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to reintroduce the bill "hopefully soon." House GOP leaders, meanwhile, have given no indication they plan to keep the chamber in session after this week to work on AI-related legislation. "I don't know that staying in more weeks in September is going to be the catalyst for that," Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), the lead Republican on the FRONTIER Act , told Axios. Between the lines: Before this weekend, much of the AI debate in Washington — and in Senate races — was focused on data centers and the amount of electricity they consume. Republicans, as well as the White House, are eager to prove to voters that they won't face higher utility bills caused by data centers and their need for megawatts. Thune left open the possibility of the Senate voting on a version of the House's Ratepayer Protection Act, which is aimed at ensuring communities are not forced to pay more for increased energy use by data centers. The House is expected to vote on the bill Tuesday. What we're hearing: Thune is uniquely prepared for the AI discussion, having worked on AI legislation for years. Before he joined leadership, he chaired the Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over AI. His familiarity with the complicated and evolving subject comes in contrast to many lawmakers who have little experience with AI. Johnson even said on a podcast he has never used an AI chatbot. "Congress is not the expert on this subject because we are not in the frontier labs with them," he told reporters Monday evening. The bottom line: Thune is signaling he's open to some regulation that wouldn't stifle innovation. "I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated," he told reporters. "I do think we are in a race with China, and I think there's huge upside, obviously, with AI as well."

f194f3824ccf.text: Data: OMB ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals Senate Republicans are doubtful — and, in some cases, dismissive — of President Trump's proposal to give Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans keep control of Congress. Why it matters: Trump's proposal isn't dead on arrival. But Republicans aren't exactly lining up behind it either. "I am withholding judgment on the bill until I see their list of pay-fors," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said. "I don't support going and borrowing $1.2 trillion to be able to write the checks." "I would need to see details on it," Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) said. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he wasn't sure about the mechanics of the proposal but that he's "also worrying about $40 trillion in debt." "You know, there's no specific proposal out there," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "And obviously, however that were to come together, Congress would have a big role in determining." Zoom in: There are two massive unknowns about the " Trump Dividend " that the president promised in Dallas last week: eligibility and price tag. Vice President Vance has suggested that wealthy Americans wouldn't receive the payment. If every "every adult citizen in the United States" were eligible, as Trump suggested, it could cost some $1.3 trillion. That would be more than three times what the U.S. collects annually from tariffs and other customs duties and fees. The intrigue: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who frequently defers to Trump, said Sunday that Congress would have to approve the payments. Asked in NBC's "Meet the Press" if he'd commit that the checks will be sent, Johnson said, "I commit that Congress will work through it and find consensus on that like they have to do everything else." Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) told Axios: "Well, if it happens, I'm recommending to people that they put it away in order to pay for the additional inflation. We will see." — Axios' Kate Santaliz contributed reporting for this story.

4e8be7ac9062.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell voted at the U.S. Capitol on Monday for the first time in three months after being hospitalized in June. Why it matters: The Kentucky Republican's return could finally unjam the farm bill — and put some MAGA world rumors to rest about his ability to do the job. McConnell arrived in a wheelchair and spoke briefly to reporters, joking that after years of avoiding their questions, he "wasn't sure how many of you would be here today. But I'm glad to see you. It's time to get back to work." He did not take questions but cast a vote Monday evening in favor of Matthew Byrne's nomination to be a district judge in Ohio. ' McConnell said he was ready to work on the farm bill, as well as on supporting NATO and Ukraine. Driving the news: " Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a Monday evening statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues." He described his recovery as "a long and often frustrating process," noting "the lingering effects of childhood polio haven't made it any easier." McConnell added, "I'm still not quite back to 100%, but I've assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." What to watch: Whether the Senate Agriculture Committee will set a hearing this week to finally move the farm bill forward with McConnell's help. Catch up quick: McConnell, 84, was last seen at the Capitol on June 11. Since then, his team has provided few details about his health, fueling rampant online speculation. McConnell said in July that he fell at his home in June, briefly lost consciousness and was treated for mild pneumonia after he was hospitalized. The last official update came Aug. 6, when McConnell's office announced that he had been discharged from a rehabilitation facility and would continue recovering at home. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) and some prominent MAGA voices have pressed for more information and questioned whether McConnell remains fit to serve. Friction point: The rumor mill kicked into overdrive in July, when Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) and former McConnell aide Scott Jennings made back-to-back statements saying they had substantive conversations with the hospitalized senator. In a reported recording of an EMS call from the day of the senator's hospitalization, a dispatcher mentions cardiac arrest and a person receiving CPR at McConnell's address. McConnell has had other health scares in the past, including freezing in front of reporters and prior falls . His office has pointed to the lingering effects of his childhood bout with polio. State of play: McConnell is set to retire when his term ends in January. Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that McConnell voted Monday.

6768bd77a6d8.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took a surprise call from President Trump onstage at the All-In Summit Monday in Los Angeles, where the two dismissed fears of an AI takeover. Why it matters: Trump and Huang are staking out an increasingly clear rejection of AI doomerism right as some of the world's most powerful CEOs and AI experts call for slower AI development over safety concerns. Driving the news: Huang appeared to receive a call from Trump in the middle of an All-In Podcast interview Monday, according to video footage circulating on social media. Huang put the president on speaker so the crowd could hear the conversation. What they're saying: Trump and Huang shared an optimistic view of AI, highlighting its potential for economic growth and national security. "The robots will not be taking over," Trump told Huang. "The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax," he said, referring to the recent wave of warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Huang told Trump: "We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people." Zoom out: Huang separately addressed the AI safety fears that erupted over the weekend, striking a more nuanced tone than Trump. He said warnings from whistleblowers should be taken seriously, praising Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon for having "great courage" to raise his concerns about the company's AI development going too quickly. Yes, but: Huang rejected predictions that AI could end the world as "not grounded in science." He said AI companies should pause or pace their work "if they feel that their company is out of control." The big picture: Huang has repeatedly dismissed AI doomer fears , suggesting that some cybersecurity alarm around AI can help drum up business for the security industry. "What better way to create demand than to create a problem," Huang said at a Goldman Sachs conference in San Francisco last week, per Forbes . "Who doesn't want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?" The bottom line: Nvidia has an enormous stake in the continued success of AI as a major supplier of the chips powering advanced AI models. Go deeper: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)

7b10be6cfc51.text: Seven weeks ago, Warsh took questions from the media, and it didn't go well . Markets sold off as he seemed vague and evasive about the reasoning behind the latest interest rate decision. Wednesday, he gets a do-over. Why it matters: Investors will be thirsty for a more detailed explanation of the Fed's decision than the one Warsh offered in late July — even while respecting his intention not to give explicit guidance about future policy moves. Markets are pricing in a quarter-point increase in rates — but the why behind that likely move is more significant than the act itself, for what it says about the Fed's analytical framework under its new leadership. And if the Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee elects to leave rates unchanged, Warsh will have an even trickier communications task, lest the bond market again start to question Warsh's willingness to use interest rate policy to keep inflation in check. State of play: Assuming the Fed raises rates, does it reflect a belief that seemingly one-off changes to prices from tariffs and the energy shock are turning out to be more prolonged than previously thought? Or is AI-fueled investment creating more sustained inflationary pressure? Is it simply that the neutral interest rate is higher than it seemed? Not all interest rate adjustments are created equal. A "mid-cycle adjustment," like the three rate cuts enacted in 2019, or a "recalibration" or an "insurance move" imply different things from something like a "normalization" or a sustained policy tightening. Between the lines: Of course, each of these potential answers has implications for what the Fed will do next, in tension with Warsh's deeply held desire to avoid anything resembling "forward guidance." Moreover, different officials on the policy committee may have different rationales for a rate hike (or for not hiking), and as chairman Warsh has an obligation to accurately describe the range of views. But there's a pick-your-poison dilemma he faces. If the Fed chairman fails to lay out a coherent framework and rationale for a policy move (or no move), people naturally start to wonder if there is one. What they're saying: "We expect that he will frame the hike as a way to ensure that inflation returns to target in an acceptable timeframe," Christopher Hodge and Selin Aker at Natixis wrote in a note out this morning. "We also think that he will emphasize that this decision was discrete and does not pre-commit the Fed to any actions in subsequent meetings, giving him and the Committee maximum flexibility to respond to shocks." The bottom line: They teach us in the journalism business to ask the "who, what, when, where and why." At Wednesday's press conference, the first four will already be known. Who = Kevin Warsh and the FOMC; what = an interest rate move or no move announced half an hour earlier; when = 2:30pm ET; where = the William McChesney Martin Jr. Building. That leaves "why," which is the question that traders worldwide will be most eager to hear.

466f1d7cc4af.text:
Mass nesting brings swarms of turtles to Mexican beach
Thousands of olive ridley turtles came to La Escobilla beach in Oaxaca, Mexico, to lay their eggs within 48 hours, according to sanctuary officials.
The natural phenomenon is known as "la arribada", meaning "the arrival", and sees hundreds of thousands of the amphibians swim ashore in southern Mexico.
This is the sixth wave of the creatures in the nesting season, which started in March.

1c0ff38bbf4a.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/supreme-court-rejects-trump-mail-ballot-restrictions-ahead-of-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterms Politics Sep 14, 2026 9:02 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already underway. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they've used for years and have accounted for nearly a third of votes cast. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It represented a stark defeat for Trump on an issue he consistently has emphasized as vital to ensuring election integrity even though there is virtually no evidence of fraud with mail ballots. The Supreme Court majority did not detail its reasoning, as is typical for its emergency docket. Two justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, publicly dissented from the brief order. The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. Alito wrote in his dissent that the Postal Service "has broad authority to regulate the mail" and likely does have the power to enforce Trump's restrictions. Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed that the restrictions should not go into effect for the midterms but indicated he might rule in favor of the Trump administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time. Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active. The administration's efforts had the potential to be especially disruptive in states like Washington and Oregon that send out ballots entirely by mail. "Washington's election workers are already hard at work preparing to carry out a safe, secure, and accurate election," Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a written statement. "Now, that work continues without having to upend our election processes to meet unrealistic ballot mail requirements." In Colorado, where voters also cast ballots almost entirely by mail, Secretary of State Jena Griswold called the court's ruling "a major victory for Colorado and American democracy. Mail ballots have been protected for Colorado voters." The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn't comply. A whistleblower report, though, said the postal system's requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn't properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out. Watch the segment in the player above. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would "virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election." Lower courts agreed and blocked Trump's plan, including a preliminary injunction issued by a judge nominated by the president. But the Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that federal control of the Postal Service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible. The federal government won an early procedural decision at the Supreme Court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan. Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year. - Published
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.
Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.
On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".
"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding "Diolch yn fawr iawn" - which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.
Other winners of the coveted US TV awards included Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Stephen Colbert, while there was an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a special humanitarian award for Michael J Fox.
Proud Rhys flies the flag
Rhys was named best lead actor in a limited series for The Beast In Me, then won best lead actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay.
A small number of actors, including Alan Alda, Sally Field, John Goodman, Elisabeth Moss and Ted Danson, have been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year, but Rhys is the first to scoop a double win.
Backstage, he said: "I'm from a small country, and I'm glad we get moments to kind of put our flag on the map and say, 'we punch higher than our weight sometimes'."
The Beast In Me follows a grieving author, played by Claire Danes, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious new neighbour suspected of murder.
Rhys said it was a "real shock" to win the award, adding: "Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast, you are an intimidating scene partner, but I'm grateful for all this."
Later in the night, accepting the comedy actor prize for playing the mayor in Widow's Bay, he thanked the family, friends and colleagues who supported his career, including his parents who "kicked me on to the stage at a very early age".
A win for 'Lancashire lass'
His Widow's Bay co-star Kate O'Flynn was among the other British winners, being named best supporting comedy actress for playing Patricia in the show about a fictional island beset by a centuries-old curse.
"I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow's Bay, in front and behind the camera," said O'Flynn, from Bury in Greater Manchester.
She added: "This is the role of a lifetime... Thank you for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia."
Smart and Janney equal Emmys record
Elsewhere, Jean Smart won best comedy actress for her role in the fifth and final series Hacks.
It is the fifth Emmy she has won for the Hollywood satire. "What a ride this has been," Smart reflected, and joked the audience only gave her a standing ovation "because I'm old".
It was Smart's eighth Emmy win in total, and The Diplomat's Allison Janney also picked up the eighth Emmy of her career, this time triumphing in the category for best supporting actress in a drama series.
Smart and Janney have now equalled the record for the most acting wins ever, shared with Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus.
Despite her past success, Janney was a surprise winner on Monday and said she was "genuinely shocked" to see off competition from four stars of hospital drama The Pitt, among others.
Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn won the first Emmy of her career for best lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus, the Apple TV show about a woman who discovers almost everyone else in the world has been taken over by a mysterious mind virus.
The Pitt scoops top prize
The Pitt won best drama, traditionally seen as the most prestigious award of the night.
And the show's leading star Noah Wyle also picked up the trophy for best lead actor in a drama series for the second year in a row.
The former ER star paid tribute to all of his fellow nominees, but singled out veteran British star Sir Gary Oldman, who was nominated for Slow Horses.
Wyle said he was inspired by Sir Gary's performance as Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious in 1986 film Sid and Nancy, recalling how at the time he thought it was "the benchmark that I want to hit one day in my career".
Hero's welcome for Michael J Fox
Michael J Fox was given a standing ovation as he received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his campaigning for support for Parkinson's disease.
The Back to the Future star, 65, who founded the Michael J Fox Foundation in 2000, said: "When it starts getting tough, you show up, you help, and if you get a little joy while you're doing it, that's even better."
Appearing in a wheelchair, he told the ceremony he initially kept his condition secret after being diagnosed at the age of 29.
But he added: "Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease. So I set out to advocate for patients' needs and raise money, and to propel us towards a cure."
Dolly Parton tribute
Actress Sally Field, who starred in Steel Magnolias opposite Dolly Parton, led a tribute to the country music star, who died last month.
Field described Parton as "genuine, humble, supportive and blisteringly funny" as she introduced a special performance by country singer Reba McEntire.
"She was a humanitarian whose contribution has made a profound difference across our country," Field said of Parton, who won an Emmy in 2021.
"God bless you Dolly Parton my friend, I am not the only one on Earth who will love you for ever and ever."
Earlier in the night, Field won best actress in a limited series or movie for Remarkably Smart Creatures, a Netflix film about an octopus who observes the staff in his aquarium.
Catherine O'Hara remembered
Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a poignant tribute to their late Home Alone and Schitt's Creek co-star Catherine O'Hara. Culkin remembered her as "our mom", and "like a good mom, she always showed up when I asked her to".
Referring to the Home Alone films, he joked: "She may have forgotten me... twice! But we will always remember her."
Noah Kaha
