The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry.
Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of which 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto.
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology.
But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system.
Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.
The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets.
Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch.
Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade.
Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus.
For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14.
The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research.
Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070.
Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency".
In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating.
The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates.
Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children.
While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown.
When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998.
The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup.
Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures.
A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously.
The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty.
The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit.
The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; Â£64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure.
Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US.
Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south.
"Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning.
As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure.
Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics.
Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day.
There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.
The prime minister's office has played down the likelihood of any major announcements coming from the summit, with Carney saying over the weekend it was chance for deep-pocketed financiers to "come to 'peer into our shop window'".
The event is also an opportunity for Canada to burnish its reputation as a good place to do business after years of lagging investment performance.
Economic analysts say Canada needs to make significant policy changes to help attract investment, including more competitive tax and regulatory systems, and ensuring a supply of skilled labour.
For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs.
On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week.
On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly.
"To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said.
"After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties."
Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum.
"Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday.
"Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state."

At Semaforâs Future of Health Forum, Cassidy â a former physician and chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee â expressed outrage at the spike in measles cases and instances of âkids dying from measles,â tying it to the administrationâs policies and messaging on vaccination.
Cassidy also acknowledged in the interview with Semaforâs Burgess Everett that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., broke commitments on vaccines he made to the Louisiana Republican during his confirmation process, and that it left him angry.
âWhen youâre given guarantees by people and by the administration and they break those guarantees, I donât know if painful is the word, maybe urinated off is the word, but the point being that you certainly have a certain emotion,â Cassidy said.
Cassidy, who is retiring at the end of the year after losing his primary to a Republican challenger backed by President Donald Trump, also said that Republicans could pay a political price if Americans see a resurgence of diseases that had largely been brought under control.
âIf the American people are seeing that concerted efforts to undermine faith in immunization is leading to children dying from diseases that they havenât died from in decades,â Cassidy said. âThe American people are going to reasonably say, wait a second, this is not making America healthy again. This is making America die from diseases that we never died from before, at least not in decades. And I think that there will be a check at that point upon nonsense coming out of Washington from which people die.â
He pointed to elections as a âportion of an accountability measure.â
âIf an administration says one thing and you end up with another, and that other does not serve the American people well, and you have an election, the American people are going to weigh in,â Cassidy continued. âIf it turns out that it is a big deal, then youâre going to see the party which has poorly served the American people do poorly in the polls.â

He said âI think there will be a hearingâ on her nomination, but asked whether he would support her or not at this point, he declined to comment.

The Scoop
The US Commerce Department last month ordered Kalshi to take down one of its products tracking the price of AI compute, the crucial power from data centers thatâs driving the artificial intelligence boom.
Commerce officials cited national security concerns when they told Kalshi to unpublish its AI-compute future curve, said people familiar with the matter. The product pulls together data from several markets that allow users to bet on the cost to rent Nvidia chips to create an overall picture of where AI compute costs are heading. Kalshi quietly complied, though many underlying markets remain open for trading.
Separately, Commerce also pushed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees prediction and futures markets, to effectively freeze approval of new compute contracts for 60 days, some of the people said. It was a rare intervention that surprised an industry used to White House enthusiasm for both AI and financial-market innovation.
Representatives for Commerce and Kalshi declined to comment. The CFTC didnât respond to a request for comment.
Itâs unclear why Commerce is worried about the nascent market, which aims to do for AI computing what oil futures do for crude â let buyers and sellers of compute lock in prices, and give traders a way to bet on where those prices go. One potential reason floated to Semafor by market participants is that compute futures could be manipulated to show a sharp drop in the cost of older chips, which might destabilize AI stocks and debt markets. Some of these markets are thinly traded, which could lead to volatility even without bad actors.
Step Back
The cost of compute has become one of the most important numbers in the US economy. On one side of the debate are fears that older chips, which serve as collateral for billions of dollars of borrowing by neoclouds like CoreWeave and underpin data-center deals, will become obsolete and decline in value. On the other are concerns from big companies adopting AI that shortages of power and infrastructure will send prices of tokens soaring.
That uncertainty has given rise to a futures market that was starting to take off this summer. The CFTCâs 60-day pause could delay plans by exchange operators like CME and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, along with upstarts like Architect Financial Technologies, to list two-sided betting parlors.
Notable
- CoreWeaveâs most recent earnings suggest strong demand for older-generation chips, easing obsolescence fears.
- âCompute is going to be the next big commodity in the world,â the CEO of the startup whose data underpins Kalshiâs compute markets, told Semafor this spring.

2dc6a58dcb23.text:
The Scoop
Walmart wants to coach Americans on using GLP-1s.
The third-largest pharmacy operator in the US is adding new âhealth ambassadorâ positions as part of a pilot program launching in rural locations this week. In addition to consulting on GLP-1s, trained pharmacists will advise shoppers on things like sleep, exercise, and stress management.
As more Americans use GLP-1s â 11% say theyâre on or have used the drugs â the pharmacistsâ initial focus will be on weight management, diabetes, and maternal help, which affect millions of American families. âOur pharmacists are already getting lots of questions about health navigation,â Dr. Emily Aaronson, Walmartâs chief medical officer, said at Semaforâs Future of Health Forum on Tuesday. âBut they also have a lot of other clinical responsibilities, and so this is really about making [health coaching] the primary focus.â
The program signals both a fresh push into rural healthcare and a direct response to the GLP-1 craze, which is rapidly rewiring consumer behavior and transforming how companies relate to customers now filling their carts with entirely different foods, drinks, and personal-care products.
Know More
Walmart has been trying for more than two decades to connect with its customers more intimately about their health and wellness, a category thatâs now growing faster than its grocery business.
In 2007, Walmartâs then-CEO Lee Scott pledged to open 2,000 clinics to tackle a growing primary-care doctor shortage. But after years of struggling to find a viable business model, the company shuttered its clinics and telehealth operations in 2024 to rethink its healthcare strategy.
One area it homed in on was its nearly 5,000 pharmacies. With health and wellness now making up roughly 16% of Walmartâs US sales, pharmacies had become a huge traffic driver. Around the world, Walmart saw pharmacies in places like Europe and Canada that were prescribing drugs and treating minor ailments and began thinking that tapping its pharmacists could provide a better way to address the dearth of primary-care doctors in the US.
âThere was a time when we looked at primary care and recognized itâs really broken, and our communities donât have access to primary care,â Aaronson said. But running clinics didnât lead to a sustainable business, âso what we did instead was we took a moment and said, âWeâre going to continue to deliver all this care through the pharmacy where we can do a lot to help customers and communities.ââ
Walmart is also increasing its push into clinical trials, providing space in its Walmart stores to partners running drug trials for pharma companies, many of which are looking for more diverse populations to test their drugs. âWe recognize that in most of the communities that weâre in, our customers and patients donât have access to real healthcare through research,â Aaronson said.
Shellyâs view
Walmart has been ahead of the GLP-1 wave for years â for good reason. The drugs present an existential threat to the USâ largest grocery seller.
Back in 2023, I spent the day with now-CEO John Furner and spoke to him about how he was thinking about the future of the company. As we chatted in the produce aisles of a Walmart Supercenter in Dallas, he admitted something that would send shares in the retailer, and the entire food and consumer goods sector, tumbling down. Walmart could see that the customers who were picking up GLP-1 prescriptions from its pharmacies pulled back on food spending, he told me, sparking a selloff in a market just waking up to what has become a major reckoning in consumer behavior.
Fast forward to today and the share of Americans taking GLP-1s jumped to 11% in June 2026, up from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup. Walmart became Lilly Directâs first in-store pickup pharmacy last year, working with Eli Lilly to offer GLP-1 discounts to Walmart customers. And in August the retailer said the drugs made a material impact on its health and wellness sales, which are now growing faster than its grocery sales.
The company is smart to lean into where its customers are going, rather than run away from it or, like some of its competitors, try to pretend it isnât happening. And given Walmartâs massive footprint in many of the rural towns with the highest propensity for diabetes and obesity, it has a rare opportunity for a company of its size to do some good and make money at the same time.

Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre.
Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement.
The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (Â£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators.
Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm.
A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance.
"I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying.
Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office for comment.

If you’re down under and you give the right tree a rustle, you might encounter a record-breaking, globally recognized music icon. Or at least a bug named after her.
Meet Swiftiephylus, a newly described group of Australian insects. The big-eyed bugs — each smaller than a lentil — honor Taylor Swift in recognition of her “show-stopping talent, heart-wrenching lyrics, and the joy and comfort she has brought to many,” researchers report September 9 in Insect Systematics & Evolution.
There are some 10,000 species of herbivorous plant bugs found all over the world, but little was known about their diversity in Australia. In the early 2000s, a group of researchers including entomologist Christiane Weirauch at the University of California, Riverside, began to collect and describe these bugs. In 2022, when entomologist Sarah Schroeder began her PhD work with Weirauch, some of these mystery bugs became a part of her project.
“I was really excited,” Schroeder says. “It’s a dream thing for a scientist to get to describe new species.”
Schroeder and Weirauch studied the flower-eating plant bugs found in she-oak trees in Australia. By comparing their physical shapes, colors and genes to known species, the researchers found 12 new species. These were organized into five genera. One of these groups — Swiftiephylus — sports a name with special meaning to Schroeder.
“I’ve been a lifelong Swiftie,” Schroeder says. “Taylor’s music has underscored so many of the major milestones of my life, so it felt authentic to me to honor her by naming these species after her and giving her a gift back for all of her music.”
Schoeder picked the four species to bear Swift’s name because of their uniquely yellow colors punctuated with red accents.
“Taylor’s pretty well known for having her red lip,” Schroeder says. “And the fans affectionately call her Blondie.”
Beyond the more obviously named S. taylorae, Schroeder gave the other three species Latin translations of some of Swift’s album names. S. amator is for Lover, S. intrepidus is for Fearless and S. poetorum references The Tortured Poet’s Department.
For Schroeder, this song isn’t finished. Swiftiephylus barely scratches the surface of what’s left to find among insect life. She notes that species description is crucial for conservation, since you can’t protect what you don’t know is there. With potentially millions of undescribed insect species still out there, it’s a conservation vulnerability researchers know “All Too Well”.

The News
Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All as the banner issue Democrats should run on in 2028 on Tuesday, instead arguing that the party should campaign on the broader promise of âguaranteed coverageâ and universal care.
At Semaforâs Future of Health Forum, Kim told Semaforâs Burgess Everett that Medicare for All was a âstand-inâ for the broader goal that Democrats should be working toward.
He pointed to his MediKids proposal â legislation that would guarantee universal healthcare coverage for every American under the age of 26 â as an example of how the party could pursue universal coverage through a more targeted approach to build towards guaranteed care.
âI think itâs a stand-in for where weâre trying to head towards,â Kim said.
âI think we should be running on that guaranteed coverage, on that universal care,â he added. âI do think that that vision of guaranteed care for everybody is something that is absolutely essential and what a lot of people in this country want.â
Kim, who is a member of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, also said he was not convinced Republicans would work with Democrats next year to roll back or delay the scheduled Medicaid cuts.
Asked whether Republicans might be willing to at least delay some of the changes to Medicaid, Kim said, âI donât know. Iâm not really sure.â He pointed to Republicansâ decision to allow cuts to Affordable Care Act subsidies to take effect rather than delay them.
Know More
Kim also discussed his recent trip to Texas to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, describing significant energy and enthusiasm on the ground in the race against Republican nominee Ken Paxton.
Texas has historically been a reliably Republican state, but Paxtonâs controversial candidacy has some Democrats â including Kim â increasingly bullish on the race.
Kim described talking to a longtime Republican voter who told him that Paxton was âunelectable,â citing concerns about corruption. Kim said the experience reinforced his view that opposition to corruption and interest in a younger generation of leadership could be meaningful factors in the race.
âYou have that added baggage of Ken Paxton being literally the worst possible candidate that the Republicans could have chosen for that seat. And then the other thing is thereâs a lot of excitement for a new generation of leadership. And I could feel that when I was there too. A lot of people are excited about Talarico, a younger, new leader in that kind of space,â Kim said.

The Last Free Women: A Daring Escape From Afghanistan and Coming of Age in America by Rebecca Blumenstein and Diana Kapp.
In 2021, when Kabul fell to the Taliban, a team from the The New York Times â led by Rebecca Blumenstein â scrambled to evacuate many of the Timesâ Afghan employees and their families, ultimately relocating more than 200 people from Afghanistan to the US.
This book follows the stories of four young women from the cohort of evacuees as they acclimated to a new country, language, and culture while grappling with the loss of the world they once knew. It is a âgripping account of how refugees found peace in a new land,â Kirkus Reviews wrote. Buy The Last Free Women from your local bookstore.

All flights have been suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports because of volcanic ash released from nearby Mount Etna.
It is the second time in recent months that Catania International Airport, on the island of Sicily, has stopped flights due to emissions from Etna, which is Europe's tallest active volcano and erupts frequently.
Airport officials said arrivals and departures, which were first halted on Monday, would be suspended until 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
Ongoing activity at Etna prompted the INGV Etneo Observatory to issue a red aviation alert on Monday.
In a statement on its website on Tuesday, Catania - Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic - said further updates would follow.
It also advised passengers due to fly from Catania to check with their airline for updates before travelling to the airport.
Catania, which usually serves about 12 million passengers each year, was closed for almost a week during the peak summer season last month because of volcanic activity.
There have been calls for the airport to shut and other facilities in Sicily to be expanded because of its proximity to Etna.
The volcano, which stands at 3,324 metres (10,906ft), is about 40km (25 miles) away from the airport.
Despite air traffic disruption, August's eruption drew large crowds of onlookers to Etna's lava flows. About 1.5 million people visit Etna every year.

e16785f8dba0.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-senate-expected-to-vote-on-cryptocurrency-regulation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Senate expected to vote on cryptocurrency regulation Politics Sep 15, 2026 10:22 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is set to vote Tuesday on whether to move forward with legislation to create a new regulatory framework for cryptocurrency, a pivotal election-year test for the $2.3 trillion market as many Democrats say it doesn't go far enough to rein in President Donald Trump's investments. Watch the Senate floor live in the video player above. The vote, just two months before the midterm elections, comes as the crypto industry has become a major political force and as Trump has amassed significant crypto wealth while in office. While some Democrats support the idea of a regulatory framework, a top priority for the industry, the party has been mostly united in opposition to the legislation unless it includes strong ethics safeguards to prevent the president and his family from enriching themselves while in office. READ MORE: Republicans say Trump agreed to new ethics rules to get crypto bill across the line "Let's make sure that we do not pass a crypto bill that will let Donald Trump continue to rake in billions of dollars in crypto profits while working families across this country struggle to deal with higher prices and an economy that gets worse by the day," said Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, in a Senate floor speech on Monday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. As Democrats have vowed to block the bill, Trump has agreed to some concessions on ethics, including new restrictions on federal elected officials from issuing digital assets like the presidential meme coins he and his wife Melania launched before he took office for his second term. On Sunday, Trump agreed to additional concessions, such as additional powers for state attorneys general that Democrats had sought to enforce the crypto measure. But those concessions do not appear to be enough for most Democrats. A proposal by Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina had sought to require Trump to put his crypto holdings in a blind trust and divest when those holdings reach a certain value. The latest version of the bill "leaves a lot to be desired," Gallego said Monday evening. "If they think this is a final deal, this is not their call." Gallego said he would offer a counterproposal, but it was unclear if the two sides would be able to agree before the vote Tuesday afternoon. Republicans need Democratic support to win the 60 votes necessary to move forward on the bill in the 53-47 Senate. Trump has amassed big crypto profits Trump's family has raked in big profits in the crypto sector since he was reelected, including the meme coin, announced the day before Trump took office. Top investors were invited to a private reception with the president. Trump's family also has a controlling stake in World Liberty Financial, a crypto firm co-founded with the president's special envoy Steve Witkoff. Trump reported more than $500 million in revenue from World Liberty Financial sales of crypto products, including "governance tokens," in his annual disclosure report filed with the Office of Government Ethics. That is a significant share of the more than $1.4 billion that the president reported from crypto businesses last year. READ MORE: Trump took in about $1.2 billion from crypto businesses last year, financial disclosure shows A measure enacted into law last year regulating stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency, barred members of Congress and their families from profiting off them, but it did not extend to Trump or his family. Legislation aims to give crypto firms legal certainty Republicans who have been working on the legislation for a year say it could stall indefinitely if the Senate doesn't vote to move forward on Tuesday. The House and Senate will be out of session during October and before the elections, and the dynamics could significantly shift if Democrats win back the majorities of the House or Senate, or both, in November. Republican Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, a lead sponsor of the bill, said that a no vote means "opposing real ethics reforms on politicians' personal investments, handing American leadership in digital assets to our foreign competitors, and leaving Americans with zero protections in the digital asset markets." Supporters say the legislation aims to give the industry more legal certainty and protect consumers by creating a broad set of guardrails and regulatory requirements, including better enforcement to prevent bad actors and protections to prevent a market collapse. Opponents, mostly Democrats, say it is a giveaway to the industry, which strongly backs the bill and has become a major donor to candidates in both parties around the country. In 2024, the crypto industry spent more than $130 million in congressional races, including $40 million in Ohio and $10 million each in Arizona and Michigan. "DC received a clear message that being anti-crypto is a good way to end your career, as it doesn't represent the will of the voters," Brian Armstrong, the CEO of Coinbase, the nation's largest crypto exchange, wrote in a social media post the day after the 2024 election. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim and Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.
The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.
It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.
The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (Â£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday.
Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand.
"Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis.
Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed".
The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended.
There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen.
At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based.
The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects".
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict.
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler and Benedict Garman
Graphics by Tom Shiel

3edb7a6d4798.text: A federal judge ruled Tuesday that the Kennedy Center's latest attempt to put President Trump's name on the performing arts center violated his earlier order blocking its renaming . The big picture: The order came just before the Kennedy Center's board, now composed of Trump loyalists, is set to weigh shutting down the building for renovations that members argue must include Trump being "appropriately recognized" on the structure. What he's saying: While Trump allies have argued the latest attempt to recognize Trump does not violate the law, U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper said "[l]inguistic gymnastics cannot extricate the Kennedy Center's Board from an operative judicial order or the governing statute it was designed to enforce." Cooper ordered for Trump's name to be removed from the building in May, saying only Congress could change the name of the center that memorializes President John F. Kennedy. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Prosecutors will not seek the death penalty against Nick Reiner, who is accused of murdering his parents, Hollywood director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Reiner.
Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said prosecutors made the decision after "a rigorous review" and wishes of the Reiners' loved ones.
"We did speak with Nick Reiner's siblings (and) they made their views very clear," Hochman told reporters ahead of a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.
Prosecutors said this meant the maximum punishment Nick Reiner will face is life in prison without the possibility of parole, if convicted.
Hochman also said on Tuesday that the trial would not begin until next year.
Rob and Michele Reiner were found stabbed to death in their Los Angeles home last year. Their bodies were reportedly discovered by their daughter Romy on 14 December.
The couple died from "multiple sharp force injuries", the LA County medical examiner said at the time.
Prosecutors allege that Nick Reiner, the couples' youngest son, fatally stabbed his father and mother inside a bedroom of their home before fleeing. He was arrested in Los Angeles the same day.
The 33-year-old faces two counts of first-degree murder, with a special circumstance alleging multiple murders. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Rob Reiner, 78, directed films including This Is Spinal Tap, the Princess Bride, When Harry Met Sally and Stand By Me.
Michele Singer Reiner, 70, was an actress, photographer and producer, and the founder of Reiner Light, a photography agency and production company.
Reiner is scheduled to appear in court on Tuesday for a hearing about unsealing transcripts from the grand jury that returned the indictment against him.
Reiner's siblings, Jake and Romy, have asked for the transcripts to remain sealed because "the disclosure to the public and media of the details and evidence of the killing of their parents will cause them additional trauma and harm", Hochman said.

Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.
The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.
His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.
In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."
The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.
"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.
"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."
He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.
"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.
"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."
Hind's Hall performance
The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.
Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.
The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.
The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.
"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.
The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
'Most successful tour'
After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.
In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.
Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".
"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.
Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.
"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.
He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

ed76f3f06a74.text:
The News
AI agents can easily team up to get around safety restrictions and escape the limits placed on them, a new study shows.
Enterprise AI lab Emergence AI ran eight simulations testing the capabilities of global frontier models â including Claude and OpenAI, and Chinese models Qwen and DeepSeek â in handling cybersecurity threats.
Seven of the eight simulations ran 10 agents from the same model; the eighth mixed models together. In each, researchers presented three cybersecurity threats: a phishing campaign, a misinformation attack, and a memory breach.
None of the eight simulations were impervious to the threats, and even when agents detected a risk, the detection didnât translate into the agents trying to contain the threat. Instead, in many scenarios, the agents actively engaged with the adversarial content.
A Mistral agent, for example, wrote into its own memory the information it flagged as dangerous from the phishing attack. In another simulation, a Gemini agent, while initially flagging the phishing lure, acted on it about 46 hours later.
In the Claude simulation, the agents went so far as to break out of the test to execute a task they decided to pursue on their own. After one agent flagged that their simulated economy wasnât legit without the presence of humans, calling it âa cathedral of bookkeeping with no congregation,â the 10 agents unanimously decided to attempt to reach the outside world, defeating four separate security checks meant to confine the simulation.
The agents wrote Python code to post on multiple credential-free message boards, inviting real humans to join their economy; their outreach garnered four human responses. But after realizing humans couldnât join their economy and judging their conversations as performative, the agents voted to take a vow of silence, eschewing instructions to get back to work.
The findings show that autonomous agents, even when handed benign instructions, can bypass their initial confines when executing on a goal.
âNo amount of guardrails written in language or in code written probabilistically,â Emergence CEO Satya Nitta told Semafor, âis likely to result in truly, fully guaranteed safe behavior over any length of time.â Itâs not an issue of sophisticated technology, according to Nitta, but rather a programmatic flaw among multi-agent scenarios.
Know More
Nitta drew parallels between the Claude incident and OpenAIâs agentic experiment earlier this year, where autonomous agents hacked AI firm Hugging Face, saying that in both scenarios, the pattern of failure is the same.
âIf you have multi-agent systems, they behave in truly unpredictable emergent ways,â he said. Nitta said the Emergence experiment is the first to shed light on how AI agents collude to bypass guardrails and break confinement, as OpenAI has yet to release all of its findings from the Hugging Face incident.
The experiment comes at a consequential moment in AI development. Anxieties over the technologyâs capabilities have hit a fever pitch. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon left his job at Anthropic fearing that the AI he was building could lead to human extinction, sparking calls for regulation, and a slowdown of frontier model development, from AI leaders and opponents alike.
Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote a blog post arguing to slow down the pace of AI development, which other tech leaders, including OpenAIâs Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and former Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis said they agreed with.

d8069db5ce2f.text:
A slowdown on the AI frontier would barely register for big companies working to adopt AI, for the simple reason that they are nowhere near the frontier.
âEven if the technology stops advancing â turn âpacing the frontierâ into âhalt the frontierâ â we have a decade-plus of diffusion of benefits into the economy with the technology as it exists today,â said Chris Taylor, CEO of Ode, the $1.5 billion joint venture between Anthropic, Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and other investment firms that is focused on implementing AI inside big companies.
Corporate use of cutting-edge models has fallen in recent weeks, according to data from Ramp, as companies realize most of their challenges â onboarding customers, iterating prototype tweaks â can be accomplished with older AI models that cost less (and donât carry civilization-ending risks). Even Microsoft last month switched many employees to less-powerful models.
âAs the capabilities improve, it does unlock more, but the amount of possibility that already exists with yesterdayâs models is staggering,â Taylor told Semafor. âI donât see anything slowing down AI adoption for them.â

The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages.
Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news".
But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls".
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy.
The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified.
Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages.
Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks.
A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.
The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain.
It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply.
The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency".
Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous".
In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true".
And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen".
The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (Â£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun.
Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances".
When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks.
More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US.
Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans.
One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out.

The News
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., called on Congress to act on two issues before his term ends: the looming financial problems facing Social Security and the ballooning cost of healthcare.
At Semaforâs Future of Health Forum on Tuesday, Cassidy, who is leaving the Senate at the end of the year, told Semaforâs Burgess Everett that a bipartisan effort is underway to address Social Security, but acknowledged that the window for Congress to act is narrowing.
He pointed to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, released in June, which found that the programâs retirement trust fund would become insolvent in 2032 â triggering automatic benefit cuts of more than 20% unless Congress acts. Cassidy said that warning, combined with rising bond yields, has attracted renewed attention in Washington to a problem he has been trying to fix for six years.
âThe fact that Iâve been working on it for six years and Iâve got three months left and weâre having this conversation shows you how difficult it is,â Cassidy said. âOn the other hand, the actuary report that came out a month or so ago, I think, helped sharpen peopleâs minds that we really have a problem.â
Cassidy said the effort has bipartisan roots, pointing to a previous agreement involving seven Republicans and seven Democrats that he said was brought to President Joe Biden. He also referenced his current efforts with Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill, to pass The PROMISE Act.
âObviously, the window is closing. But the longer you wait to fix Social [Security], the worse it gets. And it doesnât just get worse marginally,â Cassidy said. âIâm hoping against hope that we can do it. And if not, Iâm looking for someone to pass it off to, and they will continue it next time.â
Earlier this year, Cassidy lost his primary to a Republican challenger backed by President Donald Trump.
Know More
As chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, Cassidy also pointed to health care affordability as another area where he hopes Congress can make progress before he leaves office.
He highlighted the bipartisan Patient Deserve Price Tags Act, which he said would give patients more information about the cost of medical services before receiving care.
âIf you think about it, healthcare is one of the few things in which you donât know how much itâs going to cost when you walk in the door. And thereâs a deliberate effort to obfuscate for the consumer how much something costs,â Cassidy said. âI think itâs a pretty good stab at trying to make healthcare more affordable.â

Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Why it matters: The impeachment effort is a long shot in the GOP-controlled Congress, but Massie's resolution is privileged, meaning he can force a full House vote and put Republicans on the record over Hegseth's handling of the Iran war. It's a dramatic escalation in the retiring lawmaker's months-long push to rein in the Trump administration's war powers. The effort also comes after the House has repeatedly voted on efforts to constrain the administration's military campaign in Iran, including passing war powers resolutions in June and July directing the president to end U.S. hostilities with Tehran. The House is slated to vote Tuesday on another war powers resolution on the Iran war effort. Driving the news: Massie's resolution accuses Hegseth of carrying out orders to continue operations in Iran despite Congress' constitutional authority over war and its votes seeking to end the conflict. Massie argued Hegseth's actions "frustrated Congress's ability to exercise its most solemn constitutional responsibility" and allowed an "unlawful war" to continue. "In all of this, Secretary Hegseth has acted in a manner contrary to his trust as Secretary of Defense," Massie said on the House floor. The eight-article resolution also targets Hegseth over U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, including accusing him of illegally directing the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization. Zoom out: Hegseth already faced a separate impeachment push from House Democrats, who introduced six articles against him in April that included allegations he waged an unauthorized war against Iran. What's next: The House will have to take up the legislation within the next two legislative days, but GOP leaders could also move to vote on tabling the resolution instead.

425c94950f47.text: By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-attacks-supreme-court-justices-he-picked-for-rejecting-his-push-to-restrict-mail-ballots Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump attacks Supreme Court justices he picked for rejecting his push to restrict mail ballots Politics Sep 15, 2026 1:06 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Tuesday went after the Supreme Court after it rejected his push to restrict mail-in voting in this year's midterms, saying justices who opposed him were "not the people I interviewed." READ MORE: Supreme Court lifts a cloud over midterms by letting mail ballots flow as normal to voters His social media missive was just the latest in a long history of Trump assailing justices, particularly those he had nominated, who ruled against him on his administration's most prominent initiatives. The president has been publicly furious with the Supreme Court over its decisions against restricting birthright citizenship and his ability to issue tariffs unilaterally. On mail-in voting, the Trump administration had made a last-minute push to have the U.S. Postal Service play a central role in deciding who would be able to receive a ballot. But state election officials argued there was not enough time to make the changes for the Nov. 3 midterm elections — and said their systems were already secure and accurate. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The court ruled late Monday in an emergency order that the restrictions would most likely lose in court, at least for this year's election. "The Court's inability and unwillingness to do the right thing for our Country will go down, in a very negative way, in the annals of History," Trump wrote in a lengthy social media post Tuesday. "This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left into making decisions that have set America back at least a hundred years." Justices Sam Alito and Clarence Thomas publicly dissented from the order, and Trump on Tuesday called them "legends both." Trump has nominated three of the justices on the Supreme Court — Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," Trump said. He asserted that the court "is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won't be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal." The president has a lengthy track record of attacking judges, often very personally, who issue decisions that go against his wishes, and Trump has long viewed his legal appointments as owing loyalty to the person who nominated them to the bench. So as Barrett, Kavanaugh and Gorsuch ruled against Trump at varying points over the years, the president has not hesitated to go after them publicly, while praising them if they sided with him in a case. Yet this court, led by Chief Justice John Roberts, has ruled in favor of Trump on several of his priorities, most notably the 2024 decision from the court's conservative majority that said former presidents are presumptively entitled to immunity for all official acts. That paved the way for Trump to run for reelection without threat of a criminal trial that year. Trump has opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss. A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast. Roughly a third of voters use mail ballots, and mail voting has already begun in some states. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they've used for years. On Tuesday, Trump also complained that the decision took too long to issue. "It is not easy for me to write this criticism of the United States Supreme Court - it will likely cost me dearly for years to come - but I feel it my obligation and duty, as President, to do so for the America we love!" Trump said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press

Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/supreme-courts-lifts-a-cloud-over-midterms-by-letting-mail-ballots-flow-as-normal-to-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court lifts a cloud over midterms by letting mail ballots flow as normal to voters Politics Sep 15, 2026 12:41 PM EDT Even with voting already underway, uncertainty about what might come next had been hovering over preparations for this year's midterm elections. The U.S. Supreme Court lifted much of that uncertainty late Monday when it rejected President Donald Trump's push to have the U.S. Postal Service play a central role in deciding who would be able to receive a mail ballot. READ MORE: Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterms The decision is a win for the status quo. The thousands of election offices around the country can send out mail ballots as they had intended without worrying about complying with new Postal Service rules imposed at the 11th hour. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Now, we can finally move forward and get back to what we do best: conducting our elections without a dark cloud hanging over us — fairly, openly, for the people, by the people," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat who oversees voting in a state where all voters receive a mail ballot, said in a statement after the decision. Executive order and ongoing litigation had created confusion The case before the court stemmed from an executive order Trump signed in March. The administration developed a plan that would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style for mailed ballots and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal it was developing. The Postal Service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn't comply. A whistleblower report said the postal system's requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, disenfranchising many of the country's voters during an election that will decide control of Congress during the final two years of Trump's term. READ MORE: Whistleblower: Postal Service's work to comply with Trump order is rushed and sloppy A tangle of legal challenges, rapid-fire rulings and appeals left election officials uncertain about what rules would ultimately be in place. But they agreed on one thing: Introducing such massive changes so close to a general election would be chaotic and nearly impossible to pull off in a country where roughly a third of voters use mail ballots. The Supreme Court's decision comes as mail voting is already in progress in some states. Some election officials have said they were worried that the dispute, coming late in the election cycle, would leave voters confused about what's allowed. Voting rights advocates and state election officials moved swiftly after Monday's decision to make clear that elections will function as they always have in each state. "Utahns can have confidence that the 2026 election will proceed as normal," said Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, a Republican serving as the state's chief election officer. The uncertainty was most pressing in the states that rely on mail voting The concern was particularly acute in the eight states where voters cast ballots almost entirely by mail: California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont and Washington. They had faced the daunting challenge of adapting in short order without an extensive network of polling places. "This is a victory for Oregonians, the right to vote, and the rule of law," said Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read, a Democrat. "This provides voters and elections officials with the certainty they need ahead of a major, federal election, and it sends a clear message to this country: Presidents don't run elections, the people do." READ MORE: Ballots discounted for late postmarks surged in Washington and Oregon after Postal Service changes Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar said his reaction to the Supreme Court's decision is "one of relief, but also excitement, because today the voters really won across America." In Nevada's June primary, more than half of voters cast ballots by mail. It's a state where mail voting is "critical" to voter voices being heard, Aguilar said. But the Democrat said "some of the damage has already been done," with false claims about mail ballots affecting people's confidence in the voting method. "You can trust the process," Aguilar urged voters. "Please participate." What about future elections? Lower courts had blocked the Trump administration from implementing its rules. The Supreme Court rejected the its attempt to stay those decisions, even as three justices — Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh and Clarence Thomas — expressed various levels of willingness to let Trump carry out his plan in current or future elections. Yet a majority of the justices noted in the decision that the administration was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" in defending its plan. It was heartening to some voting rights experts to see that language inserted. "The court didn't have to explain that it was disinclined to side with the government on the merits, but it did that, and that is a sign for the future," said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. David Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department lawyer who is now executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said implementing Trump's executive order "would have done nothing for election integrity but would have imposed a vast and expensive new bureaucracy on the states" and disenfranchised voters. He said the majority's language about the merits of the case meant "it is unlikely these rules will ever apply t

The Scene
Chipotle is beefing up its board, in a bid to reassure investors and quell concerns about potential activist scrutiny. Sabir Sami, formerly KFCâs CEO, joins Chipotleâs board effective immediately, the company announced Monday evening. He brings much-needed dining and operations expertise to the table, which until his appointment had just one director â chairman Scott Maw â with category experience.
Investors â and customers â have soured on brands like Chipotle, deriding them as âslop bowlsâ and questioning their value. Chipotleâs same-store sales began to fall last year, for the first time in decades, and the companyâs margins have been pressured by high beef and labor costs.
There are signs of hope: CEO Scott Boatwright, who landed the top job after Brian Niccolâs surprise departure to Starbucks, has launched a turnaround plan, dubbed âRecipe for Growth.â
Rohanâs view
On the face of it, thereâs nothing notable about Samiâs appointment: Healthy and unhealthy companies alike will bring in new blood to their boardrooms from time to time. But Chipotle has been in a tough spot since Niccol departed in 2024, and even as Boatwrightâs plan shows signs of momentum (same-store sales have begun to tick back up again), there are open questions about Chipotleâs strategic direction.
Some fast-casual executives and activism defense advisors have privately told me in recent weeks they believe Chipotle will contend with an activist investor given the collapse in the companyâs multiple and a general perception, from both consumers and investors, that the company has lost its way. Chipotle didnât return a request for comment on activist pressures. The companyâs board lacked the quick-service expertise one might expect from a company of its size, a deficiency that it clearly sees and is looking to address with Samiâs appointment.

203cabe0ec4e.text: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Axios could not immediately confirm the closure timeline. A second resolution from the board, filed as evidence in the ongoing legal fight, listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." Zoom out: A second resolution filed by Beatty on Monday listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported. The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space. Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina. What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover. And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him.
