"Wouldn't it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States?" asked Finland's President Alexander Stubb this summer.
The question was rather tongue-in-cheek. US President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state - causing deep offence amongst many Canadians.
Finland is one of the EU's 27 member states and a close ally of Canada as a fellow Arctic nation. Teasing tones aside, President Stubb put his finger squarely on the pulse of deepening EU-Canadian relations. "Canada is more Europe-minded than most Europeans!" is a smiling retort you often hear in Brussels at the moment.
On Sunday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU.
The catalyst for this very public, ardent new love-in is Donald Trump. Just the other day, the US president posted a map of North America on his Truth Social site, including Canada and Greenland - a territory that's part of EU country Denmark - all overlaid with the US flag.
Trade negotiations between the US and Canada broke down late last month. European countries, which have been hit by their own Trump tariffs, have privately watched the spat play out with a mixture of interest and, for many, admiration.
While the EU, led by the European Commission, simply accepted new blanket Trump tariffs without fighting back, Carney has prominently stood up to the US president, swiftly imposing counter-tariffs on the United States.
When it comes to courting the EU, Canada appears to some to be even keener than one of the bloc's closest neighbours.
"Canada right now seems more interested than the UK to get as close to Brussels as possible, as a non member state" says Mark Lowen, director of the European Council of Foreign Relations think tank. "It's remarkable."
Canada, but not the UK, successfully joined the European Union's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence fund earlier this year. The UK remained on the sidelines following a row over costs and political tensions. A summit designed to reset and improve EU-UK relations has just been delayed - again - over cross-Channel differences.
By contrast this week, Carney is invited as a special guest to the European Commission President's annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, France on Wednesday. Carney will hold a speech in the European Parliament there on Thursday, a day after President von der Leyen outlines the EU's political and policy priorities.
Officials on both sides insist this is more than just "blah blah politics", as one EU diplomat put it to me. He was speaking on condition of anonymity so as to be able to discuss the subject freely. Carney and von der Leyen are both expected to mention plans to forge closer ties. "As close as you can get without (Canada) actually becoming an EU member," the diplomat told me.
'Trump effect' prompts efforts to diversify - but are they achievable?
In the corridors of Brussels, there's whispered talk of constructing a "special association agreement" with Canada.
The unofficial aim for both sides, I'm told, is to reduce reliance on Washington in several key areas:
- Digital and tech developments, in which the US and China dominate
- Energy: Canada is rich in liquified natural gas (LNG) the EU needs since it cut back its energy dependency on Russia
- Raw materials and critical minerals: Canada has them in abundance
- Trade and defence procurement: Canada has been on a "buy European" spree of late, purchasing German attack submarines, for example, and airborne early-warning planes from Sweden's Saab. Its view appears to be: why reward the US by buying American equipment after being slapped with trade tariffs amounting to 50% in some sectors?
A Nanos opinion poll from April suggests more than four in five Canadians favour strengthening ties with the EU.
Close to three in five support Canada actually joining the bloc, though Article 49 of the EU Constitution would appear to make that impossible. Without wanting to seem facetious, the European Union is not (yet) the Eurovision Song Contest, in which indisputably non-European Israel and Australia have - controversially - been allowed to compete.
Back to trade: ties between Canada and the EU are far from novel. The EU is already Canada's second-largest trading partner - albeit far behind the US, which buys about 70% of Canadian exports.
The far-reaching Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) trade deal was agreed just under a decade ago and has been provisionally implemented, eliminating 99% of tariffs on Canadian goods exports.
Privately, European officials admit this renewed high-level courtship between Ottawa and Brussels has everything to do with the actions of Trump's second term in office.
The US president is by now infamous amongst US allies for what they view as his unpredictability and his penchant to use trade or security ties as leverage.
There's a growing sense in Europe - which has, since World War Two, looked to the US as its closest ally abroad - and in Canada, whose economy has been intertwined with the US for decades, that neither can any longer fully rely on Washington. They believe it's time to diversify.
"The Canadian government is committed to trade diversification, doubling non-US trades in the next 10 years, and doing more with the European Union will be very key to achieving that target," Mark Camilleri, president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association (CEUTIA) told the BBC.
An even tighter Canadian-EU alliance, covering far more sectors than trade alone, would continue a recent trend of both parties to form new association agreements around the world. In Canada's case, this includes a sectoral deal with China, which raised international eyebrows earlier this year.
EU insiders put all of this down to the "Trump effect".

8bd0ff1b1777.text: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

Democratic and Republican voters agree that the American public should decide the future of AI development, not billionaires in Silicon Valley, according to new polling shared first with Semafor.
The poll was commissioned for a new organization launched by Alex Bores, who made a name for himself as a top target of the AI industry in his failed bid for Congress in New York. Though AI ranked last on a list of 13 issues that 1,502 registered voters polled this month said they care about, half said AI is moving too fast and 86% identified lack of regulation as a problem.
Only 18% of those polled think the US falling behind China competitively is a problem, a risk President Donald Trump has cited in opposing regulation.
While just 36% polled said they had heard about incidents like the Hugging Face hack, âsupport for reasonable regulations is actually quite correlated with all these other issues,â Bores told Semafor Tuesday in Washington on the sidelines of the âpro-humanâ summit attended by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The pollâs results, Bores argued, show that âif you show good work on AI, youâre winning over voters, even though AI isnât their top issue.â
Boresâ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a âshared baselineâ for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said.
âAs a Democrat, I say this with love, but we turn everything into a circular firing squad, and I think itâs really, really important that on this issue, where we have powerful, well-resourced enemies that donât want there to be any regulation whatsoever, that we are all on the same tea,â he said.

1b36061db868.text: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

States bet big on rural health startups, with a Silicon Valley twist
When Josh Fleig, Louisiana’s chief innovation officer, learned his state had set aside $20 million a year, for five years, to invest in startup rural health companies, his reaction was not surprising: “Wow!”
In rural America, where people are often reported to be sicker with poor access to healthcare, the cash influx is a relief. In the economic development space where Fleig operates, it’s an opportunity.
“Look, that’s a lot of money for what we do,” said Fleig, whose state-funded economic development office invests in corporate launches, ranging from software startups to shipbuilders.
Louisiana and a handful of other states set aside money from their share of the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program to quickly invest in new technologies, mirroring private industry moves. Lawmakers added the rural health program to offset more than $900 billion in reduced Medicaid spending expected over 10 years from Republicans’ sweeping 2025 tax and spending law.
But rather than filling the budget hole, the rural program’s assignment is to find new approaches for revitalizing rural communities where doctors are in short supply and hospitals have been downsizing and closing for decades. The federal government doled out the first-year rural health program awards to states this year, with pots ranging from $147 million in New Jersey to $281 million in Texas.
Modernizing technology infrastructure is a key pillar of the federal rural health program, and the catalyst money epitomizes the administration’s strategy to move fast and experiment with untested technology — much like the “move fast and break things” mantra during the heyday of Silicon Valley.
Instead of breaking things, though, the goal is to “move fast, fast-fail, innovate quickly, and move to sustainability,” said Aaron Bujnowski, a managing director with the healthcare industry group at the consultancy Alvarez & Marsal. “This is a transformation that is still meant to serve the people.”
Rigorous Rules and Tight Deadlines
Beyond Louisiana, Timothy Foster, a spokesperson for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, confirmed that Delaware, Georgia, Massachusetts, Nebraska, South Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia are also creating rural health tech catalyst funds.
Every year, states must compete for rural funding in the five-year federal program. Federal regulators will take money away from states that do not meet the goals promised in their applications, including whether they designated money to companies for tech innovations.
CMS, which is overseeing the program, released a seven-step guidance document for states to follow when creating the tech catalyst operations. No more than 10% of each state’s award can be spent on a rural tech catalyst fund.
States’ initial annual progress reports for the rural fund were due at the end of August. CMS has declined to publicly post those reports; it plans to publish an annual report on state progress. States must show that first-year funds will be obligated — but not necessarily spent — by Oct. 30, according to the CMS guidance document.
Daniel X. O’Neil, a technology consultant who advocates for open data and open government, created a state tracker and parsed the original state applications to find dozens that mention catalyst awards and technology funds.
O’Neil said he is “looking forward to the clawbacks and the craziness of October because, you know, that’s serious stuff.”
For the rural health catalyst funds, CMS requires states to submit the list of finalists “at least 15 business days” before announcing winners, along with “sufficient information” for the agency to “assess each proposed project,” according to the guidance document.
The document outlines intellectual property and federal rights but does not provide guidance or standards for patient rights or protections. CMS spokesperson Foster stated in an email that the technology investments must comply with federal “privacy, security, interoperability, and patient safety” requirements.
Protecting Patients
Maya Sandalow, director of the health program at the Bipartisan Policy Center and one of the leading analysts watching the rural fund, said the catalyst funds are “public dollars” and has called for more transparency in the overall rural health program. The center is a nonprofit think tank in Washington, D.C.
Accurate and timely reporting must be done to ensure “the necessary guardrails are in place” to protect patients, she said, adding that the innovation needs to be “tested in a way that’s safe for the patients that they are going to be used on.”
To apply, startups must be less than 10 years old and have raised less than $50 million in early funding. Companies that win a portion of state catalyst funds must meet predetermined milestones before being paid — and federal officials will make “targeted reviews as needed,” according to the guidance document.
Louisiana officials announced the state’s tech catalyst fund with an event in rural Natchitoches, known as the filming location of the 1989 film Steel Magnolias. The fund quickly drew more than 200 companies competing for between $250,000 and $3 million in seed money.
Tiny startup Greens Health was invited to the event. The 2-year-old company analyzes Medicare claims to identify patients with chronic diseases, such as diabetes, and works with local home health nurses and senior facilities to improve care.
“We’ve been looking for a way to launch in Louisiana,” said Kehlin Swain, co-founder and chief executive of Greens Health. The company serves about 100 patients across Texas, Alabama, and Florida and hopes to get a $250,000 investment from Louisiana.
Louisiana’s Fleig said his state is “at a really interesting turning point.” The state secured $208.4 million for the first year of the rural health program and quickly created its catalyst fund using the state’s already established innovation department

Outcome of Suit Against Department of Labor Could Boost Skimpy Employer Health Plans
A long-running lawsuit challenging what it means to be an employee and therefore have access to work-based health plans is being closely watched by health policy analysts. Its outcome could spur the availability of lower-cost but potentially skimpier health coverage that skirts some consumer protections.
Court papers indicate a settlement in the case against the Department of Labor may be in the works, although the parameters of any such deal are unknown.
It would come amid premium surges on Affordable Care Act marketplaces that have led millions to drop coverage this year. The Trump administration has also been sharply focused on expanding access to alternative coverage, such as short-term plans that avoid ACA rules on preexisting conditions and benefit requirements.
“Depending on what happens with the settlement, this could be an even bigger expansion,” said Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at the Georgetown University Law Center. “People are worried that it is the opening salvo into promoting junk plans that don’t meet the ACA requirements.”
The plaintiff, Data Marketing Partnership, filed its case against the Department of Labor in 2019, during the first Trump administration. It wants official recognition as an employer so it can continue to allow its limited partners to buy into a type of job-based health insurance that doesn’t have to comply with state insurance rules or offer coverage as robust as required under the ACA.
But to grasp the claim, one also has to understand how the coverage works.
A consumer shopping for health insurance may come across information online or from a marketer about this concept, sometimes called “limited partnership” coverage. The pitch? Buy insurance offered through Data Marketing Partnership and handled by LP Management Services. To qualify, the consumer must download an app that tracks their internet searches. The company could then sell that data.
Some potential consumers may be turned off by the thought of their internet searches being tracked, but others may find it appealing because it allows them to become a limited partner eligible to buy into the company’s employee health insurance plans. But can these partners be considered employees?
The court’s answer has potential implications for regulators and consumers. Some health policy and market experts warn that a green light could lead to a proliferation of aggressively marketed and potentially questionable insurance with limited recourse for consumers because the plans would be exempt from state oversight.
“If this took off, you logically could see the rise of a whole bunch of what, functionally, would be unregulated insurance companies,” said Ali Khawar, who was the principal deputy assistant secretary of the Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration during Joe Biden’s presidency and now runs his own consulting outfit.
No one knows if the department is going to change its long-running stance defending the case. But any settlement could add more uncertainty to insurance markets.
Already insurers are requesting double-digit increases in ACA premiums again next year, partly because declining enrollment often means that the healthiest policyholders are leaving. That trend could accelerate in coming years as more people are drawn into alternatives such as limited-partnership policies.
States Act as Federal Case Plays Out
The Department of Labor defended the case throughout the first Trump administration and the Biden era, issuing a sharply worded advisory opinion in early 2020 stating that people who simply download software to “capture data as they browse the Internet” are not “employees or bona fide partners.”
A district court judge in Texas, who had previously ruled the ACA unconstitutional in a decision ultimately rejected by the Supreme Court, called the advisory opinion “arbitrary and capricious” in a 2020 ruling in favor of the data marketer. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit largely upheld the lower court’s decision but ordered it to reconsider whether someone who downloads software is either a “working owner” or a “bona fide partner.”
The employer-employee relationship is at the heart of the case because of a 1974 federal law designed to help large, self-insured employers offer retirement and health benefits to workers without having to meet varying rules from multiple states.
That law — the Employee Retirement Income Security Act — allows such plans to avoid most rules set by the states, which generally regulate most other types of insurance and assist consumers who report problems with their policies. As self-insured employer plans, the policies also don’t have to comply with some ACA rules, such as the requirement to cover 10 broad categories of “essential health benefits.”
“If the case goes the wrong way, it could impact consumers or hamstring the states,” said Marie Grant, Maryland’s insurance commissioner.
Arguments over what constitutes an employer plan are not new, and other organizations have tried offering such coverage. Some states have taken action against purveyors of limited-partner policies.
Maryland in 2024 fined a company, The Vitamin Patch, for offering limited-partnership insurance after investigating complaints and determining it was not licensed to sell coverage in the state.
Washington in 2021 ordered another company to stop offering its plans in the state and fined it $25,000.
Maine and Connecticut in 2024 warned consumers about this type of coverage.
“These plans do not provide comprehensive medical coverage and can leave consumers with large, unpaid medical bills,” according to Connecticut’s notice.
Maine’s announcement noted that entities offering these types of health insurance included The Vitamin Patch as well as Affiliated Workers Alliance, Consumer Data Partners, Employers Business Alliance, Socios Buenos, and

In the East Tampa neighborhood where Dee Morales bought her house, residents have been asking for a supermarket for 10 years. They still don’t have one. So Morales did the math out loud: In the decade the neighborhood has spent waiting, a community garden could have grown thousands of pounds of food.
Morales runs 813 Hood Garden, a network of growing spaces across East Tampa, Sulphur Springs and Ybor City. Two of these gardens are in neighborhoods the federal government classifies as “food deserts,” places that are both low-income and far from a grocery store.
She started 813 Hood Garden during the pandemic, after discovering the only way to get her oldest son to eat vegetables was to let him grow them himself. Adults who visited, she found, had never seen a pepper on the plant.
In Hillsborough County, more than 15 percent of residents are food insecure, according to Feeding America’s 2026 Map the Meal Gap, based on 2024 data. Across Florida, there was an increase in food insecurity from about 10 percent of the population in 2020 to 15.4 percent in 2024. Food insecurity has climbed nationally since the COVID-19 pandemic as food prices surged, according to the USDA.
Yet as need grows, the government’s willingness to measure food insecurity is shrinking. Last fall, the U.S. Department of Agriculture canceled its long-running annual survey of household food security—the most authoritative national count—calling it redundant and politicized. Increasingly, the task of mapping where hunger exists is falling to nonprofits and researchers building models of their own.
Geographer Jaryd Hinch built a model that scores every neighborhood in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties for community-garden “suitability,” weighting poverty and income most heavily—above factors like transit access and available land—in what he calls an “equity-first” design meant to steer gardens toward the residents facing the steepest barriers to fresh food. The study began as a graduate course project, was not funded or requested by any agency and was written by Hinch, a doctoral candidate at the University of South Florida whose research centers on aviation sustainability.
Published this year in the peer-reviewed journal Southeastern Geographer, it maps where a garden could, in theory, do the most good, then overlays the gardens Tampa Bay already has. The match is loose. About 58 percent of existing gardens fall in the neighborhoods his model flags as “highest priority,” better than the 40 percent random placement would predict, yet still far from alignment. Maps show some of the highest-need neighborhoods have no garden, while some of the county’s most established gardens flourish in comfortable suburbs—one of the most successful sits in Carrollwood, a middle-class area that is nobody’s idea of a food desert.
Hinch’s paper frames that gap as a planning problem: The region lacks “spatially informed decision-making tools,” he wrote. But the people closest to the work describe a different problem entirely.
“The tool doesn’t matter,” said Monica Petrella, the food-systems coordinator at the University of Florida’s Hillsborough County extension office and, in effect, the audience Hinch’s model was built for. She won’t consult a suitability map, she said, until a project already has about 30 committed volunteers and $10,000 for beds, soil and water. In her day-to-day life, she isn’t looking at any map to decide where a garden goes—she’s trying to help the gardens that exist find enough volunteers to survive.
That inverts the study’s premise. The binding constraint on community gardens, Petrella said, isn’t information about where need is highest. It’s people and money. And those, she noted, tend to pool where affluence already is: Gardens demand so much volunteer labor that they thrive in neighborhoods where residents have leisure time, disposable income and the knowledge to file for nonprofit status and chase sponsors.
According to the Coalition of Community Gardens, of the 12 gardens that started in the region between 2009 and 2011, six had failed by 2015—a 50 percent failure rate. After the coalition formed to network and support them, none failed over the next six years.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Petrella is blunt in her belief that gardens won’t close the hunger gap. Food insecurity, she said, is a function of economics: Grocery chains skip low-income neighborhoods they deem unprofitable, residents without cars are left with convenience stores and no amount of backyard tomatoes changes that arithmetic.
The produce itself rarely reaches the people who need it most, she said; most gardens run on individual plots, where growers take home what they raise, leaving little surplus to give away. The connection between a community garden and a hungry household, she said, is “a scenic route.” Gardens are “a cherry on top,” she said. They’re valuable for the community they build, but not a fix.
Morales agrees a garden is “part of something bigger.”
“It’s our responsibility as the people to advocate for what we want,” she said. Community gardening, in her telling, is a short-term answer while neighborhoods keep fighting for the grocery stores, transit and wages that would actually move the needle.
Notably, Morales didn’t fault the model—she called it a promising resource, as long as it captures “the actual need of the people,” something a survey, not a spreadsheet, would catch. Her frustration runs elsewhere.
“The issue isn’t that we need more community gardens,” she said. “We need support for the gardens that exist.” Organizers like her aren’t paid for their time; she works a job and pours the rest into the garden as a passion project. The News
Jim Justice is getting the itch. And it could set up a battle of GOP titans.
The West Virginia GOP senator is considering a run for his old job as governor in 2028, which would potentially set up a race between him and incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Justice told Semafor heâs âsure thinking about itâ before quickly interjecting that he loves âwhat Iâm doing hereâ in the Senate.
He also jabbed at Morrisey but insisted he wants the governor to be successful: âGov. Morrisey has a more difficult time bonding with people and everything, but beyond that, I want him to do great, I really do. Iâm not in a food fight at all.â
âI do love the people of West Virginia, and I spent eight years trying to build it back. Got it really going,â Justice continued. âI just want goodness for West Virginia, but I want goodness for the whole nation too. Weâll make a decision.â
Know More
West Virginia is a small state thatâs also the home of bare-knuckled politics and big personalities. Republicans recruited Justice, a former Democrat, to run against former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., in 2024, though Manchin ultimately decided against seeking reelection. Manchin narrowly defeated Morrisey in 2018, but Morrisey mounted a political comeback in 2024 by emerging from a crowded GOP primary and winning the governorâs mansion.
A Morrisey ally told Semafor that Justice has myriad vulnerabilities and hasnât had to win a tough GOP primary against someone like the incumbent governor (though Justice did easily defeat former Rep. Alex Mooney, R-W.Va., in 2024). The ally added that the conservative Club for Growth is already committed to opposing Justice, put Morriseyâs war chest at nearly $5 million across several political entities, and noted that Justice is in debt and is now sharing control of his familyâs Greenbrier resort.
But Justice said people in West Virginia are encouraging him to run: âYouâre going to hear people come to you and say, âBoy, weâd love to have you back as governor.â You know, thatâs natural and everything. I donât pay a whole lot of attention.â
Manchin also flirted repeatedly with running for his old job as governor, which he used to call the âbest job in the world.â Manchin never ran after serving in the Senate, but Senate Republicans believe Justice is more likely to run than not, according to several GOP sources. Regarding the 2028 governor race, Manchin said on Tuesday: âCanât we get through this election before worrying about the next election?â

Democratsâ decision to bump up New Mexico to their fourth primary spot in 2028, right after the now-familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, bestows growing prominence and sway on congressional delegations from all four states. Populous Michigan and Virginia, fifth and sixth on the primary calendar, will be right behind them.
Democrats in the previous cast of early states are going to find new opportunities to wield their clout with a field that could easily number in the dozens. And lawmakers from states newer to the early-primary lineup are already preparing to elevate what matters to their constituents, as they get wooed by presidential aspirants.
âI want them to come to New Mexico and look at the issues that we face,â said FernÃ¡ndez, D-N.M. âI want to see the candidates inspire the kind of communities that will make a difference in both the primary election and the general election.â
With competitive midterm races happening in nearly all of the early states, potential Democratic presidential candidates are already on the trail with purple-district incumbents and candidates. Other lawmakers from early-primary states are fielding calls from 2028 contenders looking to appear with them.
To name just a recent few: California Gov. Gavin Newsom appeared at the opening of a state party campaign office with Horsford; Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has done events for Nevadaâs Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Aaron Ford; and New Mexico candidates have seen visits by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker.
âIâm not taking sides early. Theyâre all going to have to earn it,â said Horsford, whose district includes Las Vegas. He said he was hoping candidates would âunderstand that working-class people care about their healthcare, housing, childcare, elder care.â
Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who represents a Trump-won New Mexico district, said Buttigieg had recently appeared with him. He named housing, water, and immigration as the top issues for candidates âto really come and understand how tough this economy truly is and what itâs going to take to fix it.â

âCome on down and visit New Mexico, get to know the state. Get to know the people,â LujÃ¡n told Semafor. âI certainly hope that whoever the next president of the United States is a Democrat and is a Democrat that understands New Mexico.â
LujÃ¡nâs fellow New Mexico senator, Martin Heinrich, said Democrats are still working through how they will host candidates in early-primary states in 2027 and 2028. But he said the new calendar is a big deal for New Mexico, which dropped off the swing-state map in 2008 after then-Sen. Barack Obama turned it blue.
âWe have a lot of really unique issues that are not something that you learn about through osmosis in other parts of the country,â Heinrich said.
New Mexico will get âpresidential candidates to care about water, public lands, national laboratories,â he added â âthings that many of them just donât have that much familiarity with.â
LujÃ¡n also said his state has great food, but cautioned candidates about a regional tripwire: feeling compelled to choose between the stateâs famous green and red chiles.
âIt depends what theyâre eating. Anyone that gives you an answer? They donât know the state,â he said. âYou canât pick one.â
Know More
Democratic incumbents in tight races are hoping to reap electoral benefits from 2028 candidates who are coming through their districts. The visits tend to energize the base ahead of the midterms and may also broaden congressional candidatesâ appeal.
âI always look at the quality of events. Are they putting me in front of voters who I really havenât connected with before? Thatâs sort of my No. 1 goal,â said Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., who represents a purple district.
She called herself a âButtigieg fanâ this time and said she would endorse in the 2028 cycle, though she was waiting to learn more about other candidatesâ positions.
It helps that three early-primary states for 2028 are also hosting competitive Senate races this fall. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., just campaigned in New Hampshire, and heâll be heading to both Michigan and South Carolina, completing the trifecta.
âWeâve never had a problem with getting people to pay attention to our state because weâve always been a swing state. And I think the calendar probably heightens it,â said Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich. âWeâre a good microcosm and often canary-in-the-coal-mine on issues, so we want to be in the mix.â
Room for Disagreement
Not every Democrat is sold on the new calendar. Those in New Hampshire say their state law supersedes the partyâs revised order, which puts South Carolina ahead of them.
âI continue to remind folks that New Hampshire has a state law, so weâre going to have the first primary,â Hassan told Semafor. âWe are seeing a lot of people come up and campaign and support our candidates, and we continue to think that itâs really good for candidates, especially Democratic candidates, to be on the ground doing retail politics.â
Nicholas and Burgessâ View

The House is embarking on its last days in session before breaking for the midterms, with a final vote expected Wednesday on a bill ratcheting up penalties on Russia.
The procedural vote teeing up the final tally on the sanctions bill inflamed intraparty tensions when two purple-district Democrats, Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington and Jared Golden of Maine, once again broke ranks and voted with Republicans.
The White House privately reached out to some Democratic lawmakers to sway them on the procedural vote with promises like infrastructure projects, according to one lawmaker.
The Senate also advanced the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act, which the chamber will now be focused on for a few days before it passes.
There are already rumors of the Senate breaking for campaign season early, but Republican leadership still wants to confirm nominees and complete some regulatory rollbacks.
And Republicans still want to pass Ohio Sen. Jon Hustedâs data center-focused Ratepayer Protection Act.
âWhoâs going to vote against it?â said Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D. âJonâs in a tough race and itâs pretty good populist stuff.â

1883a06fccf0.text: Data: NFHS ; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago. Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process. By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations . Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport. Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport , and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26. The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs , and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials . Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport. Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports. A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell. What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom. All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology â that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" â are a hoax.
It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision â theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.
Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.
The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.
Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.
"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."
Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."
A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.
It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI
Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology â including infrastructure and equipment â has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.
The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.
Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."
The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.
Of course, Trump â who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy â is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump
Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."
Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.

Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".
The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".
"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.
Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.
There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.
Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.
The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.
Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."
The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".
Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an ongoing dispute over trade.
Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength".
She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".
Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures.
Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.
"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."
She listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation under the partnership.
The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement eliminating duties on 99% of goods exports called the Comprehensive Economic Trade Agreement (CETA).
"We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space," said von der Leyen.
The move comes as EU members have also been hit trade tariffs under Trump's administration and as the bloc faces what its chief described as "an openly hostile world".
Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.
"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.
"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."
Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.
Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.
A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.
Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.

White-tailed eagle chicks have successfully fledged from wild nests in England for the fourth consecutive year.
Two out of five pairs of eagles released by a reintroduction project successfully bred and raised young with one chick fledging from a nest in Dorset and two more in Sussex.
The project, run by Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation, aims to return the species to England. Nine birds have been born in the wild since it began in 2019.
"This year's breeding success is another important milestone in the return of this lost species to England; it shows what can be achieved by very skilled wildlife managers," Roy Dennis OBE from the foundation said.
The foundation has called the breeding attempts "remarkable", adding that one of the male adult birds has only one leg after losing it five years ago.
Human persecution had caused the bird's extinction, with the last pair breeding in southern England in 1780.
"Restoring a species takes many years and requires the support of a wide range of communities and organisations, in particular landowners and farmers," Dennis added.
Steve Egerton-Read, white-tailed eagle project officer for Forestry England, said: "We are delighted that these three chicks made it through and will be closely watching their progress as they begin to explore the landscape."
To date, 56 young white-tailed eagles have been released including, for the first time this year, additional releases of six birds at Exmoor National Park, in partnership with Exmoor National Park Authority.

Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday.
Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been".
"Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable."
The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected.
The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints.
A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."
Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too.
Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games.
Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them.
Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations".
They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said.
Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.
Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels.
Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games.
But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included.
Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes.
"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."
But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation".
"The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read.
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb".
Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October.

cdb1df3ccd14.text: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged." A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high." That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it. Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing." He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans. Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident. "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go." "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally." "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong." What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI. After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology." Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate. "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI." Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day." Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude. Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI. In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI. About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.
His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.
Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".
Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.
He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.
"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.
Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.
He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.
His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.
In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.
Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.
In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

bc03c88e2093.text:
The News
Africaâs richest man Aliko Dangote is considering plans to list shares of his Nigeria refinery business on a US stock exchange within the next four years following the launch of its initial public offering, the continentâs largest ever.
The share sale, which kicked off in Lagos on Monday, has a fundraising goal of $1.6 billion, with room to add 30% more than the target if the offer is oversubscribed. Plans for a secondary listing would extend ownership in the refinery beyond the millions of Nigerians who have swarmed onto several fintech apps to subscribe to the offer set at 40 cents a share. The refinery is valued at around $50 billion, more than twice the cost of construction.
âIn the next three, four years or thereabout, we will try and also list outside the African continent, most likely in the US,â the billionaire owner of the Dangote refinery said at the IPO launch this week.
The timeframe overlaps with the companyâs plans to double the refineryâs output to 1.4 million barrels a day by early 2029. In an interview last week before Dangoteâs address at the IPO launch, refinery chief financial officer Bruce Tanner told Semafor that the company will âdefinitely be looking for international secondary listings,â and suggested that it would be after the refinery ramps up production. He had declined to give an exact date for the listing.
The companyâs initial intent to roll-out this IPO on multiple African exchanges became unworkable âgiven the timeframe and regulatory hurdles in each of the different environments,â Tanner said. He indicated that some investment houses and pension funds that could have participated in a pan-African IPO have still bought into the offer in its current Nigeria-only form.
Know More
The Nigerian refineryâs daily capacity of 700,000 barrels puts it above every refinery that currently operates in the US. Successfully doubling its size will make it the largest in the world, displacing Indiaâs Jamnagar refinery owned by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani.
Expansion will enable Dangote to serve African fuel demand beyond Nigeria where it has become the most influential supplier to the domestic market since coming on stream in September 2024. The Dangote group also plans to set up a second refinery in Kenya to form a network capable of fulfilling the continentâs needs. Both projects will cost some $30 billion combined.
Proceeds from the ongoing IPO will be directed towards the Nigeria expansion and further fundraising is planned in future, Tanner said. The refinery recorded $13.9 billion in half-year revenue this year and has forecast annual increases for each full year up to 2030, on the assumption that added refining capacity will boost sales.
Meanwhile, the plantâs 69-year-old billionaire founder, whose decades-old empire includes giant cement and sugar subsidiaries, could see his wealth expand by more than 60% to $58 billion on the strength of the Nigerian refineryâs IPO alone, according to Bloomberg.
Step Back
Dangote is betting that scale, not sentiment, is what finally makes an African-founded company work as a US-listed stock. The refineryâs capacity doubling to 1.4 million barrels a day would mean the plant could produce roughly 10% of US refining capacity. At that scale, a US listing offers him dollar liquidity, index inclusion, and institutional capital the Nigerian Exchange canât match.
But African businessesâ record on US exchanges has been shaky. African ecommerce company Jumiaâs 2019 New York Stock Exchange debut showed how fast âAfrican growth storyâ enthusiasm evaporates even after initially hitting a record high valuation months after IPO. Today the stock still trades roughly 75% below its IPO price. Meanwhile, commodity players including Sasol, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields donât list shares directly in New York but trade as American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) â certificates issued by a US bank representing shares held abroad, letting US investors buy them in dollars without a foreign brokerage account.
But years on, their ADRs still track gold and chemical prices, not business fundamentals â proxies for commodities, not endorsements of the companies themselves. Others, including Flutterwave, have quietly shelved Nasdaq ambitions. Dangoteâs bet is that hard assets, not a growth narrative, will make the difference this time.
The View From Botswana
Neo Mooki, chairperson of the stock exchange in Botswana, said at the Lagos IPO launch that the Dangote refineryâs existence and share sale was proof that âAfricans can own Africaâs ambition.â She implored the company to work with her exchange âto make sure that this ambition can also be owned right across Africa from Gaborone to Nairobi.â
In addition to Kenya, Botswanaâs capital market was a potential destination for the refineryâs shelved pan-African IPO. The Botswana Stock Exchangeâs $70 billion equity value is smaller than Nigeriaâs $120 billion market, but the bourse lists the shares of some large companies like Anglo American, the British mining giant with extensive operations in Southern Africa.

- Published
Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external.
Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.
Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.
Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.
Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.
Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.
Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed.
Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining.
Last week, Jacob GuachetÃ¡ Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.
While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory.
Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024.
As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found.
Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders.
The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

The US Treasury secretary will hold talks with a top Chinese official as part of efforts to head off a resumption of trade conflict, while tensions mounted between the superpowers across a range of issues. The talks on Sunday come ahead of next weekâs leadersâ summit in Washington, DC; though the rhetoric between the White House and Beijing has been largely conciliatory in recent weeks, the reality has been harsher.
Along with pressuring major trading partners to curb commercial ties with China and mulling further tariffs on Chinese imports, the US has linked Chinese satellite imagery to an Iranian strike that killed American troops, and tested a space-based weapon that Beijing has warned will fuel an arms race.

The US Federal Reserve is likely to raise rates today, a move that many economists say is necessary to corral inflation, but which will put the central bankâs chair in conflict with the White House. The expected quarter-percentage-point hike is one of at least four that traders are betting on over the next year, with ING researchers arguing a 50-basis-point increase could actually be a better move today were it not for the inevitable political fallout.

The Democratic Republic of Congo sought to speed up the implementation of a strategic mining partnership with the US, which is looking to rival Chinaâs influence in Africa. The European Commission president invited Canada to become the EUâs first-ever âassociate member,â highlighting the global geopolitical realignment underway as a result of US pressure on allies.
