Here are the seven bills we have been following that the Republicans wanted to get through. You see those first two have passed, funding government. We didn't have that kind of deadline this time. Russian sanctions, that made it through. But then you see in yellow two that are still in progress, that data center bill and the college sports. But you see four of the items on this list are not yet accomplished. That includes funding the war in Iran, the crypto bill, which has hit a rough patch in the Senate, and the farm bill, as well as the SAVE Act that Republicans wanted to get through. Amna Nawaz: You pointed out there Congress has not funded the Iran war, but there was a big vote on Iran in the House this week. Tell us about that. Lisa Desjardins: Right. It was a busy week. The House voted to end the war in Iran. This is the third time that the House majority, a majority in the House has voted that way. But it's notable because of the margin, and also because these seven Republicans, the most yet, voted to bring back troops and end the war in Iran. You will note, of these seven, four of them, you see them highlighted there with yellow, are in competitive House races from Michigan to Iowa to Pennsylvania. Now, these are -- this is a symbolic vote because President Trump can veto. But it shows really the direction and the momentum in Congress is against the Iran war. More are speaking out. And we expect the Senate to take a similar vote next week. Amna Nawaz: Related to the Iran war, I know you have been following a House Republican who filed articles of impeachment against the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Lisa Desjardins: Yes. Amna Nawaz: Is that going to get a vote? Lisa Desjardins: It will. It will not until after the election, though, because the House left before that vote was going to ripen. These are impeachment articles introduced surprisingly by Thomas Massie. He did not tell Republican leaders he was going to do this. He is a Republican from Kentucky. He lost his primary. But he felt strongly that he needed to put eight charges against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Some of those deal with the war in Iran, which he says needs congressional approval, but others include that he accuses the secretary of ignoring the protocols for civilian deaths, killing civilians, including at sea with those strikes that we have seen in the Gulf. Amna Nawaz: So the House has now left. The Senate's here for one more week. Overall, where do things stand with Congress getting things done before the elections? Lisa Desjardins: Well, you will hear a lot of different versions from Republicans, but they have gotten some things done. Avoiding a government shutdown and that fiscal

802f05488795.text: September 17 is Constitution Day, a commemoration of the founding document signed on that date in 1787. But for immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards.Justice correspondent Ali Rogin reports. Geoff Bennett: Well, today is Citizenship Day, which recognizes everyone who has attained U.S. citizenship and commemorates the signing of the U.S. Constitution on this day back in 1787. Amna Nawaz: But, for immigrants, the path to naturalization has grown more difficult, as the Trump administration has added new requirements and tightened vetting standards. Our justice correspondent, Ali Rogin, has this look. Ali Rogin: In a federal courthouse in Alexandria, Virginia, 60 of the nation's newest Americans take their final steps towards citizenship, sharing where their journeys began. Woman: Venezuela. Woman: El Salvador. Woman: Korea. Ali Rogin: Before they all arrived at this moment. Judge William Fitzpatrick, Eastern District of Virginia: Please rise and raise your right hand. I hereby declare... Men and Women: I hereby declare... Judge William Fitzpatrick: ... on oath. Men and Women: ... on oath. Judge William Fitzpatrick: So help me God. Men and Women: So help me God. Judge William Fitzpatrick: Congratulations. Woman: We're super excited. Me and my husband, we both became citizens. Man: I don't think people realize how daunting this journey is. But it's -- I'm so happy to be here. Ali Rogin: For most, the journey involves applying for and holding a green card for years, lengthy applications, hundreds of dollars in fees, interviews with immigration officers, an English language test, and finally a civics test, for which applicants spend months studying. Lucio Arevalo, Green Card Holder: Definitely am nervous. The nerves are there. The stress is there. Ali Rogin: New Mexico resident Lucio Arevalo is nearing the finish line of his naturalization. A green card holder since 1998, he arrived in the U.S. with his parents from Mexico as a baby. He's awaiting his interview date. Lucio Arevalo: I am, of course, a permanent resident, but I just feel like there's still that thin line between me actually being, I guess, fully part of the country. So, decided to take that step. Ali Rogin: What will it mean to you to take that oath of citizenship? Lucio Arevalo: To be honest, it's -- it would be such a big relief. Ali Rogin: Relief because he hopes to stop living in fear of President Trump's efforts to deport noncitizens. Lucio Arevalo: It is definitely scary to know that there could be that possibility for me to get stopped, I guess, by immigration. Ali Rogin: To help prepare for the civics test, Lucio turned to Welcome.US, a national initiative that emerged after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan to help new arrivals through the complicated immigration system. That's how he met volunteer Dana Van Ostrand, who lives in Iowa and has been helping Arevalo study in virtual sessions. Dana Van Ostrand, Welcome.US: It's been a really fun process to not only go through the test, but also just hear of Lucio's life and what he's been about. Nazanin Ash, CEO and Co-Founder, Welcome.US: There are a lot of changes happening in our immigration system and in whether and how we welcome newcomers. Ali Rogin: Nazanin Ash is the CEO and co-founder of Welcome.US. Nazanin Ash: It's a process that's rigorous and has always been rigorous, and it's appropriately rigorous. Taking on the responsibilities of citizenship is a commitment that no one takes lightly, least of all the aspiring Americans who are pursuing their dreams. Ali Rogin: That dream of becoming American has become more elusive since President Trump returned to office. In the last year, the administration has introduced a harder civics test with more questions and a higher number of correct answers required to pass, implemented stricter social media vetting, proposed raising the application fee by 75 percent to nearly $1,300, and revived a defunct practice of neighborhood investigations into applicants' moral character. And the government is processing far fewer naturalization applications today than during the Biden administration, a 75 percent drop-off compared to two years ago. And the rejection rate for naturalization has more than doubled since September 2024 from 9.2 percent to more than 18 percent. Sometimes, the roadblocks continue all the way to the courthouse. Since President Trump returned to office, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has been abruptly canceling naturalization ceremonies, many of them at the last minute. In fact, today, here at this courthouse, there were supposed to be two ceremonies, but the afternoon session was abruptly canceled just last night. Immigration officials say the changes are necessary to tighten the system that has become too lax. In a statement to PBS News, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said the agency "has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify," adding that: "USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process. Naturalization is a privilege, not a right." Van Ostrand says his volunteerism is a way to respond to what he sees as this administration's hostility towards immigrants. Dana Van Ostrand: The Trump administration's rhetoric and actions have been quite dehumanizing, in my view, and I wanted to be a part of welcoming people who have already been here. Ali Rogin: Back at the Alexandria courthouse, the new citizens receive a parting message from Judge William Fitzpatrick. Judge William Fitzpatrick: What I ask of you is to keep working hard, to give life, to give meaning to the oath that you took today by making your voice heard, by making sure that government, your government, reflects your values and your vision for what America can be. I have signed the final order. It is official. Congratulations to you all. Best

Other efforts to reshape the midterms continue Politics Sep 17, 2026 6:26 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The Supreme Court this week closed the chapter on one of President Donald Trump's boldest efforts to reshape November's elections — a plan that would have demanded a dramatic overhaul of the nation's mail voting processes on what most election officials agreed was an impossibly short timeline. WATCH: Analyzing the Supreme Court's mail-in voting decision and Trump's reaction But the case was just one example of the Republican president's numerous attempts to assert federal control over the upcoming midterms. Several others remain in various states of play, even as mail ballots have been sent out in at least three states and early voting starts in others this week. Recently, the Department of Justice ordered officials in more than two dozen states to preserve records from the 2024 election as part of a campaign to force them to turn over detailed voter data despite repeated court losses. And lacking the sensitive voter data the administration wants from many states, the Department of Homeland Security has launched its own probe to find noncitizen voters on state rolls, an effort that a federal whistleblower says is rushed, error-ridden and potentially violating state laws. Meanwhile, Trump has continued to falsely claim that mail ballots are corrupt, that noncitizens are abundant on voter lists and that Democratic election fraud is widespread. During the recent Republican convention, the president goaded his fans in a verbal pledge to "cheat like hell, like they do." In response to Monday's Supreme Court ruling, Trump lashed back at the justices, saying they lacked the "courage necessary to save our America." The Constitution gives the power to run elections to states, rather than to the federal government. Election officials have said they're prepared to run a safe, secure election even if Trump continues to fan the flames. Democratic groups have signaled they are building out contingency plans in case Trump sends armed federal officers to the polls or Republicans make other attempts to improperly interfere in the election, a high-stakes contest that will determine which party controls Congress next year. With his mail ballot reforms blocked for now, here's a look at Trump's other, ongoing efforts to reshape election procedures: Trump has pressured states to use a controversial federal voter lookup tool The president insists, contrary to reams of research, that large numbers of noncitizens are illegally voting around the country. In his second term in office, he has sought to use the might of the federal government to crack down on the issue, including through a massive overhaul of a federal voter eligibility database called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE. The SAVE program was created under an immigration law mandating that the Department of Homeland Security help federal, state and local agencies prevent government benefits from going to noncitizens. Trump last year directed changes to significantly expand its abilities for mass searches by election officials. Then, his administration sent letters and filed lawsuits to push states to run their sensitive voter data through the tool – a prospect some states have agreed to, but many have resisted to keep their residents' personal information secure. Since last year, at least 67 million registrations have been scanned through the program, but critics worry it could end up purging valid voters from the rolls. Some registrants have already been wrongly flagged. A federal judge in June barred the new version of the SAVE program, calling it an illegal violation of Americans' privacy. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and block that ruling with an emergency order. The Supreme Court has yet to weigh in on the case. Meanwhile, the federal government continues to push states to give up voter registration information that contains addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July warned that state officials could lose funding or face investigations if they failed to go along with Trump's election security demands. And the DOJ last week sent letters to 29 states and the District of Columbia ordering them to preserve 2024 election documents and advising them that they were "under investigation" and subject to ongoing litigation for their failure to give up the data. Numerous investigations have found that while noncitizens have occasionally appeared on voting rolls and cast ballots, it is extremely rare. DHS is conducting its own noncitizen voter investigation In a last-ditch effort to hunt for noncitizen voters without detailed data from all states, DHS in August ordered a group of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services staff to pivot to a full-time manual investigation of state voter rolls, according to a whistleblower's report released Monday. The anonymous federal whistleblower said federal employees are being directed to misrepresent themselves on the voter lookup tools in a way that likely violates state laws as they compare DHS-provided data with state records in an attempt to identify noncitizens who are illegally registered. ab0379b1500c.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/work-has-stopped-on-system-that-was-key-to-trump-effort-to-limit-mail-voting-usps-chief-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Work has stopped on system that was key to Trump effort to limit mail voting, USPS chief says Politics Sep 17, 2026 8:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The top official at the U.S. Postal Service said Thursday that the agency has stopped work on developing a controversial computer system that was central to President Donald Trump's effort to limit mail voting after the Supreme Court rejected his executive order this week. READ MORE: Trump's push to restrict mail ballots failed. Other efforts to reshape the midterms continue "There's an injunction so we're not doing anything," postmaster general David Steiner told The Associated Press in an interview. Steiner, a onetime chief executive of Waste Management, has spent most of the past year atop the postal service navigating political and financial challenges. He's pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a "liquidity crisis." And Trump's efforts to largely eradicate mail voting turned the postal service into an unlikely arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year's critical midterm elections, a role Steiner seemingly had little interest in playing. Unlike Trump, who was sharply critical of the Supreme Court decision and ridiculed some of the justices, Steiner offered no assessment of the court's action. Steiner also declined to take a position on Trump's policy, presenting himself as the leader of an "independent agency of the executive branch" whose influence over the president's order was limited to operational concerns. "I don't get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept," he said. "I looked at it more from the execution side." The postal service has asserted its independence in the past, including during a 2019 standoff when the first Trump administration sought to pressure the agency as the president was in a dispute with Amazon. Steiner said he wouldn't get into the "nuance" of that. But the pressure has grown so intense at points that it's fueled talk of whether Steiner might resign, a notion he denied. "There's no truth to that," he said. "I think I know the motivation behind it. I think it's somebody that would like to see me out of a job." Inserting the Postal Service into elections The executive order Trump signed in March directed several federal agencies to develop state citizenship lists. Those lists would have been delivered to an online portal at the Postal Service, which would have been allowed to send mail ballots only to voters who were cleared through the process. Steiner said he knew about the order about a month before it was unveiled but said his focus was largely on implementation, not the policy's merits. A whistleblower report released earlier this month by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., argued the system was hastily built and riddled with errors. Steiner said he read "portions" of the whistleblower report and acknowledged the obstacles associated with building such a massive platform quickly. Still, he said he had confidence in colleagues working on the project and had planned to unveil it around Sept. 15. "There's absolutely no doubt that we worked fast," he said. "My personal opinion is it was a monumental task and I'm very proud of our IT department for being able to do it that fast." In addition to the voter list, Trump's order would have required states to adopt a uniform envelope style that included barcodes, something states said would have been arduous so close to the election. Following the Supreme Court's ruling, a memo sent to all postal service employees Wednesday and obtained by the AP said the agency will "not be enforcing any of these new rules in the 2026 federal election." "First and foremost, for Election Mail it is business as usual," according to the memo. "We continue to follow established protocols, and we remain entirely focused on our core mission: delivering the mail safely and securely for voters and election officials across the country." Though the Supreme Court rejected Trump's executive order for this year's election, Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated he might rule in favor of the administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time. Steiner encourages voters to cast ballots early Steiner said the postal service would still encourage the use of envelopes and barcodes in future elections, which it has long recommended. He said such changes wouldn't be required but those who don't comply may have to pay more. "If you use the barcode in the envelope, we'll charge you a lower price," he said. "If you don't, we're going to charge you a higher price because it's harder for us to process." While the postal service isn't moving forward on Trump's order, there are still concerns about postmark delays that could have an impact on this year's elections. The number of ballots rejected for late postmarks has soared in the vote-by-mail states of Washington and Oregon, according to recently released data highlighting concerns about recent changes in postal service operations. Steiner said there were no plans to alter those operations and encouraged voters who use mail to get their ballots in early. "We say seven days," he said. "Everything is solved if people vote early." Space Force braces for stalled progress amid lack of full funding
Fiscal 2027 program starts are already on hold until December.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Space Force modernization efforts could slow if Congress doesn’t pass a full budget at the end of the year, the service’s leaders said.
“We're on this ramp-up, right, consistent with our overall strategy and the recognition that the space domain is a critical domain, in and of itself, but also for the joint force,” Erich Hernandez-Baquero, the Space Force’s top buyer, told reporters Tuesday. “Now we're going to run into [fiscal year 2027]—and you saw that our budget request was to continue on that—and this [continuing resolution] is definitely going to put the brakes on that for a time period.”
The Space Force has requested $71.1 billion for 2027, including $19.1 billion for procurement. But with little time remaining before fiscal 2027 begins on Oct. 1, Congress has passed stopgap legislation—a continuing resolution—to keep funding the Pentagon at 2026 levels through Dec. 11. The CR permits no new programs to begin.
“We certainly appreciate at least not being shut down. So…that's a good thing, but on the CR, it really does pace us at a time where we really need to go faster. So we are obviously encouraging Congress to do what they can to help support the president's budget on that,” Hernandez-Baquero said. “In the meantime, we'll just do what we always do: prioritize the things that will yield the most mission capability soonest, and make sure we're executing on those.”
Hernandez-Baquero, who was sworn into the chief space acquisition role last month, declined to specify which priorities could be most affected by a continuing resolution because things were “pre-decision at this point.”
Gen. Doug Schiess, the chief of space operations, said about 10 percent of the service’s programs could be slowed down due continuing resolution.
“About 90 percent of the programs we have are programs from last year—so we can still get after those,” but there’s a remaining 10 percent of programs that require full budget funding, Schiess said. “It's going to slow us down, and the threat is not slowing down.”
Amid a broader push for acquisition reform, Hernandez-Baquero said he’s focused on streamlining and speeding up military purchasing. And when it comes to technology initiatives, there will be a new senior leadership role dedicated to it.
The Air Force’s new program acquisition executives, or PAEs, are “establishing those pathways for onboarding new technology, but I'm just conscious that that by itself is not going to support drawing in the right technologies,” he said. “I want somebody that's focused—100 percent—on looking at the most promising tech and driving the prototyping initiatives that are going to help mature it to the level where a PAE can say, ‘Ah, it meets my criteria for this onboard path, and I can go do that’.”
That person is a technology portfolio executive, who “will have the most promising technology coming out of the [research and development] side, and…will work with industry to ensure that we have the right pathways to do that. Conceptually, there would be prototype efforts that get executed out of that to support the mission areas.”
The technology portfolio executive office already exists but the role hasn’t yet been filled, he said.
“When I designate a TPE, for example, that person is going to report directly to me and represent my authority when it comes to the technology transition,” Hernandez-Baquero said. “I cannot do this without the buy-in of the PAEs that are executing the mission areas, and so my charter to them is going to be not only to deliver on those missionaries, but be part of the enterprise team that's going to deliver on those cross-cutting capabilities.”

Air Force contemplates unmanned tankers
The technology isn’t yet available to give autonomy to very large aircraft—but it’s coming.
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—With an eye on the Navy’s progress toward an unmanned aerial tanker, Air Force planners are asking questions about their own future tanker fleet.
“Thinking beyond the current KC-46 buy and the program extension. Whatever that next tanker looks like—our advanced tanker system—it's got to be connected. It's got to be able to defend itself. But it begs the question: Does it need to be manned? Could it be optionally manned, or could it be autonomous, or is there a family of solutions maybe that would answer that question?” Lt. Gen. Daniel Tulley, who leads Air Mobility Command, told reporters at the Air, Space, & Cyber 2026 conference.
The Air Force is currently buying Boeing KC-46 Pegasus tankers and spent $12 million to explore buying a new tanker this year. But it zeroed out funding to continue those explorations in the 2027 budget request and is asking instead for $13 million for “advanced tanker systems.”
Tulley said the Navy’s work on the Boeing MQ-25 Stingray suggests that his own service might eventually not need manned tankers. The Navy announced on Thursday that the MQ-25, which first flew earlier this year, has received approval to enter low-rate production. The service also ordered three more aircraft, bringing its total to 14.
“I do not believe that it has to be manned, a future air-refueling solution,” he said. “But then, how do we, the U.S. Air Force, bring that to bear in scope, scale, and range?”
A drone tanker for the Air Force would need to be a very large aircraft with the capacity for fuel and the ability to fly for a long time. The KC-46, for example, can fly nearly 7,400 miles and carry more than a thousand tons of fuel. The MQ-25 can fly about 500 miles and carry up to 7.5 tons of fuel.
“An optionally manned or an unmanned tanker at the ranges we need it to operate at is a very large aircraft. And we're not yet to where we're employing fully autonomous large aircraft,” Tulley said.
“Just about any large aircraft these days made by Boeing can take itself off with very little help, can fly on a programmed route and pretty much land itself on autopilot, bring itself to a stop on the runway. But we don't employ it that way with a system that's controlling it and then taxiing it in and making it a part of a more effective, broader system.”
One maker of autonomous-aircraft control systems said the vision of autonomy for large aircraft was getting clearer. And while the technology isn’t there yet, there’s progress, said Matthew George, CEO of Merlin Labs.
“We’re the furthest along in the world on making that real—in our opinion,” said Matthew George, CEO of Merlin Labs. “So we're going to be implementing autonomy on the C-130J, which is the same general size class” as the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker.
“And the advantage with those aircraft is you can start to implement autonomy still with human crews aboard, and you can supplement those human crews in a way that's pretty helpful. That's a way that you can start to chip away at that without actually going fully to the unmanned tanker right away,” George said. “The goal is that the unmanned tanker is ready, and the autonomy ends up being ready at the same time.”
George agreed with Tulley’s point that many aircraft can somewhat fly themselves, but there are instances, such as emergency situations, when a human needs to make a decision.
“What's really hard is those edge cases and those emergencies—or those things where there are decisions to be made. So, for instance, if you're going to a destination and then there's weather in between, how do you get around the weather?” he said.
And beyond technology, there are policy challenges.
“None of this matters unless it's certified and safe. So for us, getting certification done is important, and that's what we're working really closely with the Air Force on this year,” George said. “We're taking that [autonomous pilot] brain and putting it onto the C-130J. And as far as we know, that's going to be the first time autonomy fully takes control of an operational U.S. Air Force aircraft.”
No date was provided for when that flight will occur, but the company’s technology completed a critical design review, George said.

69bdd3e58296.text: Violence has spread across the Middle East since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran. Qatar has spent months mediating between Iran and the U.S. while also being targeted by Iranian strikes. Nick Schifrin sat down with Dr. Majed al-Ansari, adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, to discuss regional tensions and whether there is a way back to negotiations. Amna Nawaz: Today, Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen traded new strikes. The fighting is just one example of violence that's spread across the region since the U.S. and Israel launched the war in Iran. Geoff Bennett: The country of Qatar has spent months mediating between Iran and the U.S. and Iran and the region while also being targeted by Iranian strikes. This week, Nick Schifrin sat down with a key adviser to Qatar's prime minister to discuss regional tensions and whether there is a way back to negotiations. Nick Schifrin: Thank you very much, Mr. Ansari. Thanks very much. Welcome to the "News Hour." Majed Al-Ansari, Adviser to Qatari Prime Minister: Thank you for having me. Nick Schifrin: You have been in the middle of negotiations this year between Iran and the United States. Qatar was largely confident about this when the MOU was signed. But, since then, we haven't seen any progress. Iran has maintained its choke hold over the Strait of Hormuz. From where you sit, is there a path back to U.S.-Iran negotiations or not? Majed Al-Ansari: You know, Nick, one thing we can't afford to do in the region right now is despair about the diplomatic solution. There is no way out of this unless it is a diplomatic solution. And, therefore, we have been working with all our partners 24/7. Our mediation teams have been running between each capital in the region trying to get it forward, and we won't give up. We will just continue doing it until we have a solution. Nick Schifrin: Negotiations is not just U.S.-Iran. It's also Iran-GCC. It's also the Gulf Cooperation Council. We were supposed to have a meeting earlier this week. And the regional officials I was talking to before this meeting was supposed to happen on Monday were saying Iran was asking for too much. Iran was asking for control or at least some kind of access of all ships going in and out of the strait in Iranian waters. Is Iran asking for too much? Majed Al-Ansari: Now, first of all, this is -- this was supposed to be an interim solution, not the new status quo. The new status quo cannot be to deal with the Strait of Hormuz, something that can be open or closed by any... (Crosstalk) Nick Schifrin: Meaning it needs to be open, period. Majed Al-Ansari: Exactly. We need to go back. It's a matter of international maritime law. It's where all the littoral states have the right to use the Strait of Hormuz openly and not creating a new status quo that would give any of the littoral states any power over the strait. Nick Schifrin: Reuters a few weeks ago reported that Qatar's liquefied natural gas exports, which, of course, count for a large share of Qatar's GDP, have dropped 96 percent since the U.S. and Israel launched this war. Firstly, is that accurate? And, secondly, how existential a threat is it to Qatar if this war continues, if the strait continues to be closed? Majed Al-Ansari: I won't come into the specific numbers. I will leave that to QatarEnergy and the people in our energy sector. I can tell you, of course, that all of our LNG used to go through the Strait of Hormuz. And Strait of Hormuz being closed basically means that no LNG is going through. Let me say it very clearly. The effects -- we have not yet to see the real effects on international economy of this crisis. We have yet to reach the tip of the iceberg. We are looking now... Nick Schifrin: Why do you say that? Majed Al-Ansari: Because the economic effects of this war is going to go on -- if it continues like this, going to go on and affect every other sector. We have already -- are already getting reports of reduced yields from crops in countries like Somalia and other countries in Asia, where this is an issue of famine. It's not an issue of luxury, right? I think it's an existential threat for all of us collectively in the international economy. And, of course, Qatar is heavy -- heavily dependent on the Strait of Hormuz. But let me say it also very clearly. Our economy is not fragile. Those who are living in Qatar, thankfully, other than the fact that missiles were being intercepted every other day, but when it comes to commodities, when it comes to security, when it comes to everyday needs, when it comes to salaries and the economic situation, nothing was affected. Nick Schifrin: Iran hit the Al Udeid Air Base, the largest air base across the region. Do you have faith that the United States can defend the U.S. Qatari base, one of the most important spots in Doha? Majed Al-Ansari: You know, the metric that we need to consider here is the fact that more than 95 percent of every projectile that was sent towards our countries was deterred through the work of the men and women in uniform, and it's not an easy an easy number to deal with. The -- our militaries proved their worth. The cooperation with the United States proved its worth. We see the coordination and the interoperability between our militaries and the U.S. military on all fronts when it comes to defending our countries. I think we have shown that we are not an easy pill to swallow. Nick Schifrin: But do you have faith that 95 percent can be repeated if there's another cycle of Iowa? Majed Al-Ansari: One hundred percent. I can tell you that our militaries are standing ready right now for any kind of escalation. Of course, we're working diplomatically to make sure that there is no other escalation. But you have to remember 40 percent of the attacks on Qatar, for example, were on energy facilities, right? 2a83846840e0.text: Professional wheelchair tennis players are competing for their countries this week in the World Team Cup at the U.S. Tennis Association’s National Campus in Orlando. It’s part of the 50th anniversary of the sport’s creation and comes at a time when popularity is growing. Amna Nawaz reports for our ongoing coverage of the culture of sport, part of our CANVAS series. Amna Nawaz: This week, professional wheelchair tennis players are competing for their countries, part of the World Team Cup at the U.S. Tennis Association's national campus in Orlando. It's all part of the 50th anniversary of the sport's creation and comes at a time when popularity is growing. I recently took a close-up look at the U.S. Open in Flushing Meadows, New York, for our ongoing coverage of the culture of sport, part of our Canvas series. All the agility, speed, and power of tennis supercharged on two wheels. (Cheering) Amna Nawaz: The sport of wheelchair tennis has come a very long way in just 50 years. Brad Parks, Wheelchair Tennis Co-Founder: Everybody, they're just so darn good. I mean, it's just so fantastic to see how it has progressed and improved over the years. Amna Nawaz: Brad Parks, who founded the sport back in 1976, has a lot to celebrate. Today, wheelchair tennis is in more top-tier professional tournaments than ever before, including all four Grand Slams. A player development pipeline is being built, and sponsorships and broadcast deals mean the fan base continues to grow. Parks himself never expected to be here after being paralyzed in a freestyle skiing accident at the age of 18. Brad Parks: Somebody came and told me about wheelchair basketball when I was in the hospital. And I'm thinking, well, if you play wheelchair basketball, why can't you play tennis? And tennis was on my mind because I wanted to be a better tennis player than I was. Sliding into a shot, hitting a ball, recovering, coming back around, that whole feeling of movement and everything else is really, really great. Amna Nawaz: Acceptance was built one match at a time. Brad Parks: When I was first injured, we would go to a tennis court, and sometimes the pro would come over and go, what are you guys doing? Everybody was always worried we were going to damage the courts. And they -- we weren't really even accepted. Nobody could believe that we were actually wheelchair athletes, that we were athletes. Amna Nawaz: The game differs slightly from the able-bodied sport. Players use the same courts, balls, and rackets, but they're allowed two bounces of the ball. The chair is considered part of the player's body. So the same rules that apply to the body in able-bodied tennis apply to the chair. Dana Mathewson was the first American woman to win a major wheelchair tennis title, the 2022 Wimbledon doubles championship. She retired in 2024 ranked number one in the U.S. and number seven in the world. She left the court at the top of her game, but found a new role just a few feet away, hosting and commentating. Seven years ago, when you last spoke to us, you had this to say. I want to put it back to you now and get your reaction. Dana Mathewson, Professional Wheelchair Tennis Player: That's crazy it was seven years ago. Amna Nawaz: I know. You said: "The more and more I get exposed to different things..." Dana Mathewson: The more that I realize that I can do with this disability and the things that it's afforded in my life. Amna Nawaz: "The more I actually feel really grateful for it." You still feel that way? Dana Mathewson: It's a hot take, isn't it? (Laughter) Dana Mathewson: Yes. I would be lying to you if I said that I woke up every day and I saw my chair and I was like, yay. Like, that's kind of -- that's a reach. But the sentiment of what I said definitely still rings true. I think that I can guarantee that, without a disability, I wouldn't have been a professional athlete. I wouldn't have represented my country. I wouldn't have set records within a sport. I wouldn't have got the opportunity to do things like this. I wouldn't get to be an advocate for a marginalized group of people. Amna Nawaz: Advocating for and mentoring the next generation of players. Did you have the kind of mentors when you were coming up that you're trying to be for them now? Dana Mathewson: I want to say yes, but the honest answer is not really. When I first started and I went to my first ever wheelchair tennis camp, there were a couple Paralympians that I met, and they made such an impact on me, but I only got to see them for that week. The little amount that I had was so impactful to me that, if I can do that for someone else, that that means more to me than any -- it sounds cliche, but, honestly, I mean it -- any Slams or anything like that. Amna Nawaz: Among the sport's new stars, Japan's Tokito Oda, a 20-year-old with multiple sponsors who's known as much for his sartorial flair as he is for his killer serve. Oda was just 17 when he won the French Open in 2023, becoming the youngest man ever to win a Grand Slam title. He's now number one in the world, and he came to talk to us as the sun went down after another victory. Wheelchair tennis has been around for longer than you have been alive. Tokito Oda, Professional Wheelchair Tennis Player: Yes. (Laughter) Amna Nawaz: Right? But it's still pretty young in terms of a sport. How did you first come to play this sport? Tokito Oda: Yes, when I was 10, I started tennis, but I got cancer when I was 9, and I was in like A hospital, like around the one year. During the hospital, I saw the singles playing. But he says, here in the U.S., it has a long way to go. Back home in Japan, he's used to much bigger crowds. f152572142e8.text: House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is staring at a scary political environment for Republicans and claiming to see something very different: a path to 225 seats . Why it matters: Republican leaders insist they can retain the majority, but only if they drive their voters to the polls by manufacturing the kind of voter enthusiasm Democrats are generating organically. "If we make it a contrast election, we win," Scalise told Axios in an interview Thursday. "We could get to 225. It would be a good night for us if we did, but it's possible," he said. "235 is not," he said. "You're literally doing coin tosses in a couple of seats." Between the lines: Asked if he saw any signs of a blue wave forming or the map expanding, Scalise said: "Not right now. No." Reality check: Republicans know that history — and many of the indicators heading into November — is working against them. "I know what history says, you know, but history's not on the ballot," Scalise said. Still, Democrats are turning out in primaries — and special elections — as if they're getting free gas cards for showing up. Democrats lead by nearly nine percentage points on the generic ballot. President Trump's approval rating is below 40%, according to the RealClearPolitics average . And Trump is underwater by a whopping 61 percentage points on inflation in a recent poll, an apparent record . Zoom in: Republicans are examining the map with a jeweler's loupe and insist the picture isn't as bleak in the pivotal battleground seats. "We're not looking at national polls; we go district by district," Scalise said. That means trench warfare in 35 seats, where Republicans say they have proven winners, plenty of money and new rules to spend it . "We've got 20 [seats] on our side that we're fighting to hold on to that are real competitive, and 15 [seats] that we have a real chance to flip," he said. "These are knock-down, drag-out fights." What we're hearing: The White House has long thought of the midterms as a "hate election." Scalise uses the more genteel term "contrast election." But before Republicans can dream about growing their majority, they need to fix their enthusiasm problem — and match the Democratic energy showing up in many of the preelection indicators. The GOP's midterm convention in Dallas last week was the first step. "If we are able to capitalize on that kind of enthusiasm and carry that momentum into November, then we'll have the same turnout as the other side, and we'll hold the majority," Scalise said. Now comes the road show: Congressional leaders — and the president — are hitting the campaign trail. In the next two weeks, Scalise will travel to 11 states to campaign for 16 Republicans — incumbents and challengers. The bottom line: The 225-seat scenario is Scalise's high-water mark. At another point in the interview, he suggested the majority could be smaller — closer to the 220–215 split Republicans won in 2024. "This isn't going to be a 10-seat majority, but it could be a six-seat majority."

7b7dca8cc811.text: President Trump told Axios Thursday that he's approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to restart massive attacks in an effort to bring the conflict to a close. "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me." Why it matters: Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments come ahead of a planned meeting Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action. If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need buy-in from his regional allies. The president has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon. Some U.S. officials warn that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal isn't reached by then. What he's saying: Trump made clear in the interview that he wants to use the meeting at the UN to hear directly from regional allies about the war's next steps. "I want to find out where they are and how they are doing. We have been very protective of them," Trump said. Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms. Driving the news: In early August, Trump held off on resuming major combat operations after Saudi Arabia and Qatar expressed concern that Iran would bomb Saudi oil and gas facilities in retaliation. Since then, Trump has taken a "low-key" approach : suspending negotiations with Iran, launching a new economic sanctions campaign , continuing a naval blockade on Iranian ports, and focusing the U.S. military on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and increasing oil flow to the global energy market. The U.S. military has significantly increased oil and gas tanker transit through the strait. But traffic is still below pre-war levels, and oil prices remain high. State of play: Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have ordered the military to maintain its level of forces in the Middle East until the end of the year, U.S. officials say, to remain ready for a potential return to full-scale combat. The officials say Trump needs to decide soon on the way forward, partly because the U.S. military can't stay in its current holding pattern much longer. "At some point, you have to decide what is the endgame," one of the officials said. Trump told Axios he's very satisfied that the naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting its oil. "Not one ship has gone to Iran since we started. They tried and we blew them up," he said. The president added that Iran is in direct contact with the U.S. and said the Iranians still want to reach a deal. The big picture: The White House has also been working on a post-war strategy that calls for a regional effort to contain Iran while expanding normalization of relations between Israel and its neighbors. While the plan is still in the early stages of drafting, it's intended to guide the U.S. approach in the Middle East after the Iran war ends and in the final two years of Trump's term. Two big events loom over the planning: the Oct. 27 election in Israel and the U.S. midterms in November. What to watch: When asked if he will meet with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in New York next week, Trump said, "I may."

Swedish pop star Zara Larsson has condemned the White House for using one of her most recognisable songs in a social media reel.
The clip used Larsson's Midnight Sun in a video appearing to show immigration enforcement raids. The song has since been removed from the post, but the video is still visible on the White House's TikTok feed.
The video is captioned "never ending deportations", riffing on Larsson's lyrics "never-ending midnight sun".
In a three-minute reaction video posted on social media, Larsson described the clip as "dehumanising", joining a growing list of singers, including Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande, who have told the Trump administration to not use their music.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
The reel splices together multiple videos of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, as well as other US law enforcement personnel, handcuffing men and putting them into vehicles.
Larsson reposted part of the original clip, which then cuts to a selfie video of her using her fingers to hold an 'L' shape against her forehead.
In the reaction video that has already clocked up more than 4.2 million views on TikTok, she tells her followers the White House video is "so dehumanising".
Larsson continues: "These people in this video â they're real people."
"The vast majority of these people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs and they're just trying to have a better future".
"It's so crazy how everything is so memefied and so 'ha-ha-ha'," she says, accusing the White House of using her song to sow "division", despite the lyrics reflecting a connection between people and nature, according to Larsson.
Earlier this year, Larsson condemned a video of President Donald Trump dancing at various events overlayed with her hit Lush Life.
White House social media accounts have been forced to remove various songs from their feed following interventions from artists.
Taylor Swift's seasonal track August disappeared from a reel shared by the Trump administration in August, while one of Olivia Rodrigo's songs vanished from a video after the singer condemned its use for what she called "hateful propaganda".
Sabrina Carpenter and Ariana Grande have also warned the Trump administration in separate incidents to not use their music in social media content after the White House posted videos featuring their songs.

A US federal judge has ordered the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before any "demolition" occurs to the Kennedy Center, as President Donald Trump warns the Washington DC performing arts venue could be "ripped down".
The order comes after Trump was photographed onboard Air Force One looking at a poster with a headline that appeared to tout the demolition of the site.
On Thursday, US District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered a detailed report of the centre's "temporary closure" for emergency repairs, and for written notice of any change to the scope of the project.
In May, Cooper ordered the removal of Trump's name from the building.
In a document filed to court on Thursday before the judge's ruling, Kennedy Center executive director, Matt Floca, said the temporary closure was to repair safety hazards and would last seven days, "unless extended".
On Tuesday, the Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted - for the third time since February - to close the venue down for two years.
Trump then took to Truth Social to write that the board, which is chaired by Trump and includes his cabinet members and allies, voted "almost unanimously" to close the venue "for safety reasons".
He has argued that the venue is badly in need of repair, and that by adding his name to the building it will be able to secure renovation funding.
"I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," he told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Wednesday. "It'll end up being ripped down."
On Wednesday, Trump was photographed through a window of Air Force One looking at a poster with the words "Kennedy Center DEMOLIS" visible.
On Thursday, Cooper ordered the Trump administration to provide at least 30 days' notice ahead of any change in construction plans.
That order came after congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio Kennedy Center board member, asked the judge to make "crystal clear that its order prohibits demolishing the structure".
Beatty, a Democrat, had previously sued to halt changes to the Kennedy Center, and to strip Trump's name from the building.
Congress established the centre as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in 1963.
Some critics argue that congressional action is required to make changes to the building, and that the need for renovations is exaggerated.

- Published
The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.
Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.
All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.
"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".
Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.
Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.
He argued that "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum" and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.
Still, the backlash has come from all sides.
Some are upset Sheeran's tour is continuing without all the listed acts and they want refunds. It's no longer the show they paid for, they said.
Given, who is from Northern Ireland, said he's felt in two minds over the tickets he has on Saturday to see the show in Philadelphia.
It will mark Sheeran's first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled.
Given said he's felt that Macklemore was treated "very, very wrong" and thought Sheeran was not being transparent with fans.
"[Sheeran] said he was in support of Ukraine when the Ukraine-Russia war started," said Given.
"You can't just say now suddenly, 'I'm not political.'"
But he explained the poignant connection he's felt to Sheeran's music that has drawn him to Saturday's show.
The singer's hit Thinking Out Loud was the first dance at Given's wedding.
"When she danced," Given, 52, said, recalling the moment with his bride, "the first words of the song were, 'When your legs don't work like they used to before.'"
His wife, Kellie, had been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and could barely walk. She died four years later, in 2024.
Given said if it wasn't for "that connection, I would absolutely" not be attending, but "I'm probably leaning towards going".
Fellow fan Patti Ann has felt less conflicted over the backlash and instead said Sheeran was in a "no-win situation".
"I back [Sheeran] 100% for his decision," she said. "I feel like he has an obligation and a contract with his venues, and sometimes, financially, you can't get out of those types of things."
Ann, who has been a Sheeran fan for years, said she thinks a concert venue is not the place for politics.
Believe what you want, she said, "just don't press it on me".
She still plans to attend his show in Atlanta, Georgia, in October.
Matt Jaye, a Jewish-American from Florida, said he was outraged watching Macklemore's comments on a New Jersey stage earlier this month in support of Palestine.
He contacted Ticketmaster and asked for a refund for tickets he has to Sheeran's November show in Tampa, Florida.
His request was denied, which he said was "pretty upsetting".
His mood changed, though, after Macklemore was removed from Sheeran's line-up.
"I'm not in favour of a one-sided presentation of things from an artist," Jaye, 48, said. "That's not why I'm going to the concert."
Jaye said he believed Sheeran bore some culpability for Macklemore's pro-Palestinian protest.
"If [Sheeran's] saying that he's apolitical, I would expect him to maintain those same standards for the artists that he's bringing on," he said.
"I don't think he handled it in the best way possible."
He added that he would have liked Sheeran to issue an apology to the Jewish community for making part of his audience "very uncomfortable".
Some fans are worried what will become of the tour by the time Sheeran is set to play in their city.
Heather Park, who has tickets this weekend, said she's worried some shows might be cancelled.
"My main thing was to go see Ed Sheeran," she said. "Macklemore was just a bonus."
While Park, 49, believes Macklemore's ouster was unfair and a violation of free speech, she said she's mostly unbothered by the drama and prefers to separate the artist from the art.
"I still like the music," she says.

395bb8863dd8.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-rfk-jr-speaks-at-conference-for-anti-vaccine-group-he-founded Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: RFK Jr. speaks at conference for anti-vaccine group he founded Politics Sep 17, 2026 8:34 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House. Watch Kennedy's remarks in the video player above. It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy. "Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago," he said. The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration. Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge. Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations. WATCH: Pediatrician says RFK Jr. sowing doubt about measles-associated deaths That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November's midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels. Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children's Health Defense for years. He served as the group's chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking. Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode. "We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years," Kennedy told the group. Mary Holland, the CEO of Children's Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as "Bobby" and said the group has "gratitude beyond words" to the HHS secretary for "recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations." Kennedy's appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades. Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy. Shapiro blasted Kennedy's appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy "chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America." Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, "yet he couldn't bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust." A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy's appearance at the event. Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted. Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism. Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy's decision to give a speech at the conference shows "the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS." "With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside." Stobbe contributed from New York. In a border city stadium, US NFL fans sing Canada anthem with gusto
At a match between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions football teams in Orchard Park, New York, both the American and Canadian national anthems played.
The Bills chose to honour their Canadian fans amid rising tensions between the US and Canada.
President Donald Trump, who is currently locked in an escalating tariff tussle with Ottawa, has, on a number of occasions, declared his ambition to make Canada the 51st American state. He blames Canada for taking advantage of the US through unfair trade practices and trade deficits.
The BBC's Robin Levinson-King spoke to fans ahead of kickoff about the symbolism of the anthem being played.

See tiny organisms on show in microscopic video competition
Nikon's annual Small World In Motion competition is open to anyone around the world with an interest in film or time-lapse photography through a microscope.
This year's winning video was magnified to 100 times in size, and featured tiny hair-like structures, called cilia, in the airways of a child with a rare genetic disease.
It was submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, who used a series of complicated light waves to illuminate different parts of the sample in colour.
Runners up in the competition included videos of a roundworm encountering a single-celled organism and microscopic jellyfish larvae suspended in droplets of water. Clips of bioluminescent algae and a tiny sea slug were among the highly commended.

The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump's nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after a Republican senator joined Democrats in opposing his confirmation.
Richard Schroyer was serving as a senior aide to the secretary of Homeland Security when Trump picked him to lead the immigration enforcement agency in June.
The White House withdrew his nomination on Thursday in a short memo, which did not explain the decision. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
Republican Sen Rand Paul had stalled the nomination as he pressed for more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis in January.
Schroyer had worked with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol for 29 years, and also served in the US Marines. He is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department oversees ICE and other immigration and border agencies. His selection by Trump was seen as a surprise given his lack of experience overseeing such a large law enforcement agency.
The position is one of many that needs to be confirmed by the US Senate. Schroyer's nomination did not manage to make it to a full Senate vote and had stalled in the Senate's Homeland Security committee.
ICE has not been led by Senate-confirmed leader since 2017 and instead has had a host of temporary chiefs. It is currently led by David Venturella, a former private prison executive, after Todd Lyon announced his departure from the top job in April.
The withdrawal on Thursday marks a defeat for Trump and Mullin, as the White House continues Trump's campaign pledge to lead the largest deportation effort in US history.
Paul, who serves as chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings.
National protests took place earlier this year following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.
Both US citizens, the two were protesting when they were fatally shot in separate confrontations with ICE agents in January.
One of the promises that helped Trump take the White House in 2024 - cracking down on illegal immigration - has now divided voters going into the congressional midterm elections less than two months from now.
At the same time, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican from Florida, is warning that the crackdown could cause many of the Hispanic voters who supported him to turn their backs on the party when they go to the polls in November.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," she said in an advertisement filmed outside the White House that was released on Thursday. "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

The Royal Observatory Greenwich has announced the winner of its Astronomy Photographer of the Year competition for an image of the Shark Nebula.
The dark nebula is made from interstellar dust dense enough to block starlight and is 650 light years away.
Steve Marsh, one of the judges and art editor at BBC Sky at Night Magazine, said the image by Ali Alobaidly showed "flawless presentation, pin-sharp details and dynamic contrast".
He added: "The Shark Nebula is already a striking object, but when it is resolved to the point where even detail-rich distant galaxies can be seen through it, you know you're looking at something very special."
Alobaidly, who won Â£10,000 for winning the competition overall, said he hoped to use his photographs "to make astronomy more accessible, engaging and meaningful through science communication and education", and described the award as a "tremendous honour".
For the 2026 competition there were almost 4,000 entries from 66 countries.
Alobaidly's entry, taken in Kuwait, was entered in the Stars and Nebulae category.
Nikolaos Strimpoulis, 15, won for ZWO Young Astronomy Photographer of the Year for his image Mineral Moon, taken in Palaio Faliro, Athens, Greece.
The close-up image of the Moon's surface includes dark areas known as maria and bright areas known as the highlands.
The orange and blue colours on the lunar surface are caused by iron and titanium deposits and it was for that reason that the image was given its title.
Marsh said: "Many of us start our astrophotography journey with the Moon â some of us stay there forever! But often we don't delve deep into the subtle colours of its mineral deposits until much later. This amazing young astrophotographer has achieved perfectly developed colouring in this photograph."
Dr Greg Brown, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich, said the entries from the 18th year of the competition demonstrated "skill and innovation" coupled with improvements in technology.
See more of the winning images:
An exhibition of the winning and highly commended images will be on display at the National Maritime Museum, London from 18 September.

A wildlife charity fears it could lose a funding grant after a burst pipe prevented vital conservation work.
It is the fourth time Long Mead Local Wildlife Site, at Swinford in Oxfordshire, has been flooded because of a mains failure.
Although the meadow by the River Thames naturally floods in the winter, standing water at this time of year can cause damage to the rare habitat.
Thames Water said the latest leak had been fixed and it remained committed to protecting local wildlife sites.
"It's already starting to stagnate, so that's serious," said Catriona Bass, director of the Long Mead Foundation.
"Floodplain meadows are used to flooding in winter when the plants are dormant.
"These meadows don't flood typically in summer and when they do it's a disaster because the plants are growing - so it kills off the plants."
The site is central to a restoration programme that aims to boost this type of specialist habitat across the county.
There are only four square miles in total of floodplain meadow in the country - the equivalent in size to Heathrow Airport.
The rare habitat is home to deep-rooting wild flowers and grasses like great burnet and devil's-bit scabious.
Long Mead meadow acts as a donor site where seeds are gathered to help restore other similar habitats around Oxfordshire.
Volunteers have hand-grown more than 11,500 individual specialist plants.
The latest flooding was discovered on the day that restoration works were due to start after the last incident.
Conservationists have said they are worried a grant the charity had secured is at risk if the work is not completed in time.
"We planned on the 1st September to do this massive restoration project to deal with the previous floods and now we're not going to be able to," Bass said.
A Thames Water spokesperson said: "We are sorry for the disruption caused and remain committed to protecting local wildlife sites.
"We have repaired a recent burst in Bettys Meadow and traffic management equipment is due to be removed shortly.
"The repair took longer than anticipated due to heavy rainfall and the volume of water, which meant our engineers were unable to safely access and repair the pipework until conditions improved.
"We will continue to assess the condition of the water main and review any further measures needed to help safeguard the area in the future."

Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's â and continent's â richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery â representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (Â£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" â a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; Â£12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks â shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Three people have been killed and eight injured in a shooting at a high school in Banga in the province of Mindanao, southern Philippines.
Two of the victims were 14-year-old students, Banga mayor Albert Palencia told the BBC. The gunman, 16, is among the dead, he said, while four of those injured are in a critical condition.
The incident happened on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
The Department of Education said in a statement that it was "deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident".
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education ministry said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told the Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, the Banga disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.

OpenAIâs Sam Altman will attend the Sept. 24 state dinner that President Donald Trump is hosting for Xi, Semafor has confirmed, and Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang and Appleâs Tim Cook are reportedly attending, too.
