- Published
Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.
Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.
Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.
Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned, but it is believed that more than 13,000 remain in the enclave.
The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.
During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.
More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.
The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.
The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.
Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker".
"The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.
The opposition also accused SÃ¡nchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. SÃ¡nchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.
Ester MuÃ±oz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".
The incident has also created diplomatic headaches for SÃ¡nchez.
The prime minister is at odds with Italy, with the two countries earlier this week extending temporary border controls imposed on each other. He is also trying to maintain his bilateral relationship with Morocco.
The influx of migrants in late July came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.
After the ruling, some social media accounts spread misinformation and offered to help migrants cross the Spanish border for hundreds of pounds.
Thousands of people then flooded across the border fence and swam around the ocean barriers. At least 100 people died during the crossing, according to local authorities.

c7e0cbe09923.text:
- Published
The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children.
"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating.
Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window.
To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition.
The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder.
Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings.
"I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday.
"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented."
Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind.
"We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said.
The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster".
She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."
Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".
But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial.
The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations.
Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday.
In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began.
He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them".
During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis.
Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.
A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children.
However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions, while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association.
Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility.
The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial.
Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial.
He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy.
He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset."
The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts.

d382c0aab809.text:
America’s centuries-old conflict with wolves took another turn earlier this month when President Donald Trump ordered the animals be stripped of federal protections across several U.S. states, claiming the action will provide economic relief for ranchers.
Alongside a suite of regulatory reviews to “promote financial viability” for ranchers, Trump ordered the Interior secretary to begin the process of removing gray and Mexican wolves from the endangered species list, and directed the Agriculture secretary to encourage states to make it easier for ranchers to shoot wolves.
But an Inside Climate News review of state and federal data indicates that wolves account for a tiny percentage of total cattle deaths. And while some individual ranchers in areas with intense wolf-livestock conflicts may face significant losses, other factors, like climate-fueled droughts, high fuel prices, persistent inflation and the Trump administration’s decision to pause levies on hundreds of thousands of pounds of beef imports are likely applying far more economic pressure to the industry than wolves.
A wolf pack’s presence near a ranch can impact a rancher’s bottom line, even if the animals don’t kill any cattle. But the Trump administration’s focus on delisting the predators and reducing their numbers with lethal management is misdirected, experts say.
“Wolves are going to be around, listed or not listed, because they are tough. So I was surprised the White House focused so heavily on wolves’ legal status when there is so much else federal agencies could do to reduce conflict,” said Arthur Middleton, a professor of wildlife management at the University of California, Berkeley. “The Agriculture and Interior departments could tweak and expand their technical and financial assistance for affected ranchers almost overnight. Focusing just on [wolves’] legal status is a big missed opportunity, and in my view, it doesn’t actually help ranchers that much.”
Gray wolves are federally protected in all lower 48 states except Idaho, Montana and Wyoming, where they have been removed from the endangered species list and are under state management. Gray wolves also live in California, Michigan, Minnesota, Oregon, Washington and Wisconsin.
In 2023, Colorado reintroduced gray wolves within its borders, a population managed by the state.
Mexican wolves have federal protection across their habitat in Arizona and New Mexico.
Inside Climate News reviewed data on cattle confirmed lost to predation by gray wolves published by states across the West. In 2025, those numbers varied from just nine animals in Washington to 155 killed or injured in California, a number that rose to 197 when including probable wolf attacks in that state. The true numbers are likely somewhat higher, as some wolf kills are never discovered and some carcasses are so decomposed that it’s impossible to determine how the animals died.
Still, wolf predation represents a tiny percentage of all cattle losses in states that are home to the predators. In Oregon, confirmed losses to wolves accounted for just 0.2 percent of total statewide cattle losses and deaths recorded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture in 2025—the highest proportion across the six Western states for which Inside Climate News found published 2025 data on gray wolf predation on cattle.
Most cattle are raised in circumstances in which they will never encounter a wolf, so those statewide figures mask problems faced by the worst-affected ranchers. Where free-ranging cattle overlap with wolf packs, the percentage of losses attributable to wolves will be much higher. But even in the counties with the most severe wolf-livestock conflicts, total losses to wolves are still relatively small.
Across the six California counties with confirmed losses to wolves in 2025, the total cattle population stood at 176,600 at the start of 2024—the most recent data available. Sierra County, with 38 cattle confirmed lost to wolves in 2025, had 6,600 head of cattle the previous year, giving it the highest proportional predation losses. That’s still well under 1 percent.

Beef is “the predominant dietary item of wolves in Northeastern California during the summer months,” the authors wrote, though they noted that their work showed what wolves are eating, but not necessarily what they are killing—wolves could also be scavenging the carcasses of cattle that died from other causes.

“The cattle market is sort of like the stock market,” Magagna said. “It reacts as much to rhetoric as it does to reality sometimes.”

French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified.
In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had called on the French government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat.
He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response".
A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank.
"In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said.
"The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."
Macron added that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.
He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission.
"In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said.

A honeycomb-shaped pattern in marine sediments has befuddled scientists for more than 150 years, but a new study points to a potential culprit.
The formations, known as Paleodictyon, are probably burrows created by arthropods, possibly a crustacean subgroup that includes the roly-poly, researchers report August 12 in Earth-Science Reviews. The work challenges previous hypotheses about Paleodictyon, particularly that they were created by wormlike creatures.
“Our study addresses one of paleontology’s most enduring enigmas,” says Andrea Baucon, a paleontologist at the University of Cagliari in Sardinia, Italy.
Renaissance artist and inventor Leonardo da Vinci probably sketched Paleodictyon’s characteristic forms after seeing them in ancient marine sediments now on dry land. The patterns appear on seafloors today, too. In the 19th and 20th centuries, scientists attributed the patterns not only to worms, but also to chemical processes and fossilized algae, among other things.
Baucon surmised that arthropods would be a more likely cause. So he and his colleagues tested the hypothesis by investigating prior research and making observations on fossils both previously and newly discovered. Among these was a 530-million-year-old Paleodictyon — one of the oldest specimens known — that they discovered in a quarry near Torre de Moncorvo, Portugal.
They conclude that digging Paleodictyon’s sharp corners would be impossible for soft-bodied, wormlike creatures, which can only burrow where the ground is weak. In contrast, arthropods’ rigid exoskeletons and jointed appendages are well-suited to the task.
Creating such a precise hexagonal network takes mobility and cognitive skills including efficient burrowing and spatial awareness, which align with known arthropod abilities, the team concludes. Furthermore, Baucon says, Paleodictyon appears in the fossil record at roughly the same time as the earliest fossil evidence of arthropods, in the early Cambrian Period, around 530 million years ago. This coincidence in timing is not proof, Baucon says, but it is consistent with the team’s hypothesis.
Stephen Hasiotis, a geologist at the University of Kansas in Lawrence who was not involved in the study, isn’t sure arthropods are the sole creators. “Without smoking gun evidence” from across geologic time and the various marine environments where the mysterious honeycombs have been found, Hasiotis says, there is still the chance that other living things, including segmented worms, created formations past and present. Nevertheless, he says, the team’s hypothesis will doubtlessly push Paleodictyon aficionados “back onto the trail of whodunit and why.”
Baucon and his colleagues suggest that researchers could create Paleodictyon observatories to catch itsmakers in action on ocean floors. “Technologies such as artificial intelligence could help us automate the search for the creator of this mysterious structure,” he says.

One of the hottest horror directors on the planet adapting the world's most popular scary video game series?
On paper Zach Cregger and Resident Evil are the perfect unholy alliance.
The film-maker was widely praised for his original, imaginative work on horror hits Weapons and Barbarian and is a long-time fan of the video game series.
But in the lead-up to the filmâs release, Creggerâs spent a lot of time defending himself against complaints heâs cashing in on the Resident Evil name.
Speaking to BBC Newsbeat, the director says he was "not prepared" for what came his way.
First launched in 1996 on the original Sony PlayStation by Japanese developer Capcom, Resident Evil was a sensation.
Rather than casting players as super-powered characters, as was the case with most video games in the 90s, it forced them to survive with limited resources.
Thanks to smart reinventions and remakes, the series has managed to stay relevant, selling a total of 213 million copies since its debut.
Some of its characters are among the most well-known in video games, and there are whole communities dedicated to discussing the lore of their universe.
Cregger's Resident Evil follows the story of Bryan, an original character played by Austin Abrams who worked with the director on Weapons.
He's a courier who agrees to deliver a package to a hospital in Raccoon City - a key location from the games.
As Bryan makes his way to the drop-off, it becomes apparent he is caught in the middle of some sort of viral outbreak, with the infected becoming monstrous creatures.
When the first trailer appeared online, many users swamped comment sections to complain about what they'd seen.
Where were the beloved characters? The familiar monsters?
Cregger says he had little interest in simply retelling the story of the Resident Evil games, but that didn't seem to calm some fans.
"I think I was naive," he says.
"I think I was expecting people to be excited to see a Resident Evil movie that felt in the spirit of the games.
"What I was trying to do is make a movie that really honoured the experience of playing them."
According to most reviews, Cregger has achieved what he set out to do.
In its three-star review, NME , externalasked whether it was "the first great horror movie game adaptation".
"For a large chunk of the film's runtime, the answer is a resounding yes," wrote reviewer Jordan Bassett, who said Bryan's encounters become repetitive as the film wears on.
Doug Jamieson, of The Jam Report, external, awarded four stars and said Cregger "understands adaptation as translation rather than imitation".
In an eight out of 10 review, Looper, external critic Alastair Ryder wrote: "Zach Cregger has done the best job I've seen of translating the experience of playing a video game and making it feel cinematic."
The verdict from fans remains to be seen, but Resident Evil looks to be on track to have a successful opening weekend at the box office.
It follows recent video game adaptations such as the Minecraft and Super Mario Bros films, which were poorly reviewed but hugely popular.
This isn't the first adaptation of Resident Evil, which was brought to cinema screens in 2002 - the first of six films overseen by writer-director Paul WS Anderson.
His wife, Milla Jovovich, starred in each one, and while they have grown a cult following they were never a hit with critics.
A 2021 "reboot" heavily based on the games and a 2022 Netflix series also failed to impress.
The live-action rights to Resident Evil are owned by German production company Constantin Film - a fact fans have blamed for the perceived low quality of previous adaptations.
Reports online suggest the company's agreement with Capcom prevents Constantin from setting its films in the same timeline as the games.
Cregger told Newsbeat he'd had no contact with the game developer while working on the film.
"Nobody from Capcom ever reached out to me, ever, in any way," he said.
Constantin Film declined to comment, but BBC Newsbeat has been told there was co-ordination between the developer and the film's producers behind the scenes.
Cregger says it's "probably" impossible to please everyone, but it was never his intention to recreate the game on-screen.
"If I had delivered a faithful retelling of one of the stories in the games, I feel like those people would probably be upset with me for that too," he says.
"Because I would have messed it up somehow, inevitably.
"So all I can do is just tell the story that I think is going to be the very best story.
"If somebody's going to have a problem that it doesn't do exactly what they had in their mind of what a Resident Evil movie is, I can't say anything to that."

7d4621a4ce38.text: By — Nasser Karimi, Associated Press Nasser Karimi, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Lee Keath, Associated Press Lee Keath, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/iranians-rally-by-the-hundreds-of-thousands-in-biggest-show-of-defiance-since-war-began Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iranians rally by the hundreds of thousands in biggest show of defiance since war began World Sep 18, 2026 10:25 AM EDT CAIRO (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February. Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and new U.S. sanctions. On Friday, it claimed another attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway it has sought to control since the start of the war. WATCH: How nearly 7 months of war have changed daily life in Iran Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered. For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and the Basij militia, which has played a key role in quashing anti-government protests. Rally seeks to project strength under U.S. pressure Tehran's Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets. The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb, declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for "full-fledged defense" and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon. The new trainees will make a "nightmare" for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march. WATCH: Qatari spokesman on regional war and the path back to U.S.-Iran talks Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel." "I am here to tell (U.S. President Donald) Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there." The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns. Iran says it attacked another tanker in the Strait of Hormuz The Guard displayed drones that have been used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran's attacks and threats have severely affected the Gulf region's shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world. WATCH: Iran-backed Houthis seize island at entrance to Red Sea, threatening Saudi oil exports Iran said it had attacked a Togo-flagged oil tanker, the Trend, for what it called an "illegal attempt" to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the state broadcaster reported. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a tanker was hit by a projectile, sparking a fire on board that was extinguished. The UKMTO in a separate update said ship transits facilitated by the U.S. military off Oman have averaged 24 a day over the past week but overall traffic remains about 90% lower than before the war. Iran's new volunteers could help suppress future dissent Friday's events also suggested that hard-liners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy. In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained. In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran — which has a total population of some 90 million — had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy. The Associated Press could not independently confirm that. Karimi reported from Tehran, Iran, and Anna from Jerusalem. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 08df197c5f78.text: By — Michelle Chapman, Associated Press Michelle Chapman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/warren-buffett-steps-down-as-berkshire-hathaway-chairman-after-holding-the-post-since-1970 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman, after holding the post since 1970 Nation Sep 18, 2026 10:01 AM EDT Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway after serving in the role at the $1 trillion conglomerate for more than 50 years. Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately, the company said Friday. His son, Howard, will become Berkshire Hathaway's new chairman, part of a long-planned succession. Howard Buffett has been on the Berkshire Hathaway board since 1993. WATCH: News Wrap: Warren Buffett warns against U.S. using trade as a weapon Warren Buffett, known by a legion of financial market followers as the Oracle of Omaha, will remain a director. He has been Berkshire Hathaway's chairman since 1970. Greg Abel took over for Buffett as the CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate at the start of this year, even though Buffett remains one of the most influential investors in the world. WATCH: America should stand for more than just wealth, says Warren Buffett "I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. That is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next." Buffett said that he is confident with Abel and his son Howard leading Berkshire Hathaway. WATCH: Billionaire Warren Buffett says GOP health reform bills are relief for the rich "Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," he said. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against." Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, said Buffett took a deliberate approach to Berkshire Hathaway's succession plans and has carried out the transition step by step. "Buffett seems to have understood that succeeding him wasn't just about finding another extraordinary leader," he said. "It was about building a structure that could preserve what makes Berkshire different long after he has stepped away. The test moving forward will be whether Abel and Howard can honor that legacy while still giving Berkshire room to adapt to a market that looks very different from the one Buffett mastered." Buffett's fortune has been amassed through Berkshire Hathaway stock. The company, which was a New England textile firm that was built into an investing conglomerate and an icon of Wall Street. In 2024, Berkshire Hathaway became one of the first non-tech companies valued at more than $1 trillion. Buffett, a longtime philanthropist, has given away roughly $66 billion worth of stock since 2006. WATCH: How Warren Buffett's fortune is going directly to those in need Buffett's take on finance has created its own gravitational pull. When Berkshire Hathaway reveals the stocks that the company has acquired or sold in public disclosures, it can shake markets. During his time as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, the company nearly doubled the returns of the S&P 500, with a 19.9% compounded annual growth rate compared with the index's 10.4% gain. READ MORE: Some of Warren Buffett's best and worst investments in his 60 years at Berkshire Hathaway "Warren's impact on Berkshire and its owners is without parallel in the history of American business," Abel said in a prepared statement. "The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian." Shares of Berkshire Hathaway pointed lower before the opening bell Friday. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Some senators from both parties say they were left deeply unsettled Thursday after the Pentagon's top policy adviser, Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby, failed to provide an expected update on the Trump administration's National Defense Strategy at a classified briefing. The lawmakers also say they were unsatisfied with Colby's answers to questions ranging from inquiries about the Iran war to growing concerns that President Donald Trump could deploy troops to polling places during November's midterm congressional elections. Colby acknowledged that discussions about deploying the National Guard were taking place. Sen. Jacky Rosen, a Nevada Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Colby "was not forthcoming" and "did not really address our concerns or issues." Sen. Colby, who has supporters and detractors on Capitol Hill, was expected to provide a required briefing on the National Defense Strategy, a comprehensive document that provides guidance for the military. Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said he was able to ask about the strategy for the Iran war in Iran and the decision-making that has left the U.S. with what he described as a "munitions deficit." Experts say military contractors will need about three years to replenish stockpiles of certain advanced weapons, such as defensive missile interceptors. "You walk out with more questions than when you went in, and for me, that was the case today," Kelly said. He told senators that he had heard about some of those discussions taking place but that he wasn't leading on the issue. READ MORE: U.S. has no plans to send troops to the polls in November, Gen. Caine says "Never once said 'yes' or 'no,'" Cramer said. The idea of deploying troops has been gaining attention as the midterms draw closer. Sen. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., called it a "constructive, substantive" briefing that "answered all my questions." Asked if he was satisfied with the briefing, Sen. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky. ) announced Thursday they've secured commitments for the 218 signatures needed to force another vote the release of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein . The big picture: Answers about the disgraced financier and his web of wealthy connections have continued to haunt the administration, with Attorney General Todd Blanche now facing the threat of contempt proceedings over the Epstein files. This is the bipartisan duo's second push in less than a year after they forced their first Epstein transparency bill through Congress, which the president signed after initially opposing the effort. Driving the news: " Thomas Massie and I have defied history for a second time," Khanna said in a video posted to social media late Thursday afternoon. His post read that the pair had secured commitments for 218 votes on their discharge petition, including from three Republicans: Reps. Ralph Norman (R-S.C), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.). Two Democrats were sick, he added, but will sign the day the House returns. Massie also posted that he and his partner across the aisle would have enough names once lawmakers are back from a lengthy recess. Friction point: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dumped fuel on the fire blazing between him and Massie by again sending the House home early this week, Axios' Kate Santaliz reports. The more than six-week recess will also delay Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Johnson's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What's inside: Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II in July to strengthen enforcement of last year's law. It would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records. The bill would also require the attorney general provide certain unredacted documents to victims upon request. Flashback: The House voted nearly unanimously on the first transparency act last year. The DOJ released millions of pages related to Epstein — though the information drop faced criticism for puzzling redactions and allegations of withheld files . The bottom line: Massie and Khanna's victory could renew one of the most disruptive Hill fights of the president's second term — but not until after the critical midterm election. Khanna's post read, "We will not rest until the Epstein abusers are held accountable and there is justice." Go deeper: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back

The Scene
A prominent researcher is warning the world is on the verge of a massive transformation thanks to the emergence of a new technology that could drastically benefit society or cause massive destruction. No one quite understands how it works, or whether governments should step in.
Itâs 1941 in Omaha, Nebraska, where the physicist Arthur H. Compton is giving a lecture about how the possibilities of sub-atomic energy are âso breathtaking that even those who know most about it are somewhat uncertain, and a little awed, about it,â according to a writeup of the event in The Lincoln Evening Journal.
While not a perfect allegory, a review of newspaper archives from the early 1900s shows some striking parallels between the early days of atomic energy â which would later be called nuclear energy â and the public discussion around the danger of extinction from AI today. Just like there are today, there were doomers and skeptics, utopian boosters and scientists pleading for calm.
The look back shows the familiar societal cycle around powerful technology, spanning excitement, anxiety, and dread. But the past is also a warning to todayâs AI executives and government leaders that it shouldnât take mass destruction to force a consensus on human safety.
The View From 1919
In 1919, Sir Oliver Lodge, a prominent British physicist, told a British scientific society that thereâs âenough atomic energy in an ounce of matter to destroy a continent,â per an editorial in a local Iowa paper, and that he hoped âgood and wise menâ would control it, rather than evil forces. That same year, Ernest Rutherford first split the atom. H.G. Wells had coined the term âatomic bombâ just five years earlier, in his 1914 novel The World Set Free.
In 1921, an English baron worried that future wars would be fought by someone in an office pushing a button.There was also skepticism around the technology and its potential that year: A 64-year-old Nikola Tesla said in an interview that âeven if for purposes of destructive warfare we could liberate atomic energy, it does not follow that it would be deadly.â
The View From 1925
A Sunday feature that ran syndicated in newspapers across the country asked: âDare Science Release the Atomâs Power?â It spelled out âfears that this tremendous energy might destroy the world,â alongside an image of an express locomotive, the most powerful machine of the time â evoking imagery of a runaway train. Atomic energy, the piece noted, held enough power in a drop of water to run 500 locomotives for an hour.
Six years later, Compton announced he was studying the release of atomic energy, which he said could bring âradical change in civilization,â in an article in the The Associated Press. This was a time of major scientific optimism that a world-changing breakthrough was near. One wonders what these pundits would have thought about microchips and data centers.
The View From 1939
Scientists had just confirmed nuclear fission â splitting the uranium atom and releasing its energy â on both sides of the Atlantic, and found themselves looking to calm an increasingly anxious public.
Physicists wanted there to be âno public alarm over the possibility of the world being blown to bits by their experiments,â the Science Service syndicate wrote, and blamed Wells for instilling a sense of doomerism. Scientists feared a ârevolutionâ among the public, while insisting that the release of atomic energy could only be achieved âby direct intent, in the laboratory.â
The View From 1945
The atomic bomb changed everything. President Harry Truman said that scientists had created a monster that could wipe out civilization, and called for some sort of protection around the secret. Some physicists lobbied against dropping the bomb and had even previously suggested there be an international plan for controlling nuclear weapons.
Shortly after the explosions at Hiroshima and Nagasaki, media archives show there was a mix of public reassurance, worry, and debate over international nuclear governance. One physicist told a club in Australia that there was âno need to be afraidâ of atomic power, while a historian told a Rotary Club in Missouri that the world might be destroyed âby a small group with nazi ideals or by an accident,â and proposed placing all atomic information under UN control.
The US would ultimately create the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in 1975 â three decades after Hiroshima â as an independent civilian nuclear watchdog. The international picture is patchier: Various treaties govern nukes, and the major players often canât agree on terms. The last treaty limiting US and Russian strategic arsenals, New START, expired in February, leaving the worldâs two largest nuclear powers without binding limits for the first time since 1972.
J.D.âs view
It can be overwhelming to think about whether AI is going to herald the end of the world, so itâs sometimes helpful to gather perspective and realize weâre not the first generation to have these kinds of debates. Not everything weâre living through is unprecedented.
In talking with folks across the tech ecosystem over the past week, I got the sense that the industry isnât banking on US regulation, and that it will take a more drastic incident than the Hugging Face hack for lawmakers to take any sort of action. Thatâs not a comfortable thought.
The most worrying thing from reading the archives from the early 1900s was that serious discussions around governance and regulation for atomic energy didnât happen until it was used to bomb Japan and kill an estimated 200,000 people. And that even today we donât have a firm handle on nuclear weapons, let alone AI.
Room for Disagreement
There are some serious limits to the AI-nukes analogy, nuclear policy expert Ankit Panda wrote in February in his newsletter, Nukesletter. For example, unlike the fissile material at the heart of a bomb, AI compute is far harder to count and control.

Someone in 17th century Poland really did not want one particular girl rising from the dead.
In 2022, archaeologists unearthed an unsettling grave in a cemetery in Pień, north-central Poland. A young woman had been buried with the handle of a sickle driven into the dirt beside her neck so that its serrated blade hooked over her throat. The woman, who the researchers call Zosia, also wore a triangular padlock on the big toe of her left foot.
“The placement of the sickle and the padlock suggests that the purpose of these practices was to protect the living from Zosia after her death, including, without a doubt, preventing her from rising from the grave,” says Dariusz Poliński, an archaeologist at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, Poland.
Poliński and his colleagues did a sweeping set of analyses on Zosia’s grave to piece together details of her life and burial. The team first reviewed other post-medieval European tombs where sickles and padlocks had been found and historical beliefs about such items. Both types of artifacts appear to have been used to shield the living from the dead, the researchers report in the October Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. But Zosia’s grave is the first discovered with both revenant prevention measures.
Zosia’s skeleton suggests she was 17 to 19 years old when she died. Based on the arrangement of her leg bones, the padlock was likely affixed to her toe when she was originally interred — hinting that someone immediately clocked Zosia as a flight risk from the afterlife. But mixed-up soil and the odd angle of Zosia’s left arm also give the impression that her tomb was later dug up, probably to place the sickle over her throat as extra anti-resurrection protection, the researchers write.
A close look at Zosia’s skull also revealed greenish stains that could have come from some copper object — or objects — being shoved in her mouth or nose. “This may have constituted an additional protective measure against the deceased,” Poliński says. In Polish folklore, copper was thought to help ward off vampiric demons, or strzygi.
“I have seen weird. I don’t know if [I’ve seen] weirder,” says Lauren Hosek, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has studied unusual graves but was not involved in this research. “Sickle across the neck is pretty crazy,” she says. That, paired with the padlock as a restraint, “is a pretty good argument for this idea of fear of the dead.”
Graves designed to fend off specters are sometimes known as “anti-vampiric.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean that people in the 17th century thought Zosia was out for blood, Hosek cautions. “Our modern connotations for vampire are very specific, with garlic and bats and capes.” In this historical context, a vampire simply refers to some sort of malevolent undead being.
To explain how Zosia earned this anti-vampiric treatment, Poliński’s team ran chemical analyses on her skeleton and burial accessories. The isotopes of strontium and oxygen in her teeth suggest that she grew up near Pień. But Zosia’s DNA shows that her mother’s family might have come from Scandinavia. And remnants of a silk cap on Zosia’s head contained threads of pure silver and gold. She must have been a wealthy woman of high social status, the researchers suspect, to be laid to rest in such luxury attire.
With such rich context about Zosia’s life, “we can rule out some commonly suggested explanations for this kind of mortuary treatment,” says Sandra Garvie-Lok, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, who has also studied peculiar graves but wasn’t involved in this work. Historical records have shown that someone might be singled out for strange burial because they had been an outsider or lived a difficult life, Garvie-Lok notes. But if Zosia was a noblewoman who grew up near Pień, she may not neatly tick either of those boxes.
Particularly violent or strange circumstances around her death might account for her unconventional burial. But there are no obvious marks of injury or illness on her skeleton. “We’re still looking at the DNA” for clues about how she died, says study coauthor Tomasz Grzybowski, a forensic geneticist at Nicolaus Copernicus University.
The Pień cemetery is riddled with other creepy burials, too. One boy in the graveyard, for instance, was buried face down with a triangular padlock on his right foot. “Sometime later, the grave was reopened and most of his remains were removed,” Poliński says, “leaving only the lower legs and feet in place, together with the padlock.”
Even spookier: There are no written references to the graveyard. It doesn’t appear on any maps. And because it was set away from the village, it may have been on unconsecrated ground far from any church or chapel. All this points to the cemetery being specifically for people who’d been rejected by society and were feared after their deaths.
If so, Garvie-Lok says, “this would make Pień a very unusual site that we could learn a lot from.”

e38dc5548dd4.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-begins-3-days-of-voting-in-a-parliamentary-election-set-to-cement-the-kremlins-power Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia begins 3 days of voting in a parliamentary election set to cement the Kremlin's power World Sep 18, 2026 10:53 AM EDT Russians on Friday began three days of voting in the country's first wartime parliamentary election, which features virtually no opposition and is all but certain to secure the Kremlin's political dominance. Authorities spread the election over the weekend, ending Sunday, in a bid to boost turnout among the 111 million eligible voters, and they even allowed electronic balloting. The Kremlin wants the parliamentary election — the first since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — to underline public support for the war and give a veneer of legitimacy to its action. It has sought to avoid any political risks by stamping out even the slightest sign of dissent. READ MORE: Some Russians flee country, citing Ukraine war draft fears and loss of freedoms "Your choice and resolve will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our fighters, that we are a united people, bound by shared values, historical memory, and love for the Motherland," President Vladimir Putin told the nation before the vote. Russian state news agencies reported that Putin voted online Friday and released a video of him in front of a computer screen. The main Kremlin party, United Russia, is all but assured to retain its overwhelming control of the lower house, the State Duma. Several smaller parties of the "systemic opposition" that vote in sync with the government on all key issues also are expected to retain their presence. Voters cast two separate ballots, filling half of the Duma's 450 seats by selecting political parties listed on the ballot. The rest are contested in single-seat constituencies, with voters choosing individual candidates. Some Russians hope for a different future Russians interviewed by The Associated Press expressed different expectations from the election. Dmitry Kirillin in Moscow said earlier this week that he would like "to see some changes. To see a different party" at the helm. But Muscovite Alexander Vertukhin believed "what United Russia and the communists are doing is quite sufficient; their platforms cover everything." Speaking at a Moscow polling station Friday, pensioner Galina Vavilova said she thought ending the war in Ukraine "is the main thing, of course." WATCH: Russia may force more men to fight in Ukraine as military faces heavy losses "That is the most important thing right now. Everyone wants peace, that's what it comes down to. So that our guys are safe and sound," she said. Another pensioner, Lyudmila Kalinina, wished for life "to stabilize for the better" and for "an end to the big divide between the ultra-rich and the extremely poor, because, after all, many people don't live a very sweet life." Vladimir Chubarev, a 72-year-old professor, expressed hope "for all the important initiatives our government is undertaking to succeed," adding: "And, of course, for victory." Russia has silenced anti-war voices The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia's Supreme Court, and only has a few dozen candidates in the single-constituency races. Additionally, some anti-war politicians have been imprisoned or forced to flee abroad ahead of the campaign. The election follows a summer of Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on oil refineries that triggered a widespread fuel crisis. Warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon also were attacked. The damage has exacerbated problems for the Russian economy and brought the war home for millions. READ MORE: Ukraine takes aim at Russia's economy and morale by attacking online retailer Wildberries In Russia's Black Sea resort of Sochi, polling stations were briefly closed because of a threat of a drone attack, local officials said. One polling station in the Krasnodar region had to be set up in a different venue after a drone shattered windows there, said Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova. READ MORE: Russian court jails Kremlin opposition politician for opposing war in Ukraine For the first time, the parliamentary election includes residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began, but still doesn't fully control. Voting also is taking place in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Voters dropped their ballots in a box at one polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine as an armed Russian soldier stood nearby and watched. In the Russian-held Luhansk region, 14 polling stations were using backup power sources after Ukrainian drones damaged electrical lines, Pamfilova said. Separately, Russian officials said Ukrainian attacks earlier this week killed a polling station chief and wounded another in the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia region. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on the accusation. Authorities in Kyiv denounced the voting in the Russian-held areas as illegal and urged foreign governments and international organizations not to recognize the election, warning Ukrainians that taking part in organizing the balloting could carry criminal liability. European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand also called the voting in Russian-held regions "illegal" and said the European Union condemns it. "These so-called elections represent yet another blatant violation of international law. The European Union does not, and will never recognize either the holding of these, so-called elections, sham elections, in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results," he said. 8ca764ff78e4.text: A sports-betting ad featuring a semi-nude Sydney Sweeney triggered a backlash across women's sports , with female athletes flooding social media with a countermessage: This is what women in sports actually look like. The big picture: Ads have long sexualized women, but the Novig ad's appeal to the male gaze hit differently at a moment when female athletes have cultural cachet and the platforms to push back. Driving the news: Highlight reels of women diving , pitching , tackling , shredding , lifting , skating , sprinting , leaping and covering sports have flooded social media this week — all with the same core message. British sprinter Amy Hunt delivered that refrain on-air this week, smiling and out of breath after the World Athletics Ultimate Championship: "Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears," referring to American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time . Women's sports are in an era of rapid momentum: The NCAA reported record high women's participation earlier this year, while Bank of America predicted U.S. women's sports revenue will grow more than 250% by 2030. There's still a long way to go on screen time, says Purdue University professor Cheryl Cooky, who studies sports and gender. But she says traditional media increasingly covers women's sports more seriously. Still, Cooky says , "it's in some ways not surprising that we get [the] Sydney Sweeney ad at this moment," describing it as "part of a backlash to the kinds of gains that women's sports, and by proxy, women more generally, are making in our society." Some online argued the ad wasn't meant to portray a female athlete and was instead targeting sports bettors, who are more likely to be men. But Cooky says it still struck a nerve because "we thought we were past the point of having to make a case that women in sport contexts are not simply sexual objects for male consumption." Between the lines: Even if traditional media has made progress in covering women's athletics, corporate marketing tends to follow the cultural mood, explains Carly Drake, an expert on gender marketing at North Central College. When feminism is prominent, brands sell empowerment. When the pendulum swings the other way, advertising can reinforce that backlash against women. "It really legitimizes the viewpoint that women and other vulnerable groups don't belong in sports," she says. Other sports - and fitness -related ads have recently faced criticism for their portrayal of women, including apparel brand Good Good for an ad where its co-founder shoved a female golfer to the ground. Marketing in 2026 is a conversation, not a one-way channel, Drake explains, and social media offers a new generation of women in sports a way to build fan bases, shape their brands, and, in cases like these, resist. "They're not being given this power. They're taking it," Cooky says. "They're creating their own narrative on social media, as opposed to 30 or 40 years ago, having to hope that … traditional media outlets and gatekeepers would call attention to these issues." Zoom out: That's also spilled over into a boom of podcasts hosted by or about female athletes or women in the sports world, like hall-of-famer Sue Bird's "Bird's Eye View" and "We Can Do Hard Things" with soccer legend Abby Wambach, Meanwhile, Apple TV hit "Ted Lasso" has returned to fictional team AFC Richmond. But no, not the guys from last season — now, it's the Lady Greyhounds on the pitch. The bottom line: The male gaze isn't new. Women athletes' power — and access to platforms — to answer to it is. Cristiano Ronaldo has been named in the first squad selected by new Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, ending speculation the 41-year-old could retire from international football.
Ronaldo refused to confirm whether he would continue to play for his country after Portugal's World Cup round-of-16 defeat by eventual winners Spain in July.
But the Al-Nassr forward is part of a 25-man group chosen for Portugal's four Nations League games between 24 September and 4 October.
Jesus has replaced Roberto Martinez, who stepped down as Portugal coach after their World Cup exit.
The 72-year-old was Ronaldo's club boss last season, when the pair helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Pro League for the first time in seven years.
The former Manchester United Real Madrid forward, who announced that this summer's World Cup would be his last, was in tears after Portugal's World Cup exit.
When asked if he would keep playing for his country, he said: "I will meet the family and take decisions with a calm head."
This sparked speculation he could follow his great rival Lionel Messi and retire from international football.
Ronaldo will turn 42 before next summer's Nations League finals and will be 43 by Euro 2028.
The oldest player in the history of the Euros is Ronaldo's former Portugal team-mate Pepe, who was 41 and 130 days for his last game at Euro 2024.
Manchester United pair Diogo Dalot and Bruno Fernandes are also in the squad, along with Ruben Dias (Manchester City) and Pedro Neto (Chelsea).
Portugal are at home to Wales on 24 September (19:45 BST) and away to Norway three days later. They then play in Denmark on 1 October and return home to host Norway on 4 October.

9fa407e03c20.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press By — Sarah Rankin, Associated Press Sarah Rankin, Associated Press By — Sarah Raza, Associated Press Sarah Raza, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/early-voting-begins-in-u-s-midterm-elections-that-could-flip-control-of-congress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Early voting begins in U.S. midterm elections that could flip control of Congress Politics Sep 18, 2026 12:16 PM EDT HENRICO, Va. (AP) — In-person voting for this year's midterm elections began Friday, ushering in the final six weeks for Americans to decide which party they trust to lead Congress through a cost-of-living crisis, a prolonged war in Iran and other pressing issues. Election administrators say they are prepared and confident the vote will be accurate and secure. Nevertheless, President Donald Trump has continued with efforts to denigrate certain voting methods and reshape how elections are run, through court challenges, an expansive federal hunt for noncitizen voters and a pressure campaign to force election officials to share sensitive voter data. Please check your inbox to confirm. Friday marked the start of early voting in Virginia. Voters in a handful of other states, including Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota, can cast absentee ballots in person, typically at a local election office or voting center. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in those and other states in the coming weeks. At a voting location in Fairfax, Virginia, 18-year-old college student Sanya Singhal was among the first to vote early in person Friday morning, arriving well before the site opened to get in line. "Why not just have a little fun in life, you know, try to be the first early voter?" she said. "I really want to participate in my democracy." At a voting location in suburban Richmond, a poll worker rang a bell as the building opened and about a dozen voters in line began to file in. Stephen Gura was excited to be the first. "This election is critical. We need to stop the Trump agenda," said Gura, who added that he voted for U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat, and Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee against Republican incumbent Rob Wittman in the 1st Congressional District. WATCH: Trump remains focus of GOP's midterm campaign as convention wraps The Nov. 3 election includes votes for governor and state legislature in most states and will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House and Senate. If Democrats retake Congress, it will alter the trajectory of the final two years of Trump's term, most likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts. Voting underway after unusual redistricting and Trump's bid to control how elections are run At the suburban Richmond voting center, a steady stream of voters flowed in and out. William Curry, a 74-year-old retiree who described himself as a libertarian-leaning independent conservative, voted for Warner's Republican challenger, Bert Mizusawa, and Wittman. Curry said he generally approves of the job Trump has done, apart from the war with Iran. "He's in a mess he can't get rid of," Curry said of the conflict. On a rainy day in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Bill Goehring, 67, said he voted early at the county office because he will be traveling later. He voted for a mix of Democrats and independents, and said Trump's "dictatorial tendencies are bad for America." The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many Americans about issues including rising gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence and Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement campaign. WATCH: News Wrap: August inflation report shows consumer prices up 3.4% It also follows an unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the U.S. House that began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas to redraw its congressional map to help the party. California and other states followed. WATCH: Group urges Congress to adopt proportional representation to end redistricting battles The changes affect millions of people: Research shows 1 in 10 Americans this fall is a resident of a different congressional district than in 2024. Those partisan efforts are expected to continue before the 2028 elections after a landmark ruling this year from the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the federal Voting Rights Act's protections against racially discriminatory redistricting. As the start of early voting approached, Trump was focused on efforts to assert federal control over election administration, even as the Constitution bestows the power to run elections on the states and, in some cases, Congress. The nation's highest court rejected Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots this week, but several of his administration's other efforts to influence the voting process and mine state voter lists for illegitimate voters continue. WATCH: How Trump's attempt to restrict mail ballots is being challenged in court Virginia's attorney general said Thursday that Trump's administration may have violated the state's laws after a whistleblower accused federal employees of misrepresenting themselves on voter lookup tools to hunt for noncitizen voters. In a letter, Attorney General Jay Jones demanded that the Department of Homeland Security confirm in writing whether it had directed anyone to access Virginia voters' information without first obtaining permission from those voters. Trump for years has raised the specter of widespread noncitizen voting in U.S. elections, and this year is no exception. But research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. Uber has been ordered to pay $40m (Â£29m) to the family of a 23-year-old woman who was fatally struck on a California highway after the rideshare company's driver allegedly pulled over and ordered her out of the car.
Emily Normandin-Parker had booked an Uber for home with a friend on 12 August 2023, before her friend became sick and vomited in the car, court documents show.
Her parents said the driver pulled over to the side of the highway and forced the women, who were intoxicated, out of the car, after which Normandin-Parker was hit and killed by another vehicle.
Uber had argued that the driver was an independent contractor, and the company was not responsible for his actions.
"Emily did everything Uber tells riders to do - she made the responsible choice not to drive and we trusted Uber to get her home safely," her parents said in a statement about their daughter, a graduate of the University of California, Los Angeles. "That trust cost our daughter her life."
Judge Richard Stone ordered the rideshare company to pay the money to Normandin-Parker's parents after a five-day arbitration process, according to the law firm Panish, Shea, Ravipudi, which represented the family.
Arbitration is an alternative way to resolve disputes outside of court with a qualified arbitrator, in this case a retired judge.
Lawyers representing the family said that after leaving the women on the highway, the driver, Vu Tran, did not call for help for them. He instead pulled off to call Uber and demand they charge Normandin-Parker a cleaning fee, the lawyers said.
Tran showed "far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers", Judge Stone said, adding that he could have taken the exit and dropped the women off at a safe location.
Uber said it believed the arbitrator was wrong in holding the company legally responsible for the event.
"We have continued to strengthen our approach to safety over the years, through new technology, policies and safeguards informed by safety experts, including additional guidance to drivers about avoiding drop-offs in unsafe locations," the company said in a statement.
The law firm representing the family said Uber had initially proposed a settlement that would give the parents $10m and require them not to speak about the incident, which they declined.

There are no Canadian teams in the NFL - but there are millions of fans.
At the Buffalo Bills game in New York on Thursday night, plenty of Canadians wore the team's trademark red, white and blue while drinking beside their pick-up trucks, which were parked to tailgate - a very American pre-game tradition.
The Bills' stadium is only 112 miles (180 km) from Toronto - about a two and a half hour drive for fans - and right across Lake Ontario, which President Donald Trump has sought to rename Lake America.
So it was no surprise that many Canadians arrived long before kick-off to soak up the atmosphere and enjoy the sights of the new Highmark Stadium for their team 's home opener against the Detroit Lions.
What was unusual was that their national anthem rang out through the stadium.
The field was decked out with both the stars and stripes of the US flag and the maple leaf of the Canadian one, and the 1990s Canadian band The Barenaked Ladies belted out Oh Canada! in front of a massive crowd.
It was an emotional moment for many of the Canadian fans, who said they felt an extremely warm welcome even if their country's mood has recently grown more frosty towards the US.
"I've always felt welcome here," said Ben Kerr, from Bradford, Ontario.
"I think it's a nice acknowledgement," he added. "I appreciate that the Bills are doing that for Canada."
The relationship between the two countries, which began to sour when US President Donald Trump returned to office and made repeated calls to annex Canada, has frayed further with an escalating tit-for-tat tariff showdown.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada, which shares the world's longest undefended border with the US, is "at war" with its southern neighbour over trade. Trump has called Canada "nasty" and "entitled".
Both sides are feeling the economic impact, with Canadian industries reeling from tariffs and Canadians boycotting travel and spending in the US.
The ongoing tensions made the decision to travel to Buffalo a little more complicated for Kerr.
"I try to spend as little money as possible in the US," he told the BBC. "Buy our food in Canada, buy our beer in Canada, bring it across and drink it here. We're not big in supporting the American economy in this trade war."
Many Americans at the game expressed their own frustrations with the escalating trade war, and the way it has divided the two neighbours.
For Drew Grier, an American who lives eight minutes from the stadium, "the anthem playing tonight is a core part of who we are as a border city".
At a Buffalo Sabres playoff ice hockey game in April, a microphone died while the Canadian anthem was being sung and the audience's voices filled in.
"You sang the Canadian anthem because it needed to happen," Grier said.
Canadian Blake Parnham recalled that moment: "I was sobbing watching the game at home because I felt so vindicated, that Buffalo is different."
He couldn't make it to Buffalo for the Bills home opener, but he enjoyed it from his elaborately decorated backyard in Keswick, Ontario.
Grier said that singing the Canadian anthem tonight is "not that polarising of a thing".
"If anyone is polarising it, it's coming from those outside here, because those of us here, we love Canada," he said.
But some thought it was a step too far.
"The only acceptable reason to sing that anthem would be if they were playing a Canadian team, but they don't play any Canadian teams," posted one fan on social media.
"I don't think it's really necessary," said David Waring, who attended Thursday's game.
In the end, it may all come down to simple economics.
The Bills' new home, Highmark Stadium, cost $2.2bn to build. While the population of western New York is a little over 1.5 million, the nearby Toronto and Hamilton greater metro areas is home to more than 8 million. Simply put, the team needs Canadian fans.
Gavin Kemp, who has run the NFL-Canada office for eight years, told the BBC that Canada's relationship to the NFL was "extremely important".
Asked why the Bills chose this year to play the Canadian anthem, Kemp said the team was "leaning into one of their biggest parts of their market".
Canada boasts nearly 15 million NFL fans â about one-third of the country's population, and roughly 10-15% of Bills season ticket holders are Canadian, according to the team.
"Sports really transcends all of this," Kemp said. "All this politics is kind of secondary to the fact that your team is doing fantastic right now."
Even American fans who traditionally cheer for other teams found themselves siding with the Bills.
Carol Breed, who backs the Detroit Lions, considered travelling to Highmark Stadium from her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, after she heard they would play the Canadian national anthem.
"I love our country's relationship with Canada," the 74-year-old told the BBC, adding that in Michigan the country is viewed more as a "relative".
"I just hate what Trump has done to the partnership."
She wasn't able to watch the game in person, but has found other ways to scratch her O'Canada itch.
A couple of weeks ago, Breed embarked on the two-hour drive across the border, on the recently opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, which has also stoked divisions between the two nations of late.
"We sang the US anthem until we reached halfway and then started singing the Canadian anthem," she said.

Watch: Sixth batch of UFO files includes orbs from 1952
The release includes incidents dating back to 1952, including footage filmed near Tremonton, Utah, by US Navy Chief Warrant Officer Delbert C. Newhouse, who reported seeing and filming a group of bright airborne objects.
Submitted to the US Air Force shortly afterwards, the footage later became one of the visual cases reviewed by Project Blue Book, the Air Force's UFO investigation programme, which ran from 1952 to 1969.
However, the film's limited detail and lack of fixed reference points meant investigators could not reach a definitive conclusion.
After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files in a series of six drops.
The first tranche of 161 files was uploaded to the US defence department's website on 8 May, with promises of more to come.
